records.title: Images are running as root but constrained by `runAsNonRoot` in vanilla kube
records.body:
On vanilla kube the decode pod won't spin up since vanilla doesn't have any SCC that will  automatically pick a high‐numbered non-root UID from the namespace’s allowed range and inject that as the container’s user at startup, even if your image’s USER is still “root.” Because Kubernetes sees a numeric UID ≥ 100000, your runAsNonRoot: true check passes.

Current work around is removing `runAsNonRoot` but longer term we could either an account on the image to run as or set the `runAsUser` to something like `1000`, a user that exists on the image.

records.title: Define our docs strategy for llm-d
records.body:
As a project that draws from multiple upstreams to create well-lit paths, we need to work through a few open questions:

* What documents should live in our upstreams (IGW, vLLM) vs in llm-d?
  * What concepts should be explained in the upstreams?  (I.e. https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/pull/25)
  * How do we ensure mixed concepts are explained (prefix aware cache routing + a cache hierarchy)?
* Where does llm-d place its documents?
  * `docs/?`
  * The website github.com/llm-d/llm-d.github.io?
  * A new docs site?

Timeframe to settle this is by end of June.
records.author: smarterclayton

records.title: Clearly measure and articulate the key tradeoff points in disaggregated serving
records.body:
Disaggregated serving requires more hardware to serve. When supporting dynamic and heterogenous workloads (multiple types of LLM use case sharing the same hardware) the benefit may be situational or it may be a significant disadvantage.  llm-d should be able to make recommendations for deployers about when disaggregation is beneficial for distinct workload types (chat, summarization) with real world data.  That will in turn enable us to better automate the use of disaggregation - our northstar for both disaggregation and autoscaling is to move from static deployment topology to dynamic decisions on when to separate prefill from decode.

We need to measure the cost/benefit for multiple workloads, input/output distributions, and hardware.  As other optimizations show up, these break points may change.

A base llm-d deployment should be flexible to a wide range of these point and allow the workload author - not the deployer - to make informed choices based on their latency/efficiency priorities.

Extracted from the [disaggregated serving northstar](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1FNN5snmipaTxEA1FGEeSH7Z_kEqskouKD1XYhVyTHr8/edit?tab=t.0).

records.title: [Feature Request] AutoScaling
records.body:
Proposed feature description: Traffic and hardware-aware autoscaler that calculate the optimal mix of accelerators for each model server. 
For the calculation the autoscaler takes into account 
1. Traffic mix
2. Accelerator specification (such as memory, bandwidth, arithmetic intensity)
3. Model characteristics (size, density, ...)
4. prefill vs. decode needs 
5. different types of requests (ie. latency tolerant)

The approach should not rely on offline profiling/benchmarking data, i.e., there needs to be a capability to observe and adjust 
decision parameters based on model behavior while serving requests post deployment. 

Ideally, an approach to autoscaling will be modular and extensible, allowing to experiment with different autoscaling algorithms. 

An autoscaling approach should separate logic to autoscale individual models, vs logic to make global decisions ie based on priorities *across* models in case of resource contention. 

For an individual model, an autoscaler recommends optimal accelerator mix, minimizing cost, while preserving request SLOs. 

Separately, a global optimizer can decide on a global state, ie, assignment of resources to model server instances, based on global priorities. 

Approach: 

Optimization Control Loop: 

Optimization control loop: The control loop comprises (1) a Collector to get data about the inference servers through Prometheus and server deployments, (2) an Optimizer to make decisions, (3) an Actuator to realize such decisions by updating server deployments or by writing directly to Prometheus relying on HPA to affect changes, and (4) a periodic Controller that has access to static and dynamic data. 

Auto-scaling logic: We have implemented a queueing theory based logic, and a model-tuner that tunes the parameters of the auto-scaler based on model behavior and traffic patterns dynamically. 

Global optimization: we formulate the global optimization as a MILP problem. Our approach is modular and extensible and allows for different global optimizers to be used. 

Why it is needed: 
Models exhibit different characteristics and behavior under varying traffic patterns. Logic to optimize model serving autoscaling must understand the intrinsic characteristics of AI, such as distinction between prefill and decode phase, and how characteristics of models such as density, size, and architecture will affect the optimal shape and configuration. An AI specific autoscaler must also understand the relationship between batch size, accelerator capacity, ITL, TTFT, and different configuration options. It must also understand traffic shapes and patterns. 

Value: A major inhibitor for AI adoption is cost, and many AI users are struggling to run multiple AI models making maximal use of a set of accelerators. In addition, traffic patterns change dynamically, thus resources assigned to a model, and their configuration must adjust dynamically to ensure that resources are optimally utilized at all times. Additionally, requests may have different priorities or SLOs. Some request may be latency tolerant while others are not. The goal of the autoscaler is to dynamically adjust resources and configurations for each model, to minimize overall cost, and maximize use, and SLO adherence. 

User stories: 
As a user of llm-d I want to serve multiple models and have llm-d dynamically adjust resource allocation and configuration across models based on the changing traffic patterns to reduce my overall cost while meeting all SLOs.

records.title: [Bug]: EPP Container Fails with glibc Symbol Error on NixOS (unstable)
records.body:
### What happened?

## **Bug Summary**
The EPP (External Processing Pod) container fails to start with a glibc symbol lookup error when deployed on NixOS-based Kubernetes nodes, preventing advanced request routing optimizations.

Interestingly I get the same error when deploying NVIDIA device plugin v17. 

Version 16 of the daemonset works without complaining!

## **Environment**
- **OS**: NixOS 25.11 (Xantusia) 
- **Kernel**: 6.15.2
- **Container Runtime**: containerd 2.0.4-k3s2
- **Kubernetes**: v1.31.7+rke2r1
- **llm-d Version**: Chart 1.0.19
- **EPP Image**:  `ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-inference-scheduler:0.0.4`

**GPUs:**
- NVIDIA RTX 4000 SFF Ada Generation
- NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090
- **Driver**: NVIDIA 575.57.08
- **CUDA**: 12.9

## **Error Details**
```
/app/epp: symbol lookup error: /nix/store/cg9s562sa33k78m63njfn1rw47dp9z0i-glibc-2.40-66/lib/libc.so.6: undefined symbol: __tunable_is_initialized, version GLIBC_PRIVATE
```

**Exit Code**: 127  
**Pod Status**: CrashLoopBackOff

## **Reproduction Steps**
1. Deploy llm-d on NixOS-based rke2 cluster
2. Use any configuration with EPP enabled (default behavior)
3. Observe EPP pod fails immediately with glibc symbol error

## **Impact**
- ❌ EPP advanced routing features unavailable
- ❌ KV-cache aware scheduling disabled
- ✅ Core inference functionality works (direct API calls succeed)
- ✅ Basic request routing through gateway functional

## **Root Cause**
EPP binary compiled with glibc version incompatible with NixOS glibc 2.40-66. The \`__tunable_is_initialized\` symbol is a glibc private symbol that varies between distributions.

## **Suggested Fix**
- Use statically linked binary or Alpine-based container image
- Test EPP container compatibility across different Linux distributions
- Consider multi-arch builds with glibc compatibility matrix

## **Workaround**
Deploy with EPP disabled if advanced routing features aren't required - core inference remains functional.

records.title: Add background resources for new community members
records.body:
As a new community member who is not coming from an llm or kubernetes background, I often found it difficult to understand the various component descriptions and architecture documents I read. I think it would be useful to add some resources for baseline knowledge to help new members quickly acquire the context needed to engage with this project. This information could be presented in many ways, but I have a few specific ideas for what this might look like:

1. A glossary for commonly used terms or pieces of jargon. Terms can include
  a) domain-specific word meanings (e.g. "What is a pod?")
  b) acronym expansion (e.g. "What is HBM cache?")
  c) external tool descriptions (e.g., "What is Redis?")
  d) project-specific jargon (e.g. "What is E/W caching?")

2. A set of external references for tools used by llm-d, such as
  a) documentation for external tools, like Kubernetes
  b) specifications for common tools, like golang

3. A list of SIGs and the general topics they cover, and perhaps a way to link in SIG-specific information. (For instance, I think "E/W caching" is term used just by sig-kv-disaggregation?)

records.title: unify llm-d-scheduler and llm-d-sidecar repos
records.body:
This issue suggests unifying llm-d-scheduler and llm-d-sidecar to a single scheduler repo with sidecar sub-directory.

PD is the main claim of llm-d scheduler, and we can't do PD without the sidecar.
additionally, the whole point of the sidecar is to support PD.
as of today we need to:
- maintain the relevant consts twice in both places.
- make sure the releases are matching.
- for some issues that involve scheduler and sidecar we need to create issues in both repos and do cross reference while syncning on the PRs merge.

bottom line - we can't do PD without the sidecar, and the sidecar has no justification to exist without the scheduler doing PD.

this issue proposes to put both in a single repo, while defining sidecar owners using owners.md file in the relevant sub-directory.

cc: @vitabortnikov @nilig @elevran @lionelvillard

records.title: [Roadmap] `llm-d` 0.3 Release Plan
records.body:
Following our 0.2 release, we are excited to continue progress against our well-lit paths

---

- Expand hardware platform support
    - Accelerators - AMD and TPU

- Respect our upstreams
    - Remove llm-d image (upstream all changes to vLLM)

records.title: Proposal: Formalize Image Build Requirements for Multi-Vendor Hardware Support
records.body:
As `llm-d` adoption grows, we’re seeing increasing interest from contributors and downstream users who want to build and run `vLLM` images on different hardware platforms (e.g., NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, custom accelerators).  

Right now, our image build process is implicitly NVIDIA-focused, and it isn’t clear what minimal requirements a `vLLM` container image must meet to be considered **`llm-d` compatible**. To enable broader hardware vendor support, I propose we **document and formalize** the build requirements and provide a starting point for contributors.

---

### Goals
1. **Define compatibility requirements** for a `vLLM` image to work within `llm-d`.
2. **Document required environment variables** and runtime expectations.
3. **Specify PATH and runtime dependencies** so that images from different vendors behave consistently.
4. **Provide a basic template Dockerfile** as a reference for contributors.

---

### Requirements to Document

#### Environment Variables
- `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, `NVSHMEM_DIR`, etc.
- Any vendor-specific accelerator variables (CUDA, ROCm, SYCL, etc.), but must not break baseline compatibility.

#### Runtime Expectations
- `vllm` must be installed and runnable as an entrypoint or CLI command (`vllm` should be in `$PATH`).
- Python version compatibility (e.g., 3.9–3.12).
- Required system libraries must be bundled (e.g., `libcuda.so` for NVIDIA builds, ROCm equivalents for AMD).
- Entry point should be flexible enough to allow `llm-d` to override commands/args.

#### PATH Requirements
...

---

### Deliverables
- **Documentation page** in the repo (e.g., `docs/images.md`) describing the requirements above.
- **Template Dockerfile** to illustrate a minimal `llm-d`-compatible image:
  ```dockerfile
  FROM <base-runtime>

  # Install Python + vLLM
  RUN pip install vllm

  # Define environment defaults
  ENV MODEL_PATH=/models \
      VLLM_ARGS=""

  # Ensure vllm is available in PATH
  CMD ["vllm", "serve", "$MODEL_PATH", "$VLLM_ARGS"]

records.title: [Feature Request] Disaggregation scheme for Vision Language Models
records.body:
### Proposed feature description

Vision language models have additional components over text-only LLMs. A disaggregation scheme is required for vision encoders and projection layers of such models.

### Approach

Use additional modes for vLLM instances for vision-encode and projection tasks along with existing prefill and decode modes.

### Why is it needed

This feature enables distributed inference of multimodal models that are supported in vLLM, such as LLaVA, Phi-3-Vision.

### User stories

As an analytics app developer using llm-d for distributed model inference, I want to provide offline video frames or multi-camera live streams as context for prompts based on an end user query and generate fast response.

records.title: Adopt Mergify to Unblock PR Flow and Reduce Stagnation
records.body:
## Issue Summary

Over the past few weeks, we’ve seen PRs linger without review, and a few contributors have stepped away after long wait times with no path to merge. This creates frustration, slows delivery, and risks losing community momentum. We need a lightweight, automatable way to keep PRs moving once quality checks are met.

Proposal: Adopt Mergify to automate common merge workflows (e.g., auto-merge when required checks pass and approvals are present), reduce review bottlenecks, and give contributors predictable outcomes.

## Goals

- Shorten time-to-merge for low-risk PRs that meet policy.
- Reduce maintainer toil (labeling, rebasing, merging).
- Provide contributors a clear, published path from PR → merge.

## Scope (Initial)

- Auto-merge PRs that meet criteria (green CI, code owners approval, label present).
- Queueing/Batching to avoid merge race conditions and keep main green.
- Auto-update (rebase) eligible PRs when main moves.
- Enable selective rules per label or path (docs-only, chore, dependency bumps).

records.title: Inference image Readiness Probe
records.body: There are 3 different concepts of "readiness" in the llm-d system of the inference image. The first is when the container is registered as running. The second is when the basic vLLM API server comes up (health, etc.). The final is when the rest of the API routes specific to the vLLM model being served are ready, `/v1/completions`, etc. We should add a readiness probe script to our build process for some k8s sanitization. This way our E2E scripts could just consume if pod is Ready / Not Ready instead of having random timeouts and hope the model is served in that amount of time.

records.title: [Demo] Multiple model deployment
records.body:
I don't think this use-case meets our criteria for `guide` however we have gotten many question asking about if multiple models can be deployed with `llm-d`. The answer is that they can it just requires composable installations of the stack. You would need:

Per model specific inference stack:

- 1 x GAIE chart deploying `inference-scheduler` (or `epp`) with the necessary RBAC
    - 1 x `DestinationRule` (only if using Istio)
    - 1 x inferencepool
    - 1 x httpRoute (out of band, not deployed through GAIE but references the inferencepool + gateway)
- 1 x Modelservice chart installation deploying vllm with appropriate labels and selectors to get picked up by EPP

Common infra across all inference stacks:
- 1 x Gateway and relevant configurations

I think having a demo, fork, or spinout repo showing this would help drive adoption.

A minimal reproduction is attempting to load the vllm deepgemm benchmark, which also fails to load a kernel image that it has built inside the container.

* The base image is `nvidia-cuda:12.9.1-devel-ubi9`
  * A very similar container image derived from [nvidia-cuda:12.9.1-devel-ubuntu22.04](https://github.com/smarterclayton/vllm-dp-lws/blob/main/Dockerfile) does not exhibit the issue
* Appears to be related to how vLLM invokes DeepGEMM and configures the torch environment
  * Running deepgemm `tests/test_fp8.py` directly compiles kernels (cloning deepgemm, execute the test script against the venv)
* Is not related to gIB
* Occurs on a 580 and 570 drivers on GKE (1.33 and 1.32)

A reproduction environment is in https://github.com/smarterclayton/ig-load/blob/reproduce/config/deploy_vllm_repro.yaml.  The pod will start and trigger the reproduction into the logs, then sleep. To debug - start the statefulset, exec into the pod:

```
$ kubectl exec -it vllm-repro-0 -- /bin/bash
# reproducer
```

which executes

```
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 uv run /opt/vllm-source/benchmarks/kernels/deepgemm/benchmark_fp8_block_dense_gemm.py
```

in the venv and triggers the failure.  

This blocks the wide ep example from deploying on B200s.

Themes:

1. Production Readiness (GA) of the first three paths: 
    - Wide-EP
        - [ ] DP native balancing
        - [x] CPU prefix cache integrated with DP and operationally monitored

            - [ ] Graceful detection and failure for when a wide-EP pod is killed due to node death / gpu failure

        - Increasing Hardware Support

            - [x] XPU
        - Tighter Integration with Benchmarking and CI
            - [ ] Increase path testing coverage in CI (test features from PRs across all guides)

            - [x] vllm upstream p/d regression tests (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/27199)

    - [x] Well-lit path for full disagg remote w/ lustre

    - [ ] GDS with prefix caching

### Contact Details

_No response_

### What happened?

In `ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-dev:v0.2.2` when you go to specify the recommended tool call parameters for a llama and/or mistral model documented here:

https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/features/tool_calling.html

    - --tool-call-parser
    - llama3_json
    - --chat-template
    - examples/tool_chat_template_llama3.1_json.jinja

```

records.title: [Feat] API Key aware Scheduling/Load-Balancing/Rate-Limiting
records.body:
I looked into different approaches for LLM serving infrastructure, and it seems that llm-d is a good choice and implements a lot of the features I want.
However it looks like llm-d is designed to be API Key agnostic, and doesn't currently implement any logic that relates to API Key based decisions.

In the scenario where you have a single LLM deployed and different API Keys accessing it, you may want to apply different scheduling/load-balancing/rate-limiting logic, according to the API Key.
I believe this should be implemented as part of llm-d, since being API key–aware allows for smarter and more balanced scheduling decisions—something that wouldn’t be possible if implemented in a separate layer.

Although I suppose it's possible to implement this logic as new plugins, I think it might be quite cumbersome without well-designed interfaces and clear abstractions in the codebase.
So I'd love to either request this as a feature or hear from you how you would go on about implementing this without changing the core of the codebase.

records.title: [Doc] Modular recipes for user guides
records.body: ## Motivation We see lots of duplication in user guides. For example, pretty much the same gateway resources are copied in each guide. Moreover, the current "monolith" style makes it hard to combine multiple guides. For example, one can combine inference scheduling with CPU offloading. With more user guides coming such as the kv cache offloading guides, there is a strong desire to modularize these recipes so that: - Reduce duplication and its maintenance overhead - Promote composability of guides for more advanced setups ## Proposal 1. Add a new `./guides/recipes` folder, which contains **reusable** recipes for 3 types of resources: * `gateway`: Contains core gateway and httproute resources, plus any gateway provider specific resources. * `inferencepool`: Contains `values.yaml` files for the `inferencepool` chart. The main part that we kustomize a lot is the plugins config. For that reason we have various plugin config recipes, plus a common base `values.yaml`. * `vllm`: Contains vllm workload recipes including standard (non-disagg) and disaggregated flavors. It will look something like this: 2. Each guide will refer to the reusable recipes, with minimal kustomization in each guide when needed. 3. There is no one size fits all so we use `helm` for light templating and `kustomize` for heavy overlays. We use `helm` as a templating tool so we just use local charts. We are open for suggestions as well. 5. [markdown style] When users need to make a decision, such as picking a gateway provider, we use tabs so they only need to choose what they are interested in, without needing to read irrelevant information.## Principles These are **soft** principles that help guiding the implementation. * Open for changes. These are guides, not APIs, which means we don't have to argue for a specific format and get stuck. * Don't over DRY. Certain level of repeating is OK if it helps readability or ease of implementation. We modularize to help developers and users, not to make things harder. * Limit `kustomize` levels to <=3. ## Implementation Phase 1: Use the CPU offloading https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/pull/318/ as the pilot to try this pattern Phase 2: Convert wide-ep to this style Wide-ep is already written with kustomize so it's very staightforward to move reusable recipes to the `recipes` folder. In this phase the resource names can be hard coded and we rely on different namespaces for parallel installations. Phase 3: Convert other guides to this style one by one

### What happened?

After https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/pull/407 we successfully start NVSHMEM with DeepEP on GCP on the RHEL UBI image.  However, the Ubuntu image does not start with:

```
/tmp/nvshmem_src/src/modules/transport/ibgda/ibgda.cpp 3905 no active IB device that supports GPU-initiated communication is found, exiting...

/tmp/nvshmem_src/src/host/transport/transport.cpp:nvshmemi_transport_init:282: init failed for transport: IBGDA
```

From previous testing, that occurs in Ubuntu when not using the OFED libibverbs packages.

For 0.4, we need to identify whether we switch to OFED in the Ubuntu packages (likely) as NVSHEM officially requires OFED for IBGDA.

records.title: [MS] ModelService Requests and Limits is Confusing
records.body:
In `ms`, we are able to set resources and limits for various resources such as gpus. I noticed that this is not respected (overrriden by the parallelism scheme)

For example, if I set:

```yaml
decode:
  create: true
  replicas: 1
  monitoring:
    podmonitor:
      enabled: true
      portName: "metrics"  # decode vLLM service port (from routing.proxy.targetPort)
      path: "/metrics"
      interval: "30s"
  containers:
  - name: "vllm"
    image: ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-cuda-dev@sha256:ee286539334e853f8c1559e9ad0b7d5ca3a401f19a88d23aee15b897108d6654
    modelCommand: vllmServe
    args:
      - "--async-scheduling"
    ports:
      - containerPort: 8200
        name: metrics
        protocol: TCP
    resources:
      limits:
        memory: 64Gi
        cpu: "16"
        nvidia.com/gpu: 8
      requests:
        memory: 64Gi
        cpu: "16"
        nvidia.com/gpu: 8
```

the pod will be created with only 1 gpu

```bash
    Limits:
      cpu:             16
      memory:          64Gi
      nvidia.com/gpu:  1
    Requests:
      cpu:             16
      memory:          64Gi
      nvidia.com/gpu:  1
```

It turns out that we have to set the `parallelism` to get 8 gpus:

```bash
decode:
  parallelism:
    tensor: 8
    data: 1
  create: true
  replicas: 1
```

This is extremely confusing

records.title: Avoid Prefill/Decode version/configuration mismatch
records.body:
### Summary

The Endpoint Picker (EPP) will pair Prefill and Decode instances with mismatched vLLM versions or configurations during rolling updates, potentially causing crashes or other undefined behavior due to KV cache format incompatibilities, KV transfer metadata mismatches, and other version-specific issues. Further investigation is needed to understand all problematic scenarios.

### Background

In the P/D well-lit path, an `InferencePool` object defines which pods are eligible for selection via label selectors. The EPP then independently selects a pair of Decode and Prefill workers from the pool based on:
- Pod labels (`llm-d.ai/role: prefill` or `decode`)
- Load metrics
- Prefix cache hit probability

However, Prefill and Decode instances are deployed as separate Kubernetes Deployments , each with their own image and configuration specifications.

### Problem

The EPP selection logic does not verify that paired Prefill/Decode instances have matching:
- vLLM version/image digest
- Attention backend configuration (FlashAttention, etc.)
- KV cache configuration
- Other runtime parameters

This creates two high-risk scenarios:

**1. Version Upgrades**: When performing a rolling update of the vLLM image on Decode pods while Prefill pods remain on an older version (or vice versa), the EPP will pair instances with mismatched versions.

**2. Configuration Changes**: Similarly, changing configuration parameters (e.g., `--attention-backend`) on one role but not the other can create incompatible pairings.

### Suggested Approach

The EPP should only consider P/D pairs with matching version and configuration. Possible implementations:

1. **Version Label Matching**: Add a version/configuration hash label (e.g., `llm-d.ai/config-version`) to both Prefill and Decode pods. The EPP filters to only consider pairs with matching values.
2. **InferencePool per Configuration**: For each rollout, create a new InferencePool with unique label selectors (e.g., `llm-d.ai/config-hash: abc123`) that match both the new Prefill and Decode deployments. 
3. **Pod Annotation Verification**: The routing sidecar or EPP could verify compatibility by comparing pod annotations containing version/config metadata before forwarding requests.

Whichever approach is taken, the rollout of Prefill and Decode needs to be coordinated such that the new:old ratio of both matches - e.g. given 4 Prefill workers and 1 Decode workers, there would be no point in upgrading D from new to old before starting to upgrade P, and vice-versa.

At a vLLM level, all we will be able to do is identify such mismatches and reject such requests. Potentially this could form part of the solution - e.g. if the EPP was aware of the failure and rejected that P/D pair when scheduling a retry?

(_Raised by @tlrmchlsmth - I'm trying to capture the issue at a high-level._)

records.title: Multiple Model deployments under LLM-D
records.body:
@Gregory-Pereira @nilig @vMaroon 
You've previously asked me to document the process I follow to deploy multiple models under the stack and any issues I encounter along the way.  I just recently deployed multiple models under LLM-D (0.4.0).  Let me know if folks have alternative ideas. Note:  Some issues might already be documented or fixed.

I installed the LLM-D stack on a newly built IPI-installed OpenShift cluster (4.18.27) dedicated to LLM-D/WVA.  Our current Inferencing platform operates on separate cluster running the RHOAI 2.x stack.

My desired configuration:

- A single gateway deployment ('infra') with 'n' replica's
- Per Model:
  -  An EPP deployment ('gaie') with 1 replica (I understand work is ongoing to better support HA mode where each EPP replica would have a complete picture of KV-caches across all pods)
  - A model-service deployment ('ms') with 'n' replica's


I follow the guide of the` precise-prefix-cache-aware` lit-path and utilize the helm charts and scripts provide to install the stack and models.



### **Gateway and Monitoring details**
I'm using Istio as the gateway, and I follow the documentation to lay down the CRD's and istiod. I install the Grafana operator and import the dashboards provided in the repo.


### **Deploying models**
I'm currently deploying all models into the same namespace.  On our current platform, we do have situations where this is not the case, so supporting models across namespaces is something I'll need to look into.  

On our platform we also store model checkpoints on the NVMe drives of our GPU nodes.  This dramatically speeds up load time (which is important for Scale From Zero and Scale up operations). For now I'm not dealing with that added complexity and I'm configuring the LLM-D model deployments to read checkpoints from a COS bucket we maintain.  COS bandwidth/transfer speed is typically better than downloading from HF.  I create the COS PVC and Secret in advance of deploying models.




### **For each Model and EPP deployment:**

I create a unique values file for each EPP and Model service.

- Model service values file updates (under the 'ms-kv-events' folder):
  - Under modelAftifacts:
    - uri : is updated to source the model from cos (ie., "pvc://{mvc-name}/models/qwen/Qwen3-32B")
    - name: is updated to match the model-id of the model
    - Labels: I add the label with the value of the model's deployment name: (ie., llm-d.ai/model: "ms-qwen3-32b-040-llm-d-modelservice").
      - In prior llm-d releases this was automatically done, but appears it was removed.  This label is critical, and is used to bind the deployment to its endpoint picker configuration.
  - Under decode:
    - Set parallelism->tensor if the model requires more than 1 gpu
    - Containers->image - per Maroon, this value is incorrect, and needed to be updated to 'ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-cuda:v0.4.0'
    - args:
      - The argument string contains two places that requires the model's model-id
      - This may be a bug, and for models requiring more than one GPU, you must manually add the "--tensor-parallel-size {number of GPUs} \" argument manually
  - env:
    - This may be a bug, Update CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES to match your GPU requirement

Similarly, for multi GPU models, add the additional mounts:
```
  volumeMounts:
    - name: shm
      mountPath: /dev/shm

  volumes:
  - name: shm
    emptyDir:
      medium: Memory
      sizeLimit: 8Gi
```


EPP values file updates (under the 'gaie-kv-events' folder):
- I ran into an issue with the 'flags:' section.  Greg provided a fix, flags are now in the form of {name}:{value}
- I only update pluginsConfigFile and pluginsCustomConfig values when running benchmarking tests (precise vs random)
- To support multiple models I need to update the value of modelServers->matchLabels to match the label I put into the model service (decode) deployment.  This is critical for correct routing, right now, the defaulted values are too generic for multiple model scenarios.
   - For instance for the qwen3-32b model, the the label I use is: llm-d.ai/model: "ms-qwen3-32b-040-llm-d-modelservice"
 

I export a unique value for the RELEASE_NAME_POSTFIX env-var per model.  I set the NAMESPACE env-var to namespace where I'm deploying models to, then run:

`helmfile apply -n ${NAMESPACE}`




**Now some un-natural stuff(!):**
- I didn't look into how to not deploy a unique gateway per model ('infra').  I keep the first models gateway deployment; all others I 'helm uninstall infra-{name} -n ${NAMESPACE}'
- After the first model is deployed, the second models deployment will fail with:
`Error: Failed to render chart: exit status 1: Error: Unable to continue with install: Secret "prefix-routing-gateway-sa-metrics-reader-secret" in namespace "{your $NAMESPACE}" exists and cannot be imported into   the current release: invalid ownership metadata; annotation validation error: key "meta.helm.sh/release-name" must equal "{current gaie release name}": current value is "{first models release name}"`
   - My hack/work-around is to just update the existing secrets "meta.helm.sh/release-name" value.


### HTTPRoute updates per model
- Do to a bug in Istio, we must only have a SINGLE HTTPRoute CR (with rules array entries ), we cannot have multiple separate CR's (one per model)
- BBR vs URL rewriting - both approaches work, I do not see a significant performance improvement in either approach, I've chosen to use url-rewriting (less pods, hops)

- The httproute is bound to the single gateway I kept (from first model deployed).  
```
Example:

spec:
  parentRefs:
    - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
      kind: Gateway
      name: {my first models infra gateway name}
  rules:
    - backendRefs:
        - group: inference.networking.x-k8s.io
          kind: InferencePool
          name: gaie-granite-3-3-8b-040
          port: 8000
          weight: 1
      filters:
        - type: URLRewrite
          urlRewrite:
            path:
              replacePrefixMatch: /
              type: ReplacePrefixMatch
      matches:
        - path:
            type: PathPrefix
            value: /granite-3-3-8b-instruct/
      timeouts:
        request: 2700s
    - backendRefs:
        - group: inference.networking.x-k8s.io
          kind: InferencePool
          name: gaie-base-qwen-6b-040
          port: 8000
          weight: 1
      filters:
        - type: URLRewrite
          urlRewrite:
            path:
              replacePrefixMatch: /
              type: ReplacePrefixMatch
      matches:
        - path:
            type: PathPrefix
            value: /Qwen3-0-6B/
      timeouts:
        request: 2700s
    - backendRefs:
        - group: inference.networking.x-k8s.io
          kind: InferencePool
          name: gaie-qwen3-32b-040
          port: 8000
          weight: 1
      filters:
        - type: URLRewrite
          urlRewrite:
            path:
              replacePrefixMatch: /
              type: ReplacePrefixMatch
      matches:
        - path:
            type: PathPrefix
            value: /qwen3-32B/
      timeouts:
        request: 2700s

```



### (External) Route:
To simplify access to the gateway, I manually created a route to the access cluster from the outside

```
metadata:
  ...
  annotations:
    haproxy.router.openshift.io/timeout: 2700s
spec:
  host: llm-d-multi-model.apps.rits-llmd-up.fmaas.res.ibm.com
  to:
    kind: Service
    name: infra-base-qwen-6b-040-inference-gateway-istio
    weight: 100
  port:
    targetPort: default
  tls:
    termination: edge
    insecureEdgeTerminationPolicy: None
```


**Test curl:**
```
curl -H 'accept: application/json' \
-H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
-d '{"model": "ibm-granite/granite-3.3-8b-instruct",
     "max_tokens": 200,
    "prompt": "Can you play cards?"
   }' \
"https://llm-d-multi-model.apps.rits-llmd-up.fmaas.res.ibm.com/granite-3-3-8b-instruct/v1/completions"
```




**To better handle load/slow response times:**
 - Adjust Timeout the on the external Route
 - Adjust HTTPRoute timeouts
 - Adjust the number of gateway replicas (4 req'd for my load test...)
 - Adjust LoadBalancer timeout (.api traffic in)

records.title: Update inferencepool chart to v1.2.1 for GA API compatibility with Istio 1.28+
records.body:
## Problem

The inferencepool chart version v1.2.0 uses the experimental API group `inference.networking.x-k8s.io`. However, Istio 1.28+ only supports the GA API group `inference.networking.k8s.io`.

This causes issues when deploying on clusters with Istio 1.28+ as the InferencePool, HTTPRoutes, and EPP deployments need to be manually patched to use the GA API group.

## Affected files

The following helmfile.yaml.gotmpl files specify `version: v1.2.0`:
- guides/simulated-accelerators/helmfile.yaml.gotmpl
- guides/precise-prefix-cache-aware/helmfile.yaml.gotmpl
- guides/inference-scheduling/helmfile.yaml.gotmpl
- guides/workload-autoscaling/helmfile.yaml.gotmpl
- guides/pd-disaggregation/helmfile.yaml.gotmpl

## Solution

Update the inferencepool chart version from `v1.2.0` to `v1.2.1`, which includes GA API support.

## Impact

This will enable out-of-the-box compatibility with Istio 1.28+ without requiring manual patches to InferencePool resources, HTTPRoutes, and EPP deployment args.

records.title: Add a sidecar deployment option in precise-prefix-cache-aware guide
records.body:
`llm-d-kv-cache` has just been renamed and a new disaggregated tokenizer service is proposed for better tokenization.

This issue is responsible for tracking the addition of the option to deploy a disaggregated tokenizer service sidecar in the precise-prefix-cache-aware guideline.

cc @vMaroon
records.author: delavet

records.title: EPP only route requests to decode pod on single node PD disaggregation when using host network
records.body:
Hi community,

I met a bug that the request are only routed to decode pod when using host network. From my end we need to enable GPUDirect on LLMD, so we need to use `hostNetwork: true` to map the RDMA device into the pods, or it will be interpreted as a virtual network and do not function. After using `hostNetwork: true`, we need to solve the port conflicts in scale-up setting. I try hard to understand the ports mapping in the yaml and I think it should be formed like this:

```bash
EPP  --> sidecar(8000) + decode (8200)
      | --> prefill (8000)
```

And the prefill here I change it from 8000 to 8300, and after that I helm template the yaml and make sure the final ports are correctly set.

```bash
EPP  --> sidecar(8000) + decode (8200)
      | --> prefill (8300)
```

However,  finally the bug I met is that my prefill pod will never be picked by the EPP, which means the requests will be done completely on `sidecar(8000) + decode (8200)`, and there are no logs in the prefill pod.

Welcome to any possible solutions to this bug!

=== ISSUE CONTEXT ===
Date: 2026-01-26
Environment: Kind cluster with Intel XPU via DRA (Dynamic Resource Allocation)
Namespace: llm-d-xpu-pd
Model: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B
vLLM version: 0.13.0 with NIXL KV connector
image:  ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-routing-sidecar:v0.4.0

Symptom:
- routing-proxy repeatedly reports "context canceled" errors every 5 seconds
- Requests from curl pods hang indefinitely (5+ minutes without response)
- Error occurs when proxying to decode vLLM at localhost:8200
- NIXL KV transfer works (100% external prefix cache hit rate)
- Some successful requests seen earlier (throughput: 1.3-4.0 tokens/s)

Error Pattern:
- 07:14:45 - 07:15:50: Continuous errors every 5s
- 07:23:04 - 07:23:59: Continuous errors every 5s
- 07:30:10 - 07:31:10: Continuous errors every 5s (ongoing)

Stack trace points to:
- proxy_helpers.go:117 in createDecoderProxyHandler
- ReverseProxy.ServeHTTP in Go's httputil

Pod Configuration:
- Decode pod has native sidecar (routing-proxy) with restartPolicy: Always
- routing-proxy connects to vLLM decode on localhost:8200
- NIXL connector validated: nixlv2

records.title: Make storage offloading guides composable with CPU offloading
records.body:
Typically it makes sense to form a tired KV cache offloading structure: HBM - CPU - Storage.

Currently the LMCache connector based guides compose, because enabling CPU/storage requires different environment variables. The native connector, however, requires different command line args. We should document how to enable both CPU and storage with the vllm native connector, and provide example recipes.

cc @kfirtoledo
records.author: liu-cong

records.title: Update the guides to fix monitoring enablement for GKE
records.body:
In https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api-inference-extension/pull/1906 the flag for enabling monitoring for GKE was changed to align with all other providers, we should update related llm-d guides as well:

specifically, change 
```--set "inferenceExtension.monitoring.gke.enabled=true"```

to 
```--set "inferenceExtension.monitoring.prometheus.enabled=true"```

records.title: consolidate label usage in guide
records.body:
We have both 
`llm-d.ai/accelerator-variant` and `llm-d.ai/hardware-vairant` which serve the same purpose
and` llm-d.ai/accelerator-vendor `vs ` llm-d.ai/hardware-vendor` 
if we decide to use `hardware` than `acclerator` then it is good to update spec in modelservice git repo as well which is having accelerator for all variants now

One good thing is to document which labels are being used for which purpose and if mandator or optional .and we can have them updates across the projects.

records.title: [Bug :bug:]: Data Parallel + P/D Disaggregation Timeout and Crash on Concurrent Requests (RDMA/H200)
records.body:
### Contact Details

yangligt@google.com

### What happened?

## Description
When combining Data Parallelism (DP) with Prefill/Decode (P/D) Disaggregation, the server successfully handles single requests but encounters KV cache retrieval timeouts and subsequent crashes when processing concurrent requests (e.g., 8 concurrent requests).

Notably, a standard configuration using Tensor Parallel (TP=8) for both Prefill and Decode works as expected even under saturated benchmark conditions. This suggests a regression or instability specifically when DP is introduced into the P/D disaggregation.

## Environment
Hardware: 2x 8xH200 nodes connected via RDMA.
Model: gpt-oss-120B.
Images:
ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-cuda:v0.5.0
ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-routing-sidecar:v0.5.0

## Configuration
Working Setup: Prefill TP=8 / Decode TP=8 (Performance is stable).
Failing Setup (P/D + DP):
Prefill: TP=1, DP=8
Decode: TP=4, DP=2

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Deploy llm-d using the disaggregated P/D + DP configuration mentioned above.
1. Send a single inference request: Success.
1. Send 8 concurrent requests:
    * Prefill workers complete all tasks.
    * Decode workers hang/timeout while attempting to retrieve the KV cache.
    * Decode server eventually crashes.

## Relevant Log Output
Please find the attached logs for detailed stack traces:
* single request prefill log
* single request decode log
* concurrent 8 requests prefill log (All prefills completed)
* concurrent 8 requests decode log (Hang and crash)

Container Image / Build

### Problem Statement

Firstly we build nvhsmem4py bindings for a matrix including python 3.9 which slows down our build times. It also makes things confusing to have 2 separate sets of python3. Furthermore "there are actually some critical performance related things for asyncio that make Python 3.11 and Python 3.12 much faster for comm" which we might need to track if any packages are coming through 3.9 instead of 3.12.

Try to build nvhsmem without python3.9. Can potentially leverage the nvshmem3.5.19-1 new release if that will help to fix this issue. This is a spike ticket though - not sure if this is possible.

records.title: 🐛 Nightly E2E: Inference Scheduling OCP fails with CUDA OOM on sampler warmup
records.body:
## Summary

The nightly E2E inference scheduling test on OCP (pokprod) consistently fails with **CUDA out of memory** during vLLM sampler warmup. All 8 decode pods crash-loop with the same error.

## Error

```
RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory occurred when warming up sampler with 1024 
dummy requests. Please try lowering `max_num_seqs` or `gpu_memory_utilization` 
when initializing the engine.
```

## Details

- **Workflow**: `nightly-e2e-inference-scheduling-ocp.yaml`
- **Failed run**: https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/actions/runs/22115361589
- **Pod logs artifact**: `nightly-pod-logs-inference-scheduling` (attached to run)
- **Image**: `ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-cuda-dev:latest` (vLLM v0.11.0)
- **Model**: Qwen/Qwen3-32B with `tensor_parallel_size=2`
- **Config**: `--gpu-memory-utilization=0.95` (from `guides/inference-scheduling/ms-inference-scheduling/values.yaml` line 41)

## Timeline from pod logs

1. Model loads successfully
2. CUDA graphs capture completes (67/67 mixed prefill-decode + 67/67 decode)
3. KV cache allocated: 41.87 GiB per worker
4. **Fails** during sampler warmup with 1024 dummy requests → OOM
5. All 8 decode pods crash-loop

## Suggested fix

Lower `gpu-memory-utilization` from `0.95` to `0.90`–`0.92`, or add `--max-num-seqs=512` to the vLLM args in `guides/inference-scheduling/ms-inference-scheduling/values.yaml`.

## Notes

- CKS inference scheduling passed on the same commit — waldorf cluster GPUs may have more available memory
- The OCP cluster uses pokprod nodes (A100s)
- This may also affect other OCP guides using the same `0.95` utilization setting

records.title: [Upstream Breaking Change] NVSHMEM v3.4.5-0 → v3.5.19-1
records.body:
## Summary

NVSHMEM has released **v3.5.19-1** (published 2025-12-31), which includes significant API changes, library restructuring, and new features.

**Current Pin**: `v3.4.5-0`  
**Latest Release**: `v3.5.19-1` (2025-12-31)  
**Status**: Repository is ~7 weeks behind latest release

## Breaking Changes

### 1. API Renames (BREAKING)
- **`tile_allreduce`** renamed to **`tile_reduce`**
- **`tile_reduce`** renamed to **`tile_rooted_reduce`**

**Impact**: Code using these functions will fail to compile.

### 2. Static Library Removed (BREAKING)
- **Removed**: `libnvshmem.a` (static-only library)
- **Replacement**: Must link to `libnvshmem_host` and `libnvshmem_device` separately

**Impact**: Build scripts using `-lnvshmem.a` will fail.

### 3. Removed Undeclared Functions
- Removed `realloc` and `alltoalls` declarations (never implemented)

**Impact**: Code referencing these will fail to compile (unlikely in llm-d).

## New Features & Improvements

✅ **Positive changes**:
- Added qpair-specific API calls (`nvshmemx_qp_*`)
- Added tile-granular RMA routines: `tile_put`, `tile_get`, `tile_broadcast`
- Added LLVM bitcode library support for IBGDA
- Improved EFA transport with AWS performance improvements
- Updated default QPs from 4 to 8 for full bandwidth
- **Increased default `NVSHMEM_MAX_MEMORY_PER_GPU` from 128 GiB to 256 GiB**
- CUDA 13.0 and 13.1 support (experimental)
- Blackwell GPU support

## Impact Assessment

**Impact Level**: HIGH

**Affected Files**:
- `docker/Dockerfile.cuda` line 45 (`NVSHMEM_VERSION`)

**Breaking Changes Detected**: YES
- API renames: `tile_allreduce`, `tile_reduce` → new names
- Library structure change: `libnvshmem.a` removed

**Repository Usage Check**:
✅ **No direct usage found** in llm-d source code via grep:
```bash
grep -r "tile_allreduce\|tile_reduce\|libnvshmem\.a" .
# No matches
```

**Assessment**: Since llm-d does not directly call the renamed NVSHMEM APIs, the update should be **safe**, but testing is required to ensure downstream dependencies (vLLM, etc.) handle the changes correctly.

## CUDA Compatibility Note

⚠️ **CUDA 13 support is experimental**. llm-d currently uses CUDA 12.9.1, which is fully supported.

## Recommended Action

1. **Test NVSHMEM v3.5.19-1** in a non-production environment
2. **Verify vLLM compatibility** with the new NVSHMEM version
3. Update `docker/Dockerfile.cuda` line 45:
   ```dockerfile
   ARG NVSHMEM_VERSION="v3.5.19-1"
   ```
4. Run full integration tests before deploying to production

## References

- **Upstream Release**: https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvshmem/releases/tag/v3.5.19-1
- **Current Pin**: `docker/Dockerfile.cuda` line 45

records.title: 🌱 Guide improvement: inference-scheduling — align guide content with nightly E2E test patterns
records.body:
## Summary

The **inference-scheduling** guide has a comprehensive nightly E2E test suite that validates the guide's deployment on OpenShift, CoreWeave (CKS), and GKE. Based on the collection of results and repairs needed to get these tests running successfully, there are several suggestions below to improve the guide so that it more closely matches the structure, mechanics, and success patterns of the tested deployment.

The goal is to ensure every user following this guide has a smooth, successful experience — matching what the CI system has validated nightly.

## Links

- **Guide**: [`guides/inference-scheduling/`](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/tree/main/guides/inference-scheduling)
- **Nightly tests**:
  - [OpenShift](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/actions/workflows/nightly-e2e-inference-scheduling-ocp.yaml) — ✅ Passing
  - [CKS](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/actions/workflows/nightly-e2e-inference-scheduling-cks.yaml) — ✅ Passing
  - [GKE](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/actions/workflows/nightly-e2e-inference-scheduling-gke.yaml) — ❌ Failing (GPU availability)

## Recommendations

### 1. Document GPU node selector requirements for OpenShift

The nightly OCP test applies a `nodeSelector` patch to target H100-80GB-HBM3 nodes via a `pre_deploy_script` that uses `yq` to modify `ms-inference-scheduling/values.yaml`. The guide doesn't mention this requirement, which can lead to scheduling failures on multi-GPU-type clusters.

**Suggestion**: Add a section on configuring `nodeSelector` or `nodeAffinity` for specific GPU types (H100, A100, L4) in the helmfile values.

### 2. Document minimum GPU requirements vs. recommended

The test requires a minimum of 2 GPUs but recommends 4. The guide documents 8 replicas × 2 GPUs (16 total) as the default. Users on smaller clusters may not realize they can scale down.

**Suggestion**: Add a "Minimal deployment" section showing how to run with 2-4 GPUs for testing/evaluation, similar to how the nightly test configures it.

### 3. GKE GPU availability detection

The GKE nightly test currently fails with `Insufficient GPUs: need 2, have -1 available`. The `-1` indicates the GPU detection logic doesn't properly handle GKE's DaemonSet-based GPU driver installer (which may report GPUs differently than OpenShift/CKS).

**Suggestion**: Document GKE-specific GPU prerequisites including the NVIDIA GPU operator/driver DaemonSet that must be running and healthy before deployment.

### 4. Gateway type documentation

The test supports switching between `istio` (default) and `kgateway` gateway providers via workflow dispatch. The guide should clearly document both options and their prerequisites.

### 5. Pod readiness timing

The test uses a 180-second pod readiness delay after deployment. The guide should mention expected startup times so users know how long to wait before assuming something is wrong.

---

*These suggestions are based on the nightly E2E test results and the repairs/adaptations that were needed to achieve consistent test success across platforms. The guide can be improved by incorporating these patterns so that every user has a happy, successful deployment experience.*

records.title: 🌱 Guide improvement: pd-disaggregation — align guide content with nightly E2E test patterns
records.body:
## Summary

The **pd-disaggregation** guide has a comprehensive nightly E2E test suite validating prefill/decode disaggregation with NIXL KV-cache transfer on OpenShift, CoreWeave (CKS), and GKE. Based on the collection of results and repairs needed to get these tests running successfully, there are several suggestions below to improve the guide.

The goal is to ensure every user following this guide has a smooth, successful experience — matching what the CI system has validated nightly.

## Links

- **Guide**: [`guides/pd-disaggregation/`](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/tree/main/guides/pd-disaggregation)
- **Nightly tests**:
  - [OpenShift](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/actions/workflows/nightly-e2e-pd-disaggregation-ocp.yaml) — ✅ Passing
  - [CKS](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/actions/workflows/nightly-e2e-pd-disaggregation-cks.yaml) — ✅ Passing
  - [GKE](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/actions/workflows/nightly-e2e-pd-disaggregation-gke.yaml) — ❌ Failing (GPU availability)

## Recommendations

### 1. Document a minimal/slim deployment option

The nightly test uses a **slim model transform** that replaces the guide's default large model (gpt-oss-120B) with Qwen3-0.6B for resource-efficient testing. This slim variant:
- Reduces GPU requirement from multi-GPU to 1 GPU per role
- Removes RDMA resource requests
- Sets tensor parallelism to 1
- Uses 2Gi shared memory instead of larger allocations

**Suggestion**: Add a "Minimal deployment" or "Quick start" section documenting a slim configuration for users who want to validate P/D disaggregation on smaller clusters (2-4 GPUs) before scaling to production.

### 2. Document resource requirements by model size

The guide focuses on the full production deployment (8×H200, TP=4 decode, TP=1 prefill) but doesn't clearly document how to scale down for different GPU counts. The test proves P/D disaggregation works with just 2 GPUs and a small model.

**Suggestion**: Add a resource requirements table showing minimum vs. recommended GPU configurations for different model sizes.

### 3. GKE GPU prerequisites

Same as inference-scheduling — the GKE test fails with `Insufficient GPUs: need 2, have -1 available`. The GPU detection logic doesn't properly handle GKE's driver setup.

**Suggestion**: Document GKE-specific GPU prerequisites (NVIDIA GPU operator/driver DaemonSet).

### 4. RDMA/InfiniBand vs. standard networking

The guide emphasizes RDMA/InfiniBand for KV-cache transfer, but the nightly test proves P/D disaggregation works without RDMA on small models. Users without InfiniBand hardware may not realize they can still use P/D disaggregation.

**Suggestion**: Document which network configurations are required vs. optional, and how performance scales with and without RDMA.

### 5. Pod startup time expectations

The test uses a 180-second readiness delay. Document expected startup times for prefill and decode pods, and explain the startup probe configuration (600 failure threshold × 1s period = 10 min max).

---

*These suggestions are based on the nightly E2E test results and the repairs/adaptations that were needed to achieve consistent test success across platforms. The guide can be improved by incorporating these patterns so that every user has a happy, successful deployment experience.*

The nightly test currently only runs on OpenShift. The guide documents optional Intel XPU deployment (`helmfile apply -e xpu`) but this variant has no nightly test. Users deploying on CKS or GKE may encounter undocumented platform-specific issues.

**Suggestion**: Either add CKS/GKE nightly tests, or clearly document that this guide is currently validated on OpenShift only and other platforms are community-supported/experimental.

### 2. Document GPU node selector requirements

Like the inference-scheduling guide, the test applies an H100 `nodeSelector` patch via `yq` to `ms-kv-events/values.yaml`. The guide should document this requirement for multi-GPU-type clusters.

The test requires minimum 2 GPUs and uses the full Qwen3-32B model (no slim transform). Document these requirements clearly so users know what hardware they need.

The test uses a 180-second readiness delay. Document expected startup times and explain that Qwen3-32B model loading can take several minutes.

records.body:
## Summary

The **tiered-prefix-cache** guide has a nightly E2E test on OpenShift that validates CPU RAM-based prefix cache offloading with the vLLM OffloadingConnector. Based on the collection of results and repairs needed to get this test running successfully, there are suggestions below to improve the guide.

The goal is to ensure every user following this guide has a smooth, successful experience — matching what the CI system has validated nightly.

## Links

- **Guide**: [`guides/tiered-prefix-cache/`](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/tree/main/guides/tiered-prefix-cache)
- **Nightly test**:
  - [OpenShift](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/actions/workflows/nightly-e2e-tiered-prefix-cache-ocp.yaml) — ✅ Passing

## Recommendations

### 1. Document the hybrid deployment pattern (kustomize + helm + gateway)

The nightly test does NOT use helmfile. Instead, it uses a three-step deployment:
1. Gateway recipe: `kubectl apply -k guides/recipes/gateway/${GATEWAY_TYPE}`
2. Model server via kustomize: `kubectl apply -k guides/tiered-prefix-cache/cpu/manifests/vllm/offloading-connector`
3. InferencePool via helm: `helm install llm-d-infpool ... oci://registry.k8s.io/gateway-api-inference-extension/charts/inferencepool`

If the guide only documents helmfile, users may not realize this alternative deployment pattern exists and is the one actually validated by CI.

**Suggestion**: Document both deployment methods (helmfile and manual kustomize+helm) so users can choose based on their tooling preferences.

### 2. Document a minimal/slim deployment option

The nightly test uses a **slim model transform** with Qwen3-0.6B (replacing the guide's 32B focus):
- 1 GPU instead of multi-GPU
- `cpu_bytes_to_use: 10737418240` (10GB CPU RAM for cache)
- Max batch size: 64 sequences

**Suggestion**: Add a "Minimal deployment" section showing how to run with 1-2 GPUs and a small model for evaluation.

### 3. Expand platform coverage

records.title: 🐛 Guide improvement: wide-ep-lws — fix nightly E2E failures and align guide with test patterns
records.body:
## Summary

The **wide-ep-lws** guide has nightly E2E tests on OpenShift, CoreWeave (CKS), and GKE. **All three are currently failing** due to deployment issues. Based on the collection of results and repairs needed, there are critical fixes and improvement suggestions below.

The goal is to ensure every user following this guide has a smooth, successful experience — matching what the CI system validates nightly.

## Links

- **Guide**: [`guides/wide-ep-lws/`](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/tree/main/guides/wide-ep-lws)
- **Nightly tests**:
  - [OpenShift](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/actions/workflows/nightly-e2e-wide-ep-lws-ocp.yaml) — ❌ Failing
  - [CKS](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/actions/workflows/nightly-e2e-wide-ep-lws-cks.yaml) — ❌ Failing
  - [GKE](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/actions/workflows/nightly-e2e-wide-ep-lws-gke.yaml) — ❌ Failing

## Critical Issues (Blocking)

### 1. Kustomize relative path security error (OCP + CKS)

The nightly slim overlay at `guides/wide-ep-lws/manifests/modelserver/nightly/kustomization.yaml` references `../base/serviceAccount.yaml`, which kustomize rejects:

```
error: accumulating resources: accumulation err='accumulating resources from 
'../base/serviceAccount.yaml': security; file '.../base/serviceAccount.yaml' 
is not in or below '.../nightly'': must build at directory
```

Kustomize does not allow relative paths that escape the kustomization root directory. The nightly overlay needs to either:
- Copy the ServiceAccount manifest into the nightly directory, or
- Use a kustomize `resources` reference that doesn't traverse upward, or
- Use a symlink (if supported by the runner filesystem)

### 2. OpenShift Gateway API CRD conflict

On OpenShift, the Istio gateway recipe tries to apply Gateway API CRDs, but the OpenShift Ingress Operator manages these and denies modifications:

```
Error from server (Forbidden): customresourcedefinitions.apiextensions.k8s.io 
"backendtlspolicies.gateway.networking.k8s.io" is forbidden: 
ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'openshift-ingress-operator-gatewayapi-crd-admission' 
denied request: Gateway API CRDs are managed by the Ingress Operator
```

**Suggestion**: The OpenShift test should either:
- Skip CRD installation when on OpenShift (where the Ingress Operator manages them), or
- Use a gateway recipe variant that doesn't try to install CRDs, or
- Document this OpenShift-specific prerequisite in the guide

### 3. GKE GPU availability detection

The GKE test fails with `Insufficient GPUs: need 2, have -1 available` (same issue as inference-scheduling and pd-disaggregation on GKE).

## Recommendations (Non-blocking improvements)

### 4. Document the LeaderWorkerSet prerequisite

The nightly test installs LWS via helm before deployment. The guide should clearly document this as a prerequisite:

```bash
helm install lws oci://registry.k8s.io/lws/charts/lws \
  --version=0.7.0 \
  --namespace lws-system \
  --create-namespace \
  --wait --timeout 300s
```

### 5. Document a minimal/slim deployment option

The nightly test replaces DeepSeek-R1-0528 (which requires 16+ GPUs with expert parallelism) with Qwen3-0.6B (1 GPU per role, no EP/RDMA). This slim variant proves P/D disaggregation with LWS works on minimal hardware.

**Suggestion**: Add a "Minimal deployment" section for users who want to validate the LWS + P/D + routing sidecar pattern without multi-node GPU clusters.

### 6. Document the three-step deployment (not just helmfile)

The test uses kustomize + helm + gateway recipe (not helmfile). The guide should document both deployment methods.

### 7. Document routing sidecar configuration

The decode LeaderWorkerSet includes a routing sidecar (`llm-d-routing-sidecar:v0.5.0`) with specific flags (`--connector=nixlv2`, `--enable-prefiller-sampling`). These should be documented with explanations of each flag.

### 8. Platform-specific pod readiness expectations

- OCP/CKS: 20-minute pod wait timeout, 180s readiness delay
- GKE: 35-minute pod wait timeout, 480s readiness delay (significantly longer due to L4 GPU startup and model loading)

Document these differences so users on each platform know what to expect.

---

*These suggestions are based on the nightly E2E test results and the repairs/adaptations that were needed to get tests running. The critical issues (#1-#3) are blocking the nightly tests and need immediate attention. The guide can be improved by incorporating the remaining patterns so that every user has a happy, successful deployment experience.*

records.title: 🌱 Guide improvement: workload-autoscaling — align guide content with nightly E2E test patterns
records.body:
## Summary

The **workload-autoscaling** guide has nightly E2E tests on OpenShift and CoreWeave (CKS) that validate the WVA (Workload Variant Autoscaler) deployment with intelligent inference scheduling. Based on the collection of results and repairs needed to get these tests running successfully — including fixes for KEDA APIService race conditions and quay.io build failures — there are several suggestions below to improve the guide.

The goal is to ensure every user following this guide has a smooth, successful experience — matching what the CI system has validated nightly.

## Links

- **Guide**: [`guides/workload-autoscaling/`](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/tree/main/guides/workload-autoscaling)
- **WVA repo**: [llm-d/llm-d-workload-variant-autoscaler](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-workload-variant-autoscaler)
- **Nightly tests**:
  - [OpenShift](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/actions/workflows/nightly-e2e-wva-ocp.yaml) — ✅ Passing (after recent fixes)
  - [CKS](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/actions/workflows/nightly-e2e-wva-cks.yaml) — ✅ Passing (after recent fixes)
- **Related PRs**: [WVA #761](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-workload-variant-autoscaler/pull/761) (KEDA resilience), [llm-d #801](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/pull/801) (build retry)

## Recommendations

### 1. Document KEDA coexistence behavior

The nightly test discovered a critical race condition: when KEDA is installed on the cluster (common on OpenShift), KEDA's operator continuously reconciles the `v1beta1.external.metrics.k8s.io` APIService, overwriting Prometheus Adapter's registration. This causes WVA's external metrics pipeline to break.

The WVA E2E test now includes an "APIService guard" that re-patches the APIService when KEDA reclaims it. However, this is only relevant for the E2E test harness — in production, KEDA integration uses the `prometheus` trigger type which queries Prometheus directly (documented in [WVA KEDA integration docs](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-workload-variant-autoscaler/blob/main/docs/integrations/keda-integration.md)).

**Suggestion**: Add a note to the guide explaining:
- If using WVA with standalone HPA + Prometheus Adapter (as documented), KEDA must be either uninstalled or its external metrics registration must be managed
- If using WVA with KEDA (production pattern), use KEDA's `prometheus` trigger type instead of the external metrics API

### 2. Document build-from-source vs. released images

The nightly test builds the WVA controller image from the `main` branch at test time (`nightly-${SHA}` tag) because the chart on main may include flags not in the last tagged release. The guide references specific version tags (e.g., v0.5.0).

**Suggestion**: Document how to build WVA from source for users who need latest features, and clearly indicate which chart version is compatible with which controller version.

### 3. Document Prometheus/monitoring prerequisites

The test relies on Prometheus being pre-configured on the platform. The guide should clearly document:
- Required Prometheus configuration for external metrics
- Prometheus Adapter setup and configuration
- How to verify the metrics pipeline is working (`kubectl get --raw '/apis/external.metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/...'`)

### 4. Document HPA tuning parameters

The test configures:
- HPA stabilization window: 240 seconds (default)
- Max batch size (max_num_seqs): 1 (easy to saturate for testing)
- Request rate: 20 req/s

**Suggestion**: Add a section on HPA tuning with recommended values for different workload patterns (latency-sensitive vs. throughput-focused).

### 5. Add GKE platform support

The nightly test only covers OpenShift and CKS. The guide documents GKE and Kind/Minikube as supported platforms but these aren't tested nightly.

**Suggestion**: Either add a GKE nightly test or clearly mark GKE as community-supported/untested.

---

*These suggestions are based on the nightly E2E test results and the repairs/adaptations that were needed to achieve consistent test success across platforms. The guide can be improved by incorporating these patterns so that every user has a happy, successful deployment experience.*

records.body:
## Summary

PyTorch has released **2.10.0** (published 2026-02-16), which includes Python 3.14 support, performance improvements, and new features.

**Current Pin**: `2.9.1`  
**Latest Release**: `2.10.0` (2026-02-16)  
**Status**: Repository is ~3 days behind latest release

## Release Highlights

### New Features
- **Python 3.14** support for `torch.compile()` (experimental freethreaded build)
- Reduced kernel launch overhead with **combo-kernels** horizontal fusion
- New **varlen_attn()** op for ragged and packed sequences
- **DebugMode** for tracking dispatched calls and numerical divergence debugging
- **Intel GPU support** expanded (FP8, complex MatMul, SYCL on Windows)

### Performance Improvements
- Combo-kernels horizontal fusion in TorchInductor
- Efficient eigenvalue decompositions with DnXgeev
- `torch.compile()` now respects `use_deterministic_mode`

### API Deprecations (NOT BREAKING - warnings only)
⚠️ These features are deprecated but still work with warnings:
- `torch.jit` (not guaranteed in Python 3.14) - **recommend migrate to `torch.compile`**
- `torch.onnx.export` `dynamic_axes` option - use `dynamic_shapes` instead
- `fallback=False` is now default in `torch.onnx.export`
- DeviceMesh slicing of flattened dim from root mesh

### Backwards Incompatible Changes
✅ **None affect llm-d** - verified via grep:
- Removed `data_source` argument from Sampler (not used in llm-d)
- Removed deprecated imports for `torch.utils.data.datapipes.iter.grouping`
- Removed Nested Jagged Tensor support from `nn.attention.flex_attention`
- Renamed pytorch-triton package to triton (dependency management only)

## Impact Assessment

**Impact Level**: MEDIUM

**Affected Files**:
- `docker/constraints.txt` line 1 (PyTorch version constraint)

**Breaking Changes**: None affecting llm-d

**Deprecation Impact**: No direct impact - llm-d does not use `torch.jit` or ONNX export features

**Security/Performance Benefits**: 
- Performance improvements from combo-kernels and TorchInductor optimizations
- New debugging capabilities with DebugMode
- Python 3.14 support for future migrations

records.body:
# [DRAFT] llm-d 0.6 Roadmap

## Big themes

- **Engine Diversification (SGLang):** Elevating SGLang to a well-lit path alongside vLLM, focusing on radix-tree cache integration and structured generation.
- **Initial Support for RL and Post-Training**
- **Improving Operationalizability of Disaggregated Deployments**
- **Deep Stack Observability:** Transitioning from simple metrics to full distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) across the gateway, EPP, and KV-cache layers.
- **Mixture of Experts load balancing:** Router skew, etc.
- **Expanding the Inference Scheduler's Capabilities:** Managing a broader ecosystem of engines, diverse model modalities, and complex workload patterns.
- **Intelligent Resource Scaling:** Moving beyond saturation-based autoscaling to SLO-driven (ITL and TPOT) and phase-aware (prefill and decode) resource management.
- **Foundations for Agentic Inference:** Primitives for multi-step, program-structured workloads — from program-aware scheduling and semantic KV-cache management policies to benchmarking harnesses that model agentic traffic patterns.

---

## Feature Work

### Inference Scheduler and Engine Support

- [x] **SGLang Integration:** Support for SGLang metrics, native precise radix-cache-aware routing (approximate already supports SGLang), and disaggregated P and D profiles.
- [ ] **Batch and Async Serving:** Support for offline and asynchronous batch workloads via the inference gateway (OpenAI-compatible). Support for mixing batch and realtime traffic.
- [ ] **LoRA-Aware Fairness:** New scheduling logic to prevent adapter starvation and ensure equitable distribution in multi-LoRA pools.
- [x] **Multi-Modal Support:** Standardizing scheduling and resource tracking for vision-language models (VLM).
- [ ] **Multi-Modal Support: EPD Disaggregation**
- [ ] **Pluggable Request Parsing:** Allows supporting custom request formats beyond OpenAI HTTP protocol (including vLLM gRPC protocol).
- [ ] **Program-Aware Scheduling (Foundations):** Primitives for expressing multi-step workload structure in routing decisions. Initial focus on program-hint annotations for the EPP.
- [ ] **Agentic Workload Benchmarking & Simulation:** Meaningful trace replays and synthetic workload generator modeling multi-turn agentic traffic for evaluating agentic-inference efficiency and costs.

### KV Cache Management

- [ ] **KV Offloading Evolution:**
  - [ ] **vLLM Offloading Connector [RFC]:** Implementing preemption-only offloading and HMA (Hybrid Memory Allocation) support.
  - [ ] **Storage Connector:** Native GDS (GPUDirect Storage) support for high-bandwidth cache transfers.
  - [ ] **Multi-Tier Offloading**
- [ ] **Multi-Modal & HMA-Aware Precise Prefix-Cache Scheduling:** Moving from approximate estimation to precise metadata-driven scheduling using the vLLM renderer API.
- [ ] **Disaggregated Tokenization:** Offloading chat-templating and tokenization to a dedicated sidecar or service that reuses the inference-engine pipelines and optimizations to reduce engine overhead.
- [ ] **Context-Aware Cache Management Policies:** Eviction and retention logic informed by workload context — prefix soft-pinning, reuse-predicted prioritization, ephemeral vs. durable context distinction.
- [ ] **Semantic Context Taints (Experimental):** Tagging cached KV blocks with semantic metadata (tool-output, user-private, shared-system-prompt) to drive KV-cache reuse maximization policies and routing affinity.

### Ecosystem Integrations

- [ ] **KVEvents Abstraction:** Decoupling the event layer to support both SGLang (radix) and vLLM (paged) event streams.
- [ ] **vLLM Input-Processing Frontend:** Disaggregating the vLLM input processing pipelines (tokenization, rendering) for efficient and effective reuse in the llm-d-scheduler.
- [ ] **Disaggregated Tokenization:** Offloading chat-templating and tokenization to a dedicated sidecar or service that reuses the inference-engine pipelines and optimizations to reduce engine overhead.
- [ ] **NVIDIA Dynamo KVBM Integration** *(TBD)*
- [ ] **Distributed Tracing (OTel):** Full instrumentation of the KV indexer to provide visibility into lookup and offloading latencies (PR #48).

### Workload Variant Autoscaler (WVA)

- [ ] **Saturation-Based Scaling:** Shifting from percentage-based scaling to token-based scaling for better accounting of absolute available capacity.
- [ ] **SLO-Based Analyzer:** Introduce new analyzer aware of SLOs, based on observed arrival rate.
- [ ] **Independent P and D Scaling:** Ability to scale prefill and decode variants independently based on real-time phase bottlenecks.
- [ ] **Human-in-the-Loop:** Introducing manual approval flow for scaling actions in production clusters.
- [ ] **Per-Tenant Quotas:** Resource isolation and quotas for multi-tenant inference deployments.

### P/D Disaggregation

- [ ] **Well-Lit Path Expansion:** Rollouts for new versions.
- [ ] **DP-Aware Scheduling:** Wide-EP support and well-lit path.
- [ ] **Benchmarks Published:** Tradeoffs of P/D and Wide-EP.

records.title: [Upstream Breaking Change] NIXL 0.9.0 → 0.10.0
records.body:
## Summary

NIXL has released **0.10.0** (published 2026-02-18), which includes a **major breaking change with Device API V2**, along with significant cloud storage, networking, and device integration improvements.

**Current Pin**: `0.9.0`  
**Latest Release**: `0.10.0` (2026-02-18)  
**Status**: Repository is ~8 days behind latest release  
**Impact**: **HIGH** — Breaking Device API changes

## Breaking Changes

### Device API V2 (BREAKING)

The Device API has been **completely redesigned** with new interfaces for host-side and device-side operations:

- **New programming model** across the full stack
- API definition and interface updates
- Core host-side implementation changes
- UCX backend implementation changes  
- GPU and UCX device-side implementation changes
- New memory view API that simplifies device initialization

**This is a significant API change from the v1 Device API.**

**Impact**: Code using Device API v1 will need to be migrated to the new v2 interfaces.

## Affected Files

**In llm-d repository:**
- `docker/Dockerfile.cuda` line 46 (`NIXL_VERSION`)
- NIXL headers installed to `/usr/local/include/nixl*` (lines 408-423)
- NIXL libraries installed to system lib paths

## Repository Impact Analysis

````bash
# Check for direct NIXL Device API usage in llm-d
grep -r "nixl.*device" --include="*.py" --include="*.cpp" --include="*.c" .
# (Results to be verified)
````

**Likely Impact**: NIXL is built from source and integrated into the Docker image. The Device API changes may not directly affect llm-d if vLLM and other dependencies handle the NIXL interface abstraction. However, testing is required to ensure compatibility.

## Major New Features

✅ **Positive additions**:
- **Azure Blob Storage Plugin** — New cloud object storage backend
- **S3 CRT Client Support** — Higher throughput S3 transfers with automatic multipart upload/download
- **Hierarchical Object Storage Architecture** — Refactored for modularity with support for future RDMA S3 backends
- **Libfabric Slingshot/CXI Support** — HPE Slingshot interconnect support
- **AWS Neuron Device Support** — OFI support for Trainium/Inferentia accelerators
- **Performance improvements** — GIL release in Python, CQ batch reads, improved threading model

## Compatibility Notes

- **Python**: 3.10+ required (llm-d uses Python 3.12 ✅)
- **CUDA**: No breaking changes for CUDA integration
- **UCX**: UCX plugin reorganized and improved

## Recommended Action

**Priority**: HIGH  

**Testing Steps**:
1. **Build NIXL 0.10.0** in a test Docker image
2. **Verify vLLM compatibility** — Check if vLLM uses NIXL Device API directly
3. **Run integration tests** with vLLM and NIXL 0.10.0
4. **Check for Device API usage** in dependent libraries (InfiniStore, LMCache)

**If Device API is not used directly**, the update should be safe. If it is used, migration to Device API V2 will be required.

**Update Command**:
````dockerfile
# In docker/Dockerfile.cuda
ARG NIXL_VERSION="0.10.0"
````

## References

- **Upstream Release**: https://github.com/ai-dynamo/nixl/releases/tag/0.10.0
- **Current Pin**: `docker/Dockerfile.cuda` line 46
- **Device API V2 PRs**: #1229, #1230, #1245, #1255

records.title: Tracking issue for modular installation architecture
records.body:
This is the tracking issue for implementing the [llm-d Modular Installation Architecture](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1UAfp9BUoeEt_dp4qaiJFKmOOtFi9iQYBT-BMCviQeSY/edit?tab=t.0) proposal.  For context, https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/issues/405 is the initial experimental proposal.


## Summary

Convert the following guides to the Kustomize-first modular installation architecture (as piloted by tiered-prefix-cache and wide-ep-lws), following the phased migration plan referenced by the parent tracking issue (#850):

- inference-scheduling
- pd-disaggregation
- simulated-accelerators
- workload-autoscaling
- precise-prefix-aware

This work should preserve the existing Helm-based guides during the transition, then switch the repo defaults to the Kustomize-first approach once CI/CD and benchmark tooling are migrated.

## Goals / Success Criteria

- Each target guide has a **Kustomize-based `v2`** implementation (side-by-side with existing guide, initially).
- CI/CD and any deployment validation for these guides uses **v2**.
- The repo documentation and guidance **switches to v2** as the default path.
- A separate tracking issue exists for converging on a **benchmark-oriented `deployer`** abstraction (to support parameter sweeps without reintroducing monolithic Helm complexity).

## Scope (per guide)

For **each** of the guides listed above:

### Phase 1 — Parallel Implementation (Side-by-Side)
- Implement a `v2` Kustomize overlay structure for the guide (keeping the classic/Helm flow intact).
- Ensure the guide composes cleanly with the modular layers (prereqs / primitives / well-lit paths / workload patterns).

### Phase 2 — Dependency Migration (CI/CD + Benchmarks)
- Update CI workflows and any benchmark pipelines to deploy and validate via the guide’s `v2` Kustomize manifests/overlays.
- Ensure deployments are reproducible and debuggable (manifests remain transparent; use Helm-generated patches only if needed for parameter sweeping).

### Phase 3 — Deprecation & Switch
- Mark Helm-based guide and templates as deprecated.
- Update docs to make `v2` the recommended/official approach.
- Ensure downstream references (README links, guide index, examples) are updated accordingly.

## Additional Notes / Context

- Motivation: reduce duplication and opacity from monolithic Helm charts; improve composability and readability; support measurable benchmarking by isolating variables.
- User feedback supports Kustomize-first modularization, with a request to keep docs navigable (modular code, potentially flatter documentation).
- Parent tracking issue: https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/issues/850
