records.title: Proposal to Move EPP to the llm-d Repo
records.body:
### Feature Area

Inference Scheduling

### Problem Statement

We currently have two repositories each producing an EPP image, the upstream [inference gateway](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api-inference-extension) and the [llm-d-scheduler](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-inference-scheduler/tree/main). The llm-d inference scheduler extends the IGW with a set of plugins (basically using it as a library). 

Advanced plugins (like P/D and precise kv-cache aware scheduling) as well as recent scheduling framework enhancements have mostly been driven by the llm-d project, with most new plugins being hosted in the llm-d repo. This created a suboptimal situation, fragmented code and duplicate maintenance and documentation. 

This not only created confusion among developers on what to put where, but also confusion among end users as well. 


This issue mirrors the one created in https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api-inference-extension/issues/2430


### Proposed Solution

### Proposal
Move the Endpoint Picker code from its [current repo under kubernetes org](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api-inference-extension) to the[ llm-d scheduler repo](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-inference-scheduler). The InferencePool API and the EPP protocol definition along its conformance tests will stay in k8s, and ideally move eventually to the Gateway api repository.

The two APIs, InferenceObjective and InferenceModelRewrite APIs would also move with EPP since they don’t spec any behavior related to the Gateway itself, rather to the EPP only.

### Rationale
The Inference Gateway (IGW) project is split into three distinct functional parts:
- An API ([InferencePool](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api-inference-extension/tree/main/docs/proposals/002-api-proposal)) and protocol ([endpoint picker protocol](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api-inference-extension/tree/main/docs/proposals/004-endpoint-picker-protocol)) that extends the Kubernetes Gateway API. These spec how a Gateway should configure an external callout service—the endpoint picker—for inference-optimized request scheduling. Crucially, the API and protocols remain agnostic of the selection logic, leaving the specific endpoint selection algorithm to the picker implementation.
- A conformant Gateway ecosystem that supports the InferencePool API and Endpoint Picker protocol. As of this proposal, this includes GKE Gateway, Istio, kGateway, and NGINX Gateway Fabric.
- An implementation of the endpoint picker service, known as [epp](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api-inference-extension/tree/main/pkg/epp).

Beyond standard protocol implementation (primarily ExtProc gRPC handling), the core value of the epp lies in its inference-specific optimizations. These include routing requests based on LoRA adapter affinity, lowest KV-cache utilization, and predicted latency to pick the most efficient endpoint for efficient serving.

Advancing these optimizations requires deep AI/ML domain expertise and tight integration with model server implementations. Consequently, the ideal community to drive the endpoint picker forward is one that actively involves model server developers (such as the vLLM and sglang communities) and model developers, ensuring the scheduler evolves alongside the underlying serving technology.

As such, llm-d (under CNCF sandbox project application) offers this community and the ideal home for epp to continue to evolve and adapt to new innovations in GenAI serving.

### Alternatives Considered

_No response_

### Willingness to Contribute

Yes, I can submit a PR

### Additional Context

_No response_

records.title: [Upstream Breaking Change] Gateway API v1.4.0 → v1.5.0
records.body:
## Summary

Gateway API has released **v1.5.0** with **breaking changes** that affect installation and upgrade procedures. This supersedes issue #832 which only tracked the v1.4.1 update.

**Current Pin**: `v1.4.0`  
**Latest Release**: `v1.5.0` (published 2026-02-16)  
**Upstream**: [kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api)

## Breaking Changes

### 1. TLSRoute API Changes
- **TLSRoute `v1alpha2` removed** from Experimental channel (graduated to Standard as `v1`)
- **TLSRoute CEL validation requires Kubernetes 1.31+**
- Impact: Any experimental TLSRoute usage will break

### 2. New ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
- Gateway API 1.5 introduces `safe-upgrades.gateway.networking.k8s.io` VAP that:
  - **Prevents installing Experimental CRDs after Standard CRDs are installed**
  - **Prevents downgrading to versions prior to 1.5**
- **Workaround**: Delete the VAP before performing these operations

### 3. Installation Method Change
- **Experimental channel CRDs are now too large for standard `kubectl apply`**
- **Required**: Use `kubectl apply --server-side=true`
- **Alternative**: Use [`kuberc`]((kubernetes.io/redacted) to make server-side apply the default

## Affected Files

- `guides/prereq/gateway-provider/install-gateway-provider-dependencies.sh` line 39:
  ```bash
  GATEWAY_API_CRD_REVISION=\$\{GATEWAY_API_CRD_REVISION:-"v1.4.0"}
  ```
  Needs `--server-side=true` flag added to kubectl apply

- `docs/upstream-versions.md` line 45: Update pin from v1.4.0 → v1.5.0

## Suggested Fix

1. Update `install-gateway-provider-dependencies.sh` line 43:
   ```bash
   kubectl $MODE -k https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/config/crd/\$\{GATEWAY_API_CRD_REF} --server-side=true || true
   ```

2. Update documentation and add warning about:
   - Kubernetes 1.31+ requirement for TLSRoute
   - One-way upgrade (cannot downgrade from v1.5.0)
   - Need for server-side apply

## Additional Context

### New Features (Graduated to Standard):
- Gateway Client Certificate validation (GEP-91, GEP-3567)
- Certificate selection for Gateway TLS origination (GEP-3155)
- ListenerSet support (GEP-1713)
- HTTPRoute CORS filter (GEP-1767)
- TLSRoute v1 (GEP-2643)
- ReferenceGrant → v1

### Dependency Updates:
- Kubernetes dependencies: k8s.io/* v0.34.1 → v0.35.1
- Envoy go-control-plane: v0.13.4 → v1.35.0
- controller-runtime: v0.22.1 → v0.23.1

## References

- **Release Notes**: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/tag/v1.5.0
- **Full Changelog**: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/compare/v1.4.1...v1.5.0
- **Current Usage**: `guides/prereq/gateway-provider/install-gateway-provider-dependencies.sh:39`

## Summary

vLLM has released **v0.16.0** with several **deprecations and removals** that may affect builds or runtime behavior. This supersedes issue #781 which only tracked to v0.15.1.

**Current Pin**: `1892993bc18e243e2c05841314c5e9c06a80c70d` (around v0.15.1)  
**Latest Release**: `v0.16.0` (published 2026-02-25)  
**Upstream**: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/releases/tag/v0.16.0

## Breaking Changes & Deprecations

The following features were **removed** in v0.16.0:

1. **BitBlas quantization** ([#32683](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/32683))
2. **Marlin 24** ([#32688](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/32688))
3. **`reasoning_content` message field** ([#33402](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/33402))
4. **Deprecated pooling items** ([#33477](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/33477))
5. **`VLLM_ALL2ALL_BACKEND` environment variable** ([#33535](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/33535))

The following feature was **deprecated**:

6. **IPEX for XPU** - switched to vllm-xpu-kernels ([#33379](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/33379))

## Impact Assessment

Checked llm-d codebase for usage of removed features:
````bash
grep -r "reasoning_content\|VLLM_ALL2ALL_BACKEND\|BitBlas\|Marlin.*24" \
  --include="*.py" --include="*.yaml" --include="*.yml" --include="*.md" --include="Dockerfile*"
````

**Result**: ✅ No usage detected in llm-d codebase

## New Features (Highlights)

- **Async scheduling + Pipeline Parallelism**: 30.8% E2E throughput improvement
- **Realtime API**: WebSocket-based streaming audio interactions
- **RLHF workflow improvements**: Native NCCL-based weight syncing
- **Unified Parallel Drafting** for speculative decoding
- **Major XPU platform overhaul**: vllm-xpu-kernels
- Many new model architectures and performance improvements

## Affected Files

- `docker/vllm-version` (line 2: `VLLM_COMMIT_SHA`)
- `docs/upstream-versions.md` (line 14: vLLM pin documentation)

## Recommendation

Update to v0.16.0 after testing. The removed features are not used by llm-d, so upgrade should be safe. Test thoroughly for:
- Disaggregated serving features (Mooncake, NIXL)
- EPLB functionality
- Performance regressions
- Quantization workflows (FP8, FP4)

## Related Issues

Supersedes #781 which only tracked to v0.15.1.

records.title: Migrate key guides to Kustomize-first (v2 overlays), update CI/CD, and switch defaults
records.body:
## Summary

Convert the following guides to the Kustomize-first modular installation architecture (as piloted by tiered-prefix-cache and wide-ep-lws), following the phased migration plan referenced by the parent tracking issue (#850):

- inference-scheduling
- pd-disaggregation
- simulated-accelerators
- workload-autoscaling
- precise-prefix-aware

This work should preserve the existing Helm-based guides during the transition, then switch the repo defaults to the Kustomize-first approach once CI/CD and benchmark tooling are migrated.

## Goals / Success Criteria

- Each target guide has a **Kustomize-based `v2`** implementation (side-by-side with existing guide, initially).
- CI/CD and any deployment validation for these guides uses **v2**.
- The repo documentation and guidance **switches to v2** as the default path.
- A separate tracking issue exists for converging on a **benchmark-oriented `deployer`** abstraction (to support parameter sweeps without reintroducing monolithic Helm complexity).

## Scope (per guide)

For **each** of the guides listed above:

### Phase 1 — Parallel Implementation (Side-by-Side)
- Implement a `v2` Kustomize overlay structure for the guide (keeping the classic/Helm flow intact).
- Ensure the guide composes cleanly with the modular layers (prereqs / primitives / well-lit paths / workload patterns).

### Phase 2 — Dependency Migration (CI/CD + Benchmarks)
- Update CI workflows and any benchmark pipelines to deploy and validate via the guide’s `v2` Kustomize manifests/overlays.
- Ensure deployments are reproducible and debuggable (manifests remain transparent; use Helm-generated patches only if needed for parameter sweeping).

### Phase 3 — Deprecation & Switch
- Mark Helm-based guide and templates as deprecated.
- Update docs to make `v2` the recommended/official approach.
- Ensure downstream references (README links, guide index, examples) are updated accordingly.

## Additional Notes / Context

- Motivation: reduce duplication and opacity from monolithic Helm charts; improve composability and readability; support measurable benchmarking by isolating variables.
- User feedback supports Kustomize-first modularization, with a request to keep docs navigable (modular code, potentially flatter documentation).
- Parent tracking issue: https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/issues/850

records.title: [Bug :bug:]: 7 nightlies fail - CUDA image missing
records.body:
### Contact Details

andy@clubanderson.com

### What happened?

All 7 nightly failures have the same root cause: ImagePullBackOff — the container image ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-cuda-dev:latest has no amd64/linux variant in its manifest.

  OCP error (pok-prod-01):

   Failed to pull image "ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-cuda-dev:latest":
   choosing an image from manifest list: no image found in manifest list
   for architecture "amd64", variant "", OS "linux"

  CKS error (CoreWeave):

   Failed to pull image "ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-cuda-dev:latest":
   rpc error: code = NotFound desc = no match for platform in manifest: not found

  Summary: The llm-d-cuda-dev:latest image was published without an amd64 variant (possibly only arm64, or the manifest was corrupted). Every nightly guide (IS, PD, PPC,
  WVA on OCP; IS, PD, WVA on CKS) uses IMAGE_OVERRIDE: ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-cuda-dev:latest, so they all hit the same ImagePullBackOff → pods stuck in Pending → timeout →
  failure. The WVA OCP run additionally shows orphan install.sh/sleep processes killed at cleanup, consistent with the deployment timing out.

  Fix: Someone needs to rebuild/republish the ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-cuda-dev:latest image with a proper linux/amd64 manifest entry.

records.title: [Upstream Update] NIXL 0.10.0 → 0.10.1
records.body:
## Summary

NIXL has released **0.10.1** (latest), which is a maintenance release focusing on improvements to Rust bindings, Python packaging, and testing infrastructure.

**Current Pin**: `0.10.0` (in `docker/Dockerfile.cuda` line 49)  
**Latest Release**: `0.10.1`  
**Upstream Repo**: https://github.com/ai-dynamo/nixl  
**Release Date**: 2026-03-03

## Changes in 0.10.1

### Rust Bindings
- **Runtime Library Resolution**: Introduced `libnixl_capi.so`, a shared library that exports `nixl_capi_*` C symbols
- Allows downstream consumers of the `nixl-sys` Rust crate to load NIXL at runtime without requiring build-time linking
- NIXL stubs rewritten to use `dlopen`/`dlsym` for lazy forwarding
- Added `libnixl.so` existence check in `build.rs` before attempting to link

### Python Packaging & Testing
- **Exact Version Pinning**: Pinned Python CUDA-specific dependencies (`nixl-cu12` and `nixl-cu13`) to exact versions in the `nixl` meta-package
- Prevents version mismatches and ensures consistent environments
- Added support for running Python tests with pre-created virtual environment (supports both standard `pip` and `uv pip`)

## Impact Assessment

**Priority**: MEDIUM  
**Breaking Changes**: None

This is a maintenance release with backward-compatible improvements. The changes focus on:
1. Better runtime library resolution for Rust bindings
2. Improved Python dependency management (exact version pinning)
3. Enhanced testing infrastructure

## Affected Files

- `docker/Dockerfile.cuda` line 49: `NIXL_VERSION="0.10.0"` → should be updated to `0.10.1`
- `docker/scripts/cuda/builder/build-nixl.sh`: Build script (no changes needed - compatible)

## Recommendation

Update NIXL pin to 0.10.1 when convenient. The exact version pinning for Python CUDA dependencies improves build reproducibility and prevents version mismatches.

- **Release Notes**: https://github.com/ai-dynamo/nixl/releases/tag/0.10.1

records.title: Adopt vLLM's --shutdown-timeout for graceful Model Service upgrades
records.body:
## Description

As of vllm-project/vllm#34730, `vllm serve` now has a `--shutdown-timeout` parameter that will be included in the v0.18.0 release.

llm-d should adopt this parameter for vLLM Model Service instances to ensure graceful shutdowns during upgrades.

## Proposal

1. **Add `--shutdown-timeout` to vLLM Model Service configuration**
   - Set the timeout to an appropriately long interval to allow most requests to complete
   - Make this configurable via helm charts

2. **Update pod `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`**
   - Set this value greater than the `--shutdown-timeout` value
   - Ensures Kubernetes doesn't force-kill the pod before vLLM's graceful shutdown completes

## Benefits

- Minimizes user traffic disruption during Model Service upgrades
- Allows in-flight requests to complete gracefully
- Provides operators with predictable upgrade behavior

## Implementation Notes

The relevant helm charts are in https://github.com/llm-d-incubation/llm-d-modelservice

## References

- vLLM PR: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/34730
- Available in: vLLM v0.18.0+

records.title: [CI] Refresh stale EC2 Wide EP workflow to match current wide-ep-lws guide
records.body:
## Summary

The EC2 Wide EP workflow in [`.github/workflows/e2e-wide-ep-accelerator-test.yaml`](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/blob/main/.github/workflows/e2e-wide-ep-accelerator-test.yaml) is still wired to an older `wide-ep-lws` layout and should be refreshed before adding support for additional self-installed inference gateways such as standalone `agentgateway`.

## Current problems

While reviving PR #421 / issue #399, I reviewed whether this workflow should be extended beyond Istio but it's stale:

- It still transforms `guides/wide-ep-lws/ms-wide-ep/values.yaml`, but that path no longer exists in the repo.
- It runs `helmfile apply -e ${GATEWAY_TYPE}` inside `guides/wide-ep-lws`, but the current `guides/wide-ep-lws` guide does not have a helmfile in that directory.
- It assumes an older modelservice/helmfile deployment shape instead of the current guide structure under `guides/wide-ep-lws/manifests/...`.
- The experimental DP-aware Wide EP guide still documents multi-port support as an Istio requirement today, so there is not yet a clear basis for claiming agentgateway support in this EC2 workflow.

## Recommendation

1. Rewrite the EC2 Wide EP workflow against the current `guides/wide-ep-lws` guide layout.
2. Decide whether the workflow should target the default `wide-ep-lws` guide, the `experimental-dp-aware` guide, or a dedicated CI overlay.
3. Rework the slim-transform logic so it patches files that actually exist in the current guide.
4. Only after the workflow is aligned with the current guide should we add `agentgateway` is support.

## References

- [`.github/workflows/e2e-wide-ep-accelerator-test.yaml`](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/blob/main/.github/workflows/e2e-wide-ep-accelerator-test.yaml)

records.title: Prevent GHCR auto-generated semver tags when pushing release candidate images
records.body:
## Problem

When pushing a release candidate (RC) git tag like `v0.6.0-rc.1`, the `ci-release.yaml` workflow triggers (matching `v*`) and builds container images tagged with the RC version. GHCR automatically parses semver-like image tags and generates additional package version entries. For example, pushing `v0.6.0-rc.1` causes GHCR to create:

| Auto-generated tag | Issue |
| ------------------ | ----- |
| `v0` | **Production tag** — should not be updated by an RC |
| `v0.6` | **Production tag** — should not be updated by an RC |
| `v0.6.0` | **Production tag** — should not be updated by an RC |
| `v0.6.0-rc` | Unintended — needs manual cleanup |
| `v0.6.0-rc.1` | The actual RC tag |

Additionally, the workflow unconditionally tags images as `latest`, so an RC build overwrites the current production `latest` tag.

This requires manual cleanup of both the auto-generated package versions and the `latest` tag after every dry-run, which is error-prone and could impact production users pulling `latest` or pinned semver tags.

## Proposed Options

### Option A: Use a non-semver git tag format for RCs

Instead of `v0.6.0-rc.1`, use a tag format that GHCR does not recognize as semver, such as:

- `rc-v0.6.0-1`
- `dev-0.6.0-rc1`
- `release-test-0.6.0-1`

The workflow trigger (`v*`) would need to be updated (or a new trigger pattern added) to also match the chosen RC format.

**Pros:**
- Solves both the GHCR auto-tag problem and the `latest` overwrite (if combined with a condition on `latest`)
- Simple conceptually

**Cons:**
- Needs empirical validation — GitHub does not clearly document the exact parsing logic GHCR uses for semver detection, so we need to test which formats avoid auto-tag generation
- Changes the established RC tag naming convention

**Validation needed:** Push a test image to a throwaway GHCR package with candidate tag formats and verify which ones avoid auto-generated semver versions.

### Option B: Decouple container image tags from the git tag for RCs

Keep the git tag as `v0.6.0-rc.1`, but change `ci-release.yaml` to detect RC tags and use a non-semver container image tag instead. For example:

- Git tag: `v0.6.0-rc.1` (triggers the workflow)
- Container image tag: `rc-v0.6.0-1` or `sha-<short>` (what actually gets pushed to GHCR)

This can be implemented by adding a step that transforms the tag:

```yaml
- name: Determine image tag
  id: image-tag
  run: |
    TAG="${{ github.ref_name }}"
    if [[ "$TAG" == *"-rc"* ]]; then
      # Transform to non-semver format for GHCR
      IMAGE_TAG="rc-${TAG}"
      IS_RC=true
    else
      IMAGE_TAG="$TAG"
      IS_RC=false
    fi
    echo "tag=${IMAGE_TAG}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
    echo "is_rc=${IS_RC}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
```

Then use `steps.image-tag.outputs.tag` for image tagging and skip `latest` when `is_rc == true`.

**Pros:**
- Git tag convention stays unchanged (`v0.6.0-rc.1`)
- Solves both the GHCR auto-tag and `latest` overwrite problems
- RC images are still built and pushed — the workflow still triggers

**Cons:**
- Adds conditional logic to the release workflow
- The resulting image tag (`rc-v0.6.0-rc.1`) still needs validation that GHCR won't parse it as semver

## Recommendation

Option B is the least disruptive since it preserves existing git tag conventions while solving the problem at the container image level. However, both options require testing to confirm which tag formats GHCR does not auto-parse as semver.

## Next Steps

1. Push test images with candidate tag formats to a throwaway GHCR package to validate GHCR behavior
2. Decide on an option based on test results
3. Update `ci-release.yaml` and `RELEASE.md` accordingly

records.title: Add post-release image verification step to ci-release workflow
records.body:
## Summary

After the latest release, we discovered that one container image was missing from the published set. This was only caught because a community member reported it on Slack. We should add an automated verification step to the `ci-release` workflow that confirms **all expected images exist in the registry** before considering a release complete, and optionally rebuilds any missing images.

## Problem

The current `ci-release.yaml` workflow builds and pushes 6 image families across multiple platforms:

| Image | Registry Path | Platforms |
|-------|--------------|-----------|
| CUDA (RHEL) | `ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-cuda` | amd64, arm64 |
| CUDA (Ubuntu) | `ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-cuda-ubuntu` | amd64, arm64 |
| AWS/EFA | `ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-aws` | amd64 |
| CPU | `ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-cpu` | amd64 |
| ROCm | `ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-rocm` | amd64 |
| XPU | `ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-xpu` | amd64 |
| HPU | `ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-hpu` | amd64 |

While individual build jobs have `success-check` gates and digest verification, there is **no single step at the end of the workflow that validates the complete set of expected images and tags are present in the registry**. If a job is skipped, silently fails, or a manifest push doesn't propagate, the release can be published incomplete.

## Proposal

Add a **`verify-release-images`** job at the end of the `ci-release` workflow that:

1. **Defines the expected image matrix** — a canonical list of all `image:tag` + platform combinations that constitute a complete release.
2. **Probes the registry** for each expected image/tag/platform using `docker buildx imagetools inspect` or `skopeo inspect` (or equivalent).
3. **Reports results** — outputs a summary table indicating which images were found and which are missing.
4. **Optionally triggers rebuilds** — if any images are missing, either:
   - (a) Fail the workflow with a clear error listing missing images, so the release team can re-trigger builds manually, **or**
   - (b) Automatically re-trigger the build jobs for just the missing images.

### Possible implementation sketch

```yaml
verify-release-images:
  name: Verify all release images exist
  needs:
    - release-cuda-manifest
    - release-aws-manifest
    - release-cpu-llm-d
    - release-rocm-llm-d
    - release-xpu-llm-d
    - release-hpu-llm-d
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  steps:
    - name: Verify images in registry
      run: |
        TAG="${{ github.event.release.tag_name }}"
        IMAGES=(
          "ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-cuda:${TAG}"
          "ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-cuda-ubuntu:${TAG}"
          "ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-aws:${TAG}"
          "ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-cpu:${TAG}"
          "ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-rocm:${TAG}"
          "ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-xpu:${TAG}"
          "ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-hpu:${TAG}"
        )
        MISSING=()
        for img in "${IMAGES[@]}"; do
          if ! docker buildx imagetools inspect "$img" > /dev/null 2>&1; then
            echo "MISSING: $img"
            MISSING+=("$img")
          else
            echo "OK: $img"
          fi
        done
        if [ ${#MISSING[@]} -gt 0 ]; then
          echo "::error::Missing ${#MISSING[@]} image(s) from release"
          exit 1
        fi
        echo "All release images verified successfully"
```

## Open questions for the release team

1. **Fail vs. auto-rebuild**: Should the verification step just fail the workflow (letting maintainers re-trigger manually), or should it automatically kick off builds for missing images?
2. **Scope of verification**: Should we verify just the release tag, or also `latest` and branch tags?
3. **Multi-arch manifest verification**: For CUDA images, should we also inspect individual platform manifests (amd64/arm64) or is verifying the combined manifest sufficient?
4. **Tooling preference**: `docker buildx imagetools inspect` vs `skopeo inspect` vs `crane` — any preference?
5. **Standalone workflow**: Would it be useful to also have this as a separate `workflow_dispatch` workflow that can be run on-demand against any release tag for auditing purposes?

## Additional context

- The existing `success-check` jobs use `if: always()` and check matrix job results, but they don't verify the image is actually *pullable* from the registry after push.
- The Trivy scanning jobs already depend on manifest creation, so verification could run in parallel with scanning.
- The `build-image.yml` reusable workflow has change-detection logic that could be adapted for selective rebuilds.

records.title: Proposal: Inference Resilience Operator (IRO): automated hardware fault recovery for wide-EP deployments
records.body:
# Inference Resilience Operator (IRO): automated hardware fault recovery for wide-EP deployments

## Request

We are proposing IRO as a new incubating component in the llm-d ecosystem.
We are seeking community review of this proposal and approval to begin development
under the llm-d-incubation org.

## Summary

Add a new Kubernetes-native component to llm-d - the Inference Resilience
Operator (IRO) - that automatically coordinates hardware fault events with the
inference engine, sequencing the right engine-side response and
infrastructure-side recovery action to minimize serving interruption and restore
full capacity without manual intervention.

## Motivation

Production llm-d deployments running wide Expert Parallelism across multiple
nodes face a class of hardware failures that no existing component handles
end-to-end. When a hardware fault occurs - an accelerator error, a NIC failure,
a kernel panic - two things must happen in a specific order: the inference engine
must be told to stop routing traffic to the affected rank and drain in-flight
requests, and the infrastructure layer must execute the appropriate recovery
action (reset the device, reboot the node, or replace the node entirely).

These two concerns are completely decoupled today. Infrastructure fault detection
agents can cordon and drain nodes but have no awareness of the inference engine
running on them. The inference engine detects internal failures and exposes
recovery APIs but has no awareness of what the infrastructure layer is doing. No
component coordinates between them.

The consequence is a choice between two bad outcomes: the engine crashes and the
entire instance restarts with minutes of full downtime and all in-flight requests
dropped, or an operator is paged to manually sequence the recovery steps.

Every vLLM fault tolerance RFC published in the past few months - [#27866](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/27866),
[#27774](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/27774), [#27908](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/27908), [#20323](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/20323), and [#28243](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/28243) - explicitly assumes an external orchestrator
will own this coordination. None of them build it. IRO is that component.

### Goals

- Automatically coordinate engine-side response and infrastructure-side recovery
  for hardware faults, without manual operator intervention.
- Match recovery action to fault severity - a transient device error must not
  trigger the same engine response as a node replacement.
- IRO's sole responsibility is engine coordination, with a strong sequencing
  guarantee: IRO acts on the engine before or in parallel with infrastructure
  recovery, and resumes the engine only once infrastructure recovery is confirmed
  complete. The sequencing contract between the two layers is the core value.
- The infrastructure recovery controller owns all fault-to-action mapping and
  operator override logic. IRO trusts the resolved action it receives.
- Restore full serving capacity automatically after infrastructure recovery
  completes.
- Work identically across GKE, EKS, bare-metal, and on-premises deployments.
- Work with any inference engine (initially focusing on vLLM) via swappable adapters.

### Non-Goals

- IRO does not perform fault detection. It consumes signals from existing
  infrastructure agents.
- IRO does not decide what recovery action to take for a given fault code, and
  does not provide an operator policy override mechanism. Both belong to the
  infrastructure recovery controller.
- IRO does not execute cloud-provider-specific recovery actions directly. It
  coordinates the engine while the infrastructure recovery controller executes
  the action.
- IRO does not handle planned node maintenance or lifecycle events in v1.
- IRO does not implement general cluster autoscaling. IRO scales the inference
  serving group only in response to hardware faults, never in response to load.

## Proposal

IRO sits between the infrastructure layer and the inference engine. When a
hardware fault occurs, the infrastructure recovery controller creates a
`RecoveryRequest` CRD carrying the resolved recovery action. IRO watches
`RecoveryRequest`, coordinates the engine-side response, and restores serving
capacity once infrastructure recovery completes.

The infrastructure recovery controller owns the fault-to-action mapping and all
operator override logic. IRO trusts `requestedAction` on `RecoveryRequest` as
the final resolved decision.

Engine recovery tracks are determined entirely by `requestedAction`:

- **RESET_DEVICE → Track A**: pause engine, reset device, resume engine (seconds)
- **REBOOT_NODE → Track B**: pause engine, reboot node, resume engine (minutes).
  For long reboots where serving at reduced capacity is preferable, operators can
  configure the infrastructure recovery controller to use REPLACE_NODE instead.
- **REPLACE_NODE → Track C**: pause engine, scale down, replace node, scale up
  (many minutes; serves at reduced capacity during replacement)

All engine-specific logic is encapsulated in swappable `EngineAdapter`
implementations. The vLLM adapter is the initial implementation, targeting the
fault tolerance and elastic EP APIs being developed in RFC #27866 / PR #34833,
RFC #28243, and RFC #20323.

### User Stories

#### As an inference platform team running wide-EP in production

I can trust that when a single node in my serving group experiences a hardware
fault, IRO will automatically coordinate with the inference engine, trigger the
appropriate infrastructure recovery action, and restore full capacity once
recovery completes - without my team being paged or manually intervening.

#### As an infrastructure provider or cloud vendor

I can integrate my fault detection agent with llm-d by writing an infrastructure
recovery controller that creates `RecoveryRequest` CRDs, populating `errorCode`
and `requestedAction` based on my hardware knowledge and any operator-configured
overrides. My controller does not need to know which inference engine is running
or call any engine-specific API - IRO handles that entirely.

#### As an inference engine team

I can integrate with IRO by implementing the published `EngineAdapter` interface,
without modifying IRO's core recovery logic. My engine's specific API surface is
entirely encapsulated in the adapter.

## Design Details

### CRD

IRO is defined by one CRD. The infrastructure recovery controller creates
`RecoveryRequest` when it detects a hardware fault on a node running an inference
workload. IRO watches it, coordinates engine recovery, and tracks infrastructure
recovery completion via it.

**RecoveryRequest** (created by infrastructure recovery controller, consumed by IRO):

- `nodeName`
- `deviceID` (optional)
- `errorCode` (optional, carried for observability — IRO does not interpret it)
- `requestedAction` (RESET_DEVICE | REBOOT_NODE | REPLACE_NODE — resolved by the
  infrastructure recovery controller before creation)
- `status.phase` (Pending | InProgress | Completed | Failed — written by the
  infrastructure recovery controller; IRO watches for Completed to resume the engine)
- `status.conditions[EngineReadyForRecovery]` — optional; see open question below

### EngineAdapter interface

The interface exposes operations such as `PauseEngine`, `ResumeEngine`,
`ScaleDown(new_world_size)`, `ScaleUp(new_world_size)`, `FaultEvents`, and
`EngineStatus`, mapped to the fault tolerance and elastic EP APIs being developed
in the vLLM RFCs (PR #34833, RFC #28243, RFC #20323). The exact operations and
their mapping to engine APIs are subject to refinement as those APIs stabilize.

### Dual input channels

IRO receives fault signals from two independent directions with distinct,
non-overlapping responsibilities:

- **RecoveryRequest** (infrastructure-initiated) — the primary input channel. IRO
  coordinates the full engine recovery sequence: pause engine, coordinate with
  infrastructure recovery, then resume or scale up the engine once
  `RecoveryRequest.status.phase` reaches Completed.
- **Engine fault events via ZMQ** (engine-initiated) - when the engine's internal
  fault monitoring pushes a fault notification with no corresponding
  `RecoveryRequest`, the fault is treated as transient and engine-internal. IRO
  tells the engine to retry without triggering any infrastructure recovery action.

### Open question: should infrastructure recovery gate on IRO?

The `EngineReadyForRecovery` condition on `RecoveryRequest` is designed to be
**optional**. This is the key open design question.

**Without gating** - the infrastructure recovery controller creates
`RecoveryRequest` and immediately proceeds with the recovery action. IRO
independently watches `RecoveryRequest`, pauses the engine on the remaining
healthy ranks, and resumes once phase reaches Completed. Because PauseEngine and
ScaleDown only need to talk to the surviving ranks, IRO can act in parallel with
infrastructure recovery even if the faulted chip is already gone. This is simpler
and has no coordination overhead.

**With gating** - the infrastructure recovery controller creates `RecoveryRequest`
with `EngineReadyForRecovery: False` and waits for IRO to set it to True before
acting. This provides a stronger guarantee: the engine is in a clean paused state
before the chip is touched. This may be required if vLLM cannot handle a rank
disappearing mid-collective without hanging.

**The deciding factor** is vLLM's behavior when a rank disappears suddenly: if
PR #34833's internal fault detection catches and handles a sudden rank loss
gracefully (pausing the remaining ranks automatically), gating adds overhead for
no benefit. If vLLM hangs waiting for the dead rank until IRO intervenes, gating
is necessary.

We will be seeking input from the vLLM team on this before finalizing the
coordination contract. The `RecoveryRequest` CRD is designed to support both
models - the condition is present if the infrastructure recovery controller opts
in to gating, absent if not.

For more details, please refer to the [WIP design doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1q4V2CcWMSrufy5LJE_Fv49kwCoFoPSTrBrrayzNxRqY/edit?usp=sharing).

## Alternatives

### Extend an existing infrastructure agent

Infrastructure agents have hardware domain knowledge but no inference engine
awareness. Adding engine coordination to an agent would create a reverse
dependency - infrastructure code depending on inference engine APIs - and would
need to be duplicated per cloud provider. The coordination layer should be
cloud-agnostic and engine-agnostic by construction.

### Build recovery logic into the inference engine (vLLM)

Each vLLM fault tolerance RFC explicitly defers recovery orchestration to an
external orchestrator. Adding recovery logic into vLLM itself would tightly
couple hardware recovery to a specific engine, making it unavailable for other
engines and requiring infrastructure knowledge to live in the model server.

### Extend other existing controllers (such as LWS)

LWS is responsible for pod group lifecycle - creating, scheduling, and restarting
groups of pods as a unit. Adding IRO's responsibilities to LWS would conflate pod
lifecycle management with inference engine coordination in a single component, and
would require LWS to grow awareness of hardware fault signals and engine-specific
APIs. IRO instead treats LWS as one actuation target it coordinates alongside the
other layers.

records.title: [Docs]: Rename Envoy proxy references
records.body:
"Envoy" or "Envoy proxy" is used throughout the project documentation and should be updated:

1. The GAIE EPP protocol spec is based on Envoy ext-proc and not Envoy proxy.
2. Non-Envoy implementations such as agentgateway conform to the EPP protocol spec and are supported by llm-d.

A more abstract representation should be used such as:

1. Inference Gateway
2. proxy
3. others?
records.author: danehans

records.title: Add more cases to the inference-scheduling well lit path
records.body:
The default inference-scheduling well lit path's [benchmark](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/tree/main/guides/inference-scheduling#benchmarking) is intentionally crafted to show a substantial benefit in prefix aware routing. 

While this is great, it may not be indicative of a more reasonable, production workload. To support this, we should add additional benchmarks to the well lit path, as well as their outputs.

We should consider adding test case(s) for:

- The hot-node, sticky node problem. Which can be briefly described as: In a workload with a single, large prefix-match, routing can be too sticky, and cause a single 'hot' model server, leaving the other servers idle, which can result in worse performance than a standard L4 load balancer
- A benchmark with a smaller ISL, but still high prefix match, to show the benefit of prefix exists in less extreme cases also
- A decode heavy benchmark; this should have less benefit than the prefill benchmarks will, but should still be showcased as this is a valid usecase

Not all of these benchmarks need to be implemented, but our current single benchmark data can provide a skewed view of the benefits of inference scheduling

records.title: [Feature]: Make Standalone mode the default for inference-scheduler
records.body:
### Feature Area

Inference Scheduling

### Problem Statement

Not all users are necessarily accustomed to everything k8s, while most know how to deploy simple things on k8s, advanced features like Gateway is a friction point. 



### Proposed Solution

We should make [the standalone deployment mode](https://gateway-api-inference-extension.sigs.k8s.io/guides/standalone/) the default for llm-d docs; the gateway-based ones (GKE, Istio etc.) are advanced options.

For production deployments, llm-d should recommend the gateway mode; the inference-scheduler offers this native integration with Gateway which differentiates it compared to other solutions like smg, sglang-router, vllm-router or even dynamo (though they are trying to address that).

### What happened?

The `Inter-Token Latency` (ITL) panel in the `llm-d Performance Dashboard` is blank because it still queries the deprecated vLLM metric `vllm:time_per_output_token_seconds_bucket`.

This appears to affect both `v0.6.0` and `main`.

### What did you expect to happen?

The `Inter-Token Latency` panel in the `llm-d Performance Dashboard` should render data using the current vLLM metric name.

```shell
histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(vllm:time_per_output_token_seconds_bucket{namespace=~"llmd-is"}[5m]))

{"status":"success","data":{"resultType":"vector","result":[]}}

Working query:
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by(le) (rate(vllm:inter_token_latency_seconds_bucket{namespace=~"llmd-is"}[5m])))
```

records.title: Add UCCL to docker image
records.body:
Currently, The [Docker](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/blob/main/docker/Dockerfile.cuda) images contain UCX and NIXL build. 

Would be great to add [UCCL](https://github.com/uccl-project/uccl) transport built-in to the docker images so that vllm's NIXL Connector can be launched with UCCL backend to support efficient RDMA/TCP/TCP-X transfers.

Example Usage: 
```
    vllm serve <MODEL> \
      --port <PORT> \
      --tensor-parallel-size <TP_SIZE> \
      --enforce-eager \
      --block-size <BLOCK_SIZE> \
      --kv-transfer-config \
        '{"kv_connector":"NixlConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":
        {"backends":["UCCL"]}}'
```

Refer to UCCL NIXL Support roadmap [here](https://github.com/praveingk/nixl/tree/uccl-local-xfer/src/plugins/uccl)

records.title: [Feature]: Capture GenAI prompts and completions as events or attributes
records.body:
### Feature Area

Observability / Monitoring

### Problem Statement

llm-d supports distributed tracing: https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/blob/main/docs/monitoring/tracing/README.md but tracing now only provides limited information (latency,  span attributes and resource attributes). We can unblock more with logs && traces correlation like embedding the prompts and responses from model into the trace span.

Current trace structure lacks the support for supporting large texts or multimodal prompts and responses. OpenTelemetry community has a discussion about it and already sets up semantic convention for placing prompts and responses as events and store them into a bucket: https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions/issues/2010

This feature request aims to start the discussion of whether llm-d would like to adding this support to extract all prompts and response processed by the llm-d stack.

### Proposed Solution

It will capture the input && output passing through llm-d stack, and upload them to a backend storage (e.g. GCS bucket). The trace span will have an attribute that links to the object storing the input && output. It provides reference to input && output from the model, which can later be used by evaluation or other purposes.

records.title: Switch to consuming upstream images instead of building our own
records.body:
## Context

We currently build and maintain 5 device-specific container images (`llm-d-cuda`, `llm-d-rocm`, `llm-d-xpu`, `llm-d-cpu`, `llm-d-hpu`) plus an `llm-d-rdma-tools` diagnostic image. This involves ~6 Dockerfiles, ~15 build scripts, NVSHMEM patches, constraint files, and ~2,500 lines of CI workflows — all layering customizations on top of upstream vLLM.

The maintenance cost is significant and growing. Many of the customizations we carry (NIXL, DeepEP, FlashInfer, etc.) are being upstreamed into vLLM. We should stop building these images and consume upstream vLLM images directly.

## Scope of changes

### 1. Inventory what our images add over upstream

Before removing anything, we need a clear picture of what upstream vLLM images already include vs. what we add. Current customizations by category:

| Customization | Devices | Upstream status |
|---|---|---|
| NVSHMEM (with CoreWeave/RoCE patches) | CUDA | Not in upstream images |
| DeepEP, DeepGEMM, FlashInfer wheels | CUDA | FlashInfer in upstream; DeepEP/DeepGEMM not yet |
| GDRCopy + custom UCX | CUDA, ROCm | Not in upstream |
| llm-d-kv-cache offloading connector | CUDA, CPU | llm-d-specific, never upstream |
| NIXL / RIXL | CUDA, ROCm, CPU, HPU | Being upstreamed into vLLM |
| LMCache + InfiniStore | CUDA | Not in upstream |
| EFA (AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter) | CUDA | Not in upstream |
| OTEL tracing packages | All | Not in upstream |
| RHEL UBI9 base | CUDA | Upstream is Ubuntu only |
| Debug builds (NVSHMEM logging) | CUDA | Not in upstream |
| tcmalloc LD_PRELOAD | CPU | Not in upstream |
| Custom vllm-gaudi plugin wiring | HPU | Separate upstream image exists |

### 2. Decide on a strategy for llm-d-specific components

Components that will never be upstream (primarily the `llm-d-kv-cache` offloading connector) need an alternative delivery mechanism:

- [ ] **Option A**: Thin addon layer — a minimal `FROM vllm/vllm-openai:vX.Y` Dockerfile that only adds llm-d-specific bits
- [ ] **Option B**: Init container that pip-installs wheels at pod startup
- [ ] **Option C**: Volume-mounted plugin directory

Trade-offs: Option A still requires image builds but dramatically reduces scope. Options B/C add cold-start latency.

### 3. Track upstream inclusion of key components

Before we can drop our images, we need these to land in upstream vLLM images (or decide we can live without them):

- [ ] NIXL — track upstream vLLM inclusion
- [ ] DeepEP — track upstream vLLM inclusion
- [ ] DeepGEMM — track upstream vLLM inclusion
- [ ] NVSHMEM patches — contribute upstream or to vLLM image build
- [ ] LMCache / InfiniStore — track upstream vLLM inclusion
- [ ] OTEL tracing packages — propose as optional layer or accept runtime install

### 4. Start with XPU (zero-risk)

XPU already uses the upstream Dockerfile as-is (fetched via `make xpu-prepare`). This is the easiest starting point:

- [ ] Update XPU guide manifests to reference upstream `vllm/vllm-openai` directly
- [ ] Remove XPU-specific build logic from Makefile (`xpu-prepare` target)
- [ ] Remove XPU jobs from `build-image.yml` and `ci-release.yaml`
- [ ] Update E2E workflows (`e2e-inference-scheduling-xpu.yaml`, `e2e-pd-xpu.yaml`, `e2e-prefix-cache-xpu.yaml`)

### 5. Remove Dockerfiles and build scripts

Once upstream images cover our needs (per device):

- [ ] `docker/Dockerfile.cuda` (527 lines)
- [ ] `docker/Dockerfile.cpu` (157 lines)
- [ ] `docker/Dockerfile.rocm` (158 lines)
- [ ] `docker/Dockerfile.hpu` (84 lines)
- [ ] `docker/Dockerfile.rdma-tools` (124 lines)
- [ ] `docker/scripts/` (entire directory — 15+ build scripts)
- [ ] `docker/packages/` (constraint files, RPM caches)
- [ ] `docker/build-constraints.txt`, `docker/constraints.txt`
- [ ] `patches/` (4 NVSHMEM patches)
- [ ] `docker/common-versions`

### 6. Remove or simplify CI workflows

- [ ] `.github/workflows/build-image.yml` (~1,474 lines) — remove or reduce to addon-layer-only
- [ ] `.github/workflows/nightly-build-image.yaml` — remove
- [ ] `.github/workflows/ci-release.yaml` (~1,000+ lines) — remove image-build jobs, keep non-image release steps

### 7. Simplify the Makefile

Remove image-build targets: `image-build`, `image-push`, `image-retag`, `buildah-build`, `xpu-prepare`, and related variables/checks.

### 8. Update all image references (65 files)

All guides, deployment manifests, benchmark templates, and E2E workflows reference `ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-{device}:vX.Y.Z`. These need updating to point to upstream image names.

**Guides** (~30 values files):
- `guides/pd-disaggregation/ms-pd/values*.yaml`
- `guides/inference-scheduling/ms-inference-scheduling/values*.yaml`
- `guides/precise-prefix-cache-aware/ms-kv-events/values*.yaml`
- `guides/tiered-prefix-cache/cpu/manifests/`
- `guides/wide-ep-lws/manifests/`
- `guides/simulated-accelerators/`
- `guides/workload-autoscaling/`
- `guides/benchmark/`

**E2E / CI workflows** (~20 files):
- `nightly-e2e-*.yaml` workflows
- `e2e-*.yaml` workflows

**Docs**:
- `RELEASE.md`
- `docs/infra-providers/digitalocean/README.md`
- `guides/simulated-accelerators/README.md`

### 9. Validate E2E tests still pass

- [ ] Audit which E2E tests depend on packages only present in our custom images
- [ ] Update test assumptions or add runtime-install steps as needed

## Risks to track

- **RHEL/UBI base**: Upstream vLLM only provides Ubuntu. If users/partners require RHEL-based images (OpenShift), we need an alternative path.
- **Version pinning**: We currently pin exact commits of vLLM + kernel libraries together. With upstream images, we lose control over which versions ship together — need a compatibility matrix.
- **NVSHMEM patches**: These fix real infrastructure bugs (RoCE device creation on certain kernels). If not accepted upstream, P/D disaggregation breaks on affected hardware.
- **Cold-start latency**: Runtime-installed components add startup time, which matters for autoscaling.

## Suggested execution order

1. **XPU** — already upstream, zero risk
2. **HPU** — upstream `vllm-gaudi` image exists, minimal delta
3. **ROCm** — upstream `vllm-openai-rocm` exists, main delta is RIXL/UCX
4. **CPU** — small image, few customizations
5. **CUDA** — most complex, most customizations, do last

cc @llm-d/maintainers

records.title: Guided llm-d install missions in KubeStellar Console
records.body:
We built guided install missions for llm-d inside [KubeStellar Console](https://console.kubestellar.io?utm_source=github&utm_medium=issue&utm_campaign=cncf_outreach&utm_term=llm-d), a standalone Kubernetes dashboard (unrelated to legacy kubestellar/kubestellar, kubeflex, or OCM — zero shared code).

→ **[Browse the llm-d mission catalog](https://console.kubestellar.io/missions?tag=llm-d&utm_source=github&utm_medium=issue&utm_campaign=cncf_outreach&utm_term=llm-d)**

### What the missions do

The Console ships nine specialized install missions covering llm-d's well-lit paths — single-node, disaggregated prefill/decode, tensor parallelism, and the companion Inference Scheduler. Each mission runs against your live cluster via kubeconfig, checks prerequisites, applies the corresponding manifests or Helm chart, validates pod readiness and CRD registration, and ships a rollback path.

### Why we're reaching out

llm-d is part of the Console's broader local-LLM strategy, which covers Ollama (dev), llama.cpp (minimal), LocalAI (CPU-first), vLLM (GPU throughput), Red Hat AI Inference Server (OpenShift enterprise), LM Studio (workstation GUI), and Open WebUI (frontend). llm-d slots in as the \"multi-node inference scheduling\" option for operators running GPU clusters at scale. See the [Local LLM Strategy](https://docs.kubestellar.io/console/local-llm-strategy?utm_source=github&utm_medium=issue&utm_campaign=cncf_outreach&utm_term=llm-d) docs page for the full decision matrix.

Separately, the Console's [workload-variant-autoscaler nightly E2E harness](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-infra?utm_source=github&utm_medium=issue&utm_campaign=cncf_outreach&utm_term=llm-d) is already wired into llm-d-infra and has been running since 2026-03. This issue is about the install-mission surface, which is a separate touchpoint.

### Install

Local (connects to your current kubeconfig context):
```bash
curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubestellar/console/main/start.sh | bash
```

Deploy into a cluster:
```bash
curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubestellar/console/main/deploy.sh | bash
```

---

Mission definitions are open source — PRs welcome at [fixes/llm-d/](https://github.com/kubestellar/console-kb/tree/master/fixes/llm-d?utm_source=github&utm_medium=issue&utm_campaign=cncf_outreach&utm_term=llm-d). Feel free to close if not relevant.

records.title: [Feature]: Check Validity of a Shared Multimedia and Model Download Service
records.body:
### Feature Area

Other

### Problem Statement

**Description**
Currently, the llm-d ecosystem lacks a centralized mechanism for handling external assets. As we move toward complex multi-modal benchmarks (e.g., Qwen-VL with multiple images) and larger model deployments, individual components are redundantly downloading the same content, leading to inefficiencies.

**Why is this needed**:

- Centralized Caching: To prevent unnecessary network traffic by caching frequently accessed assets.
- Protocol Support: To provide native support for both http:// and https:// endpoints.
- Performance Optimization: To improve Time to First Token (TTFT) by ensuring multimedia content is cached locally before the inference request reaches the engine.


### Proposed Solution

**What would you like to be added**:
I propose the implementation of a Shared Download Service, as an **optional** component. This service will act as a centralized gateway for fetching and caching multimedia content (images and videos) and, optionally, model weights.

**Suggested implementation**:
The proposed solution is to deploy an existing open-source forward proxy (such as Squid) as a local service. We can leverage the fact that vLLM’s download logic relies on the Python requests library, which natively supports standard environment variables like `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, and `NO_PROXY`. By configuring these variables, the caching layer remains transparent to vLLM, allowing us to implement centralized caching with zero code changes to the inference engine itself.

### Alternatives Considered

_No response_

### Willingness to Contribute

Yes, I can submit a PR

### Additional Context

_No response_

records.title: [Bug :bug:]: Automatic PD path does not produce effective PD header / KV reuse in v0.7.1, while manual PD data plane works
records.body:
### Contact Details

wukehu3@gmail.com

### What happened?

# llm-d automatic PD path does not produce effective PD header / KV reuse in `v0.7.1`, while manual PD data plane works

## Summary

We verified that the `llm-d + vLLM + PD` data plane is healthy, but the automatic
`Gateway -> Envoy ext_proc -> EPP -> header mutation -> decode sidecar` path is
still failing.

Manual PD verification passes consistently when `x-prefiller-host-port` is
injected directly into the decode sidecar request:

- `delta_queries > 0`
- `delta_hits > 0`
- `delta_external_kv_tokens > 0`

Automatic Gateway path still fails:

- `delta_queries > 0`
- `delta_hits = 0`
- `delta_external_kv_tokens = 0`

The remaining failure point appears to be inside **EPP request-level processing /
header generation / ext_proc response handling**, rather than in Gateway wiring
or the vLLM/NIXL data plane.

## Environment

- Framework: `llm-d`
- Runtime: `vLLM`
- PD mode: prefill/decode disaggregated serving
- EPP image: `ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-inference-scheduler:v0.7.1`
- Routing sidecar image: `ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-routing-sidecar:v0.7.1`
- Gateway ext_proc: Envoy self-managed gateway
- Upstream repo release context:
  - `llm-d/llm-d` release `v0.6.0` lists:
    - `llm-d-inference-scheduler v0.7.1`
    - `llm-d-routing-sidecar v0.7.1`
    - `vllm-project/vllm v0.17.1`

## Why We Believe This Is Not Just Outdated Configuration

We checked the current docs / repo direction and aligned with it:

- Current docs describe all disaggregation topologies as driven by the unified
  `disagg-profile-handler`.
- The docs PR in `llm-d/llm-d` also explicitly replaces:
  - `pd-profile-handler` -> `disagg-profile-handler`
  - `prefill-header-handler` -> `disagg-headers-handler`
- `llm-d-inference-scheduler` PRs also describe:
  - PR `#732`: unified disaggregation handler
  - PR `#758`: combined header handler with legacy alias compatibility
  - PR `#756`: prevent mismatch between new and deprecated APIs

So we tested both:

1. older/deprecated-compatible PD handler chain
2. newer `disagg-*` handler chain

and both still failed on the automatic path in our environment.

## What We Verified

### 1. Manual PD data plane works

Directly sending a request to the decode sidecar with
`x-prefiller-host-port=<prefill-pod-ip>:8001` succeeds.

Observed successful signal:

- `vllm:external_prefix_cache_queries_total` increases
- `vllm:external_prefix_cache_hits_total` increases
- `vllm:prompt_tokens_by_source_total{source="external_kv_transfer"}` increases

This confirms:

- decode sidecar accepts the PD header
- prefill/decode pods can perform KV transfer
- vLLM/NIXL/routing-sidecar data plane is functional

### 2. Gateway live ext_proc config is correct

Verified from live Envoy `config_dump`:

- `envoy.filters.http.ext_proc` is present
- `request_body_mode: BUFFERED`
- `failure_mode_allow: true`
- `allow_all_routing: true`
- `allow_envoy: true`

We tested both:

- `message_timeout: 10s`
- `message_timeout: 30s`

In both cases, automatic PD still failed.

### 3. EPP receives the request

EPP logs show the request arrives with the forwarded request id:

```text
{"msg":"EPP received request","x-request-id":"pd-auto-..."}
```

### 4. Pool and backend discovery look healthy

Verified:

- route pool and scheduler pool are both created
- route pool selects decode on port `8000`
- scheduler pool selects both prefill and decode on port `8001`
- Services, Endpoints, and EndpointSlices exist for both prefill and decode
- EPP metrics report:
  - `inference_pool_ready_pods{name="...-scheduler-pool"} 2`
  - queue metrics for both prefill and decode pods

### 5. Envoy waits for EPP and times out

Observed from Envoy live stats:

- `http.ingress_http.ext_proc.message_timeouts` increases
- `http.ingress_http.ext_proc.failure_mode_allowed` increases
- `http.ingress_http.ext_proc.rejected_header_mutations = 0`
- `http.ingress_http.ext_proc.http_not_ok_resp_received = 0`

This strongly suggests:

- Envoy is successfully talking to EPP
- EPP is not returning a usable ext_proc response before timeout
- Envoy then allows the request through due to `failure_mode_allow`

## Experiments We Already Ran

### A. Deprecated-compatible PD chain

We tested an EPP chain equivalent to the older PD configuration style:

- `prefill-header-handler`
- `prefix-based-pd-decider`
- `pd-profile-handler(primaryPort: 0)`

Result:

- manual path: pass
- automatic path: fail
- Envoy `message_timeouts` and `failure_mode_allowed` both increase

### B. New unified disaggregation chain

We then switched to the newer docs-aligned chain:

- `disagg-headers-handler`
- `prefix-based-pd-decider`
- `disagg-profile-handler`

Result:

- manual path: pass
- automatic path: fail
- Envoy `message_timeouts` and `failure_mode_allowed` both increase
- EPP still logs only request receipt

### C. Partial `v0.6.0` rollback experiment

We also tested keeping the routing sidecar on `v0.7.1` while downgrading only
the EPP / ext_proc image to `v0.6.0`.

Result:

- deployment succeeded
- automatic path still failed with the same timeout / failure-mode pattern

This is why we are not currently treating this as a simple “`v0.7.1` only”
regression.

## Minimal Reproduction

### Passing manual control

Send a request directly to the decode sidecar with:

```http
x-prefiller-host-port: <prefill-pod-ip>:8001
```

Result:

- external prefix cache queries increase
- external prefix cache hits increase
- external KV transfer tokens increase

### Failing automatic path

Send the same request through Gateway with ext_proc enabled.

Result:

- request returns `200`
- EPP logs `EPP received request`
- Envoy ext_proc `message_timeouts` increments
- `failure_mode_allowed` increments
- no external KV hit/token growth is observed

## Expected Behavior

For a valid automatic PD request routed through Gateway:

- EPP should complete request-level processing
- Envoy should receive a valid ext_proc mutation response
- decode sidecar should receive effective PD routing information such as
  `x-prefiller-host-port`
- external KV hits and transferred KV tokens should increase

## Actual Behavior

Even with:

- correct pool wiring
- correct EndpointSlices
- correct live Envoy ext_proc config
- healthy EPP pod
- healthy manual PD data plane
- `message_timeout` increased from `10s` to `30s`

the automatic path still times out waiting for EPP and falls back through
`failure_mode_allow`.

## Current Assessment

The issue appears to be inside the EPP request-level processing path, likely in
the request-scoped PD decision/profile/header generation flow, or in the
ext_proc response returned to Envoy, rather than in:

- Gateway ext_proc attachment
- Kubernetes Services/Endpoints/EndpointSlices
- pod label selection
- Envoy header mutation policy
- decode sidecar / vLLM / NIXL data plane

## Useful Evidence

- Manual PD path: pass
- Automatic PD path: fail
- EPP sees request: yes
- EPP sees scheduler pool ready pods: yes
- Envoy mutation rejection: no
- Envoy ext_proc timeout: yes
- Raising timeout to `30s`: still fails
- `disagg-*` chain tested: yes, still fails
- EPP-only `v0.6.0` rollback tested: yes, still fails

## Question

Are there known cases in this component combination where EPP:

- receives the ext_proc request,
- sees the scheduler pool and ready pods,
- but does not return a request-level ext_proc response in time for PD header
  injection?

More specifically:

1. Are there additional prerequisites beyond the published `EndpointPickerConfig`
   examples that are required for automatic `x-prefiller-host-port` injection?
2. Is there a known issue where `disagg-profile-handler` / `disagg-headers-handler`
   succeeds logically but the ext_proc response is not returned or not applied in time?
3. Is there a required version matrix across:
   - `llm-d-inference-scheduler`
   - `llm-d-routing-sidecar`
   - Gateway / GIE / Gateway provider
   - vLLM runtime packaging
   that is stricter than what is implied by the top-level release summary?
4. Is there any recommended way to log or trace the exact generated header
   mutations for a single request in `v0.7.1`?

## References

- llm-d release summary:
  - https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/releases
- P/D disaggregation guide:
  - https://llm-d.ai/docs/guide/Installation/pd-disaggregation
- Disaggregation architecture docs:
  - https://llm-d.ai/docs/architecture/Components/disagg_prefill-decode
- llm-d docs deprecation tracking:
  - https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/issues/1155
  - https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/pull/1170
- llm-d-inference-scheduler PRs:
  - https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-inference-scheduler/pull/732
  - https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-inference-scheduler/pull/758
  - https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-inference-scheduler/pull/756


### Version

records.title: [bugfix] Fixing CI to build from forks
records.body:
The issue is that we had support for both Opening PRs from an upstream branch (eg: `llm-d:feature-a` --> `llm-d:main`) as well as from forks, with the default being upstream branches. This meant that we needed to give everyone permissions to push to the repo, and more generally this is not a good way to do things. This compatibility for both required that we did builds, would be that we have to find the version of the action that got ran from upstream rather than from the fork, and then re-run it every time (it does not pickup synchronization changes). This is a big issue

What we should do: Drop support for building from upstream branches. Make everything build from forks and scope permissions appropriately

records.title: Validate llm-d with shared storage across multiple vendors
records.body:
## Summary

Validate and document llm-d running with shared storage across multiple vendors. The [tiered prefix cache storage guide](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/blob/main/guides/tiered-prefix-cache/storage/README.md) shows how to connect a storage connector (llm-d FS / LMCache) to a shared POSIX volume, but today only covers **GCP Lustre** as a concrete backend. We want to guide how llm-d works on other POSIX-backed storage systems, surface any implementation gaps, and extend the guide with a path per backend. Beyond functional validation, each backend should be configured for high-bandwidth access so the storage can sustain the throughput required for KV-cache reuse 

## Backends

- [ ] GCP Lustre - [existing guide](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/blob/main/guides/tiered-prefix-cache/storage/manifests/backends/lustre/README.md)
- [ ] IBM Storage Scale
- [ ] Azure
- [ ] AWS 
- [ ] VAST
- [ ] CephFS

## Scope per backend

- Provisioning (StorageClass / CSI) + RWX PVC.
- High-performance configuration for storage to sustain KV-cache reuse bandwidth.
- Smoke test: KV blocks written and reused across vLLM pods.
- Short TTFT + throughput benchmark.
- File any llm-d implementation issues uncovered during bring-up.

records.title: [Bug]: llm-d-cuda:v0.6.0 DeepGEMM FP8 JIT crash on H100 — works in upstream vllm/vllm-openai:v0.17.1
records.body:
## Describe the bug

The `ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-cuda:v0.6.0` image crashes with a DeepGEMM JIT kernel assertion error when serving FP8 quantized models on NVIDIA H100 GPUs. The same vLLM version (v0.17.1) from the upstream `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.17.1` image works without issues on identical hardware and configuration.

Both prefill (TP=1) and decode (TP=4) pods crash with the same error during the profiling/warmup phase after model weights are loaded successfully.

## vLLM CLI args

```
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-32B-FP8 \
  --port 8200 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --block-size 128 \
  --max-model-len 32000 \
  --served-model-name Qwen/Qwen3-32B-FP8 \
  --disable-uvicorn-access-log \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"NixlConnector", "kv_role":"kv_both"}'
```

## Error trace

The crash occurs during `profile_run()` → `_dummy_run()` when the compiled model graph invokes DeepGEMM's FP8 GEMM kernel:

```
(Worker_TP0 pid=749) ERROR [multiproc_executor.py:880] WorkerProc hit an exception.
  ...
  File "vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py", line 390, in determine_available_memory
    self.model_runner.profile_run()
  File "vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py", line 5308, in profile_run
    hidden_states, last_hidden_states = self._dummy_run(...)
  ...
  File "vllm/compilation/piecewise_backend.py", line 343, in __call__
    return range_entry.runnable(*args)
  ...
  File "/torch-compile-cache/.../c6noqaysmlhazjh2sxpvvi5uhyftbcznzuq3w2xpccunzmcsrmmr.py", line 1058, in call
    buf5 = torch.ops.vllm.flashinfer_fp8_blockscale_gemm.default(buf4, arg4_1, arg5_1, 128, True)
  File "vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/utils/fp8_utils.py", line 315, in _flashinfer_fp8_blockscale_gemm_impl
    return torch.cond(...)
  File "torch/_higher_order_ops/cond.py", line 186, in cond
    return false_fn(*operands)
  File "vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/utils/fp8_utils.py", line 300, in run_deepgemm
    fp8_gemm_nt(...)
  File "vllm/utils/deep_gemm.py", line 211, in fp8_gemm_nt
    return _fp8_gemm_nt_impl(*args, disable_ue8m0_cast=not use_ue8m0, **kwargs)
RuntimeError: Assertion error (csrc/apis/../jit_kernels/impls/../../jit/kernel_runtime.hpp:45): exit_code == 0
```

Full decode and prefill crash logs are attached.

## To Reproduce

1. Deploy P/D disaggregation with `ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-cuda:v0.6.0` and `Qwen/Qwen3-32B-FP8` on H100 GPUs using the CLI args above
2. vLLM v0.17.1 starts, loads model weights successfully (~2.7s), then crashes during DeepGEMM JIT kernel compilation in the profiling phase

## Comparison matrix

| Image | Model | Result |
|-------|-------|--------|
| `ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-cuda:v0.6.0` (vLLM v0.17.1) | Qwen/Qwen3-32B-FP8 | **CRASH** — DeepGEMM JIT assertion |
| `ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-cuda:v0.6.0` | Qwen/Qwen3-32B (non-FP8) | **WORKS** |
| `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.17.1` (upstream, same vLLM) | Qwen/Qwen3-32B-FP8 | **WORKS** |
| `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.19.1` | Qwen/Qwen3-32B-FP8 | **WORKS** |

The critical finding is row 1 vs row 2: same vLLM version, same model, same hardware — only the container image differs. This isolates the bug to the llm-d image build.

## Environment

- **Image**: `ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-cuda:v0.6.0`
- **vLLM version in image**: v0.17.1
- **GPU**: NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3
- **NVIDIA Driver**: 580.126.20
- **CUDA**: 13.0
- **NCCL**: 2.27.5
- **Model**: Qwen/Qwen3-32B-FP8 (quantization=fp8, DeepGEMM E8M0 enabled)
- **Platform**: OpenShift 4.21.7
- **Tensor parallelism**: Tested with both TP=4 (decode) and TP=1 (prefill) — same crash

## Root cause hypothesis (from CLAUDE - Please Ignore/Note in comment if it's irrelevant and I'll strike it out)
It doesn't seem to be narrowing down on anything much anyway.

The `llm-d-cuda:v0.6.0` image includes custom-built components (NIXL, UCX, DeepSeek kernels, NVSHMEM patches) that ship a different DeepGEMM build or CUDA/nvcc environment than the upstream vllm image. Since upstream `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.17.1` works on the same hardware with the same model, the issue is specific to the llm-d container build environment, not upstream vLLM.

The DeepGEMM JIT compiler within the llm-d image produces kernels that fail at runtime (`exit_code != 0`), while the upstream image's DeepGEMM JIT succeeds.

Related upstream vLLM issue with same error signature (different root cause — their bundled DeepGEMM, not container build): https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/36718

records.title: [Docs] Discussion: Where to put provider specific docs in the guides
records.body:
## Description:

### Context 
Currently, the "Google TPU optimized baseline Deployment Guide" ([README.tpu.md](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/blob/main/guides/optimized-baseline/README.tpu.md)) lists the following as the first two installation steps:

Step 1: Prepare the GCS Bucket and Model (Run:ai Model Streamer) ([link](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/blob/main/guides/optimized-baseline/README.tpu.md?content_ref=step+1+prepare+the+gcs+bucket+and+model+run+ai+model+streamer))
Step 2: Configure Workload Identity for GCS Access ([link](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/blob/main/guides/optimized-baseline/README.tpu.md?content_ref=step+2+configure+workload+identity+for+gcs+access))

### The Dilemma 
We have two conflicting user experiences that we need to balance:

1. Simplicity and Quick Start (The "Getting Started" path): Steps 1 and 2 are infrastructure optimizations and are not strictly required to get a TPU stack up and running. Having them at the very beginning of the TPU guide makes the setup confusing and adds friction for users who just want to test things out. Ideally, a user should be able to directly follow the main Optimized Baseline guide ([ README.md](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/blob/main/guides/optimized-baseline/README.tpu.md?content_ref=for+broader+context+on+optimized+baseline+gateway+options+and+architecture+refer+to+the+main+optimized+baseline+guide)) and successfully run a TPU stack out of the box (e.g., pulling weights directly from Hugging Face).

2. Practicality and Production Readiness (The "Day 2" path): On the other hand, anyone actually running llm-d for real workloads (not just giving it a try) should absolutely be caching the model weights in GCS. Downloading massive FP8 models from Hugging Face every time  is slow and inefficient. In practice, setting up the Run:ai Model Streamer to load weights from GCS is highly recommended.

### Open for Discussion: 
Where should this live? How can we best restructure the documentation so that new users aren't blocked by infrastructure setup, but production users still easily find this critical optimization?

Some potential options:
* Move to a generalized "Production Best Practices" guide. 

Thoughts and feedback on the best approach are highly appreciated!

records.title: Transitioning to "llm-d Router"
records.body:
# Problem
Our current nomenclature and architectural definitions didn’t keep pace with the expansion of llm-d's deployment capabilities. Specifically, we face two primary challenges:

- Terminology Overlap and Confusion: The term "inference scheduling," currently used in llm-d to describe request routing, frequently conflicts with standard Kubernetes terminology. Users often conflate "inference scheduling" with standard K8s Pod or process scheduling. While our component does manage request timing and prioritization, its primary responsibility is high-level traffic routing, not cluster-level workload scheduling. This overlap has caused significant confusion.
- Scope Mismatch: We have evolved our inference-optimized load balancing capabilities. Historically, we relied on a Kubernetes Gateway-based approach. However, to support more flexible deployments, we now offer these capabilities via a standalone proxy, independent of a formal K8s Gateway. Consequently, the term "Inference Gateway"—heavily tied to the Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extension—is too narrow to describe all our deployment modes. We require a terminology that captures the broader architecture regardless of whether the proxy is deployed as a standalone sidecar or via a gateway.

# Proposed Solution
To address these challenges, we are rebranding the core component to the llm-d Router. This term more accurately reflects its primary function: intelligently forwarding inference requests to the optimal endpoint.

The llm-d Router is defined as the functional combination of a Proxy and an Endpoint Picker (EPP). This composition allows for flexible deployment based on infrastructure requirements:

- Standalone Mode: The proxy is deployed as a sidecar container within the same Pod as the EPP. This is the default, lightweight deployment model for llm-d.
- Gateway Mode: The proxy is provisioned as a formal Kubernetes Gateway (leveraging the Gateway API Inference Extension) that calls into a separate, provisioned EPP service. In this context, the term "llm-d Inference Gateway" remains valid, but it is explicitly a specific deployment pattern of the llm-d Router (the "Gateway Mode").

This transition addresses the problem by:
- Eliminating Ambiguity: By separating our routing logic from Kubernetes "scheduling" terminology, we clear up misconceptions about the component’s scope.
- Aligning with Industry Standards: Using "Router" aligns llm-d with industry standards for traffic direction logic, similar to how other systems (e.g., Dynamo, SMG) describe their intelligent prompt-directing layers.
- Branding and Clarity: "llm-d Router" elevates our brand and provides a clear, distinct identifier that applies consistently whether you are running a simple standalone proxy or a sophisticated, multi-tenant Kubernetes Gateway deployment.

records.title: [Feature]: Bidirectional KV Transfer for Multi-Turn Conversation Optimization
records.body:
## Overview
vLLM's bidirectional KV transfer feature (merged in [vllm#32553](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/32553), expected in v0.21.0) optimizes multi-turn conversations in P/D disaggregated deployments by enabling bidirectional NIXL-based KV cache transfers between prefill and decode nodes.

**The problem:** In current P/D disaggregation, when a user sends a new message in an ongoing conversation, the prefill node must recompute KV projections for all assistant response tokens from previous turns, even though those KV blocks already exist in the decode node's cache. This wastes GPU compute cycles, particularly for reasoning models that generate hundreds or thousands of tokens per turn.

**The solution:** Enable the prefill node to pull KV blocks from the decode node via RDMA (bidirectional NIXL transfer) instead of recomputing them. The prefill node only processes new prompt tokens, then combines the pulled KV blocks with newly computed ones before sending the complete KV cache to decode.

**Expected benefits:**
- 18-41% TTFT improvement for multi-turn conversations with prefix caching
- >2× improvement without prefix caching
- Eliminates wasted prefill compute cycles in multi-turn workloads

## Integration Required for llm-d

The **pd-sidecar** (in llm-d-inference-scheduler) orchestrates P/D request flow and needs to implement conversation state management:

1. **Conversation tracking** - Accept `conversation_id` in requests to associate conversation turns
2. **Metadata caching** - Cache decode node's `kv_transfer_params` from response stream (block IDs, request ID, host/port)
   - Cache key: `conversation_id`
   - TTL: ~450s (< 480s NIXL timeout)
3. **Metadata injection** - On turn N+1, inject cached params from turn N into prefill request so P can pull D's KV blocks via NIXL RDMA
4. **Session isolation** - Prevent cross-conversation cache contamination

The sidecar only handles metadata coordination—actual KV data transfer happens directly between P and D nodes via NIXL RDMA.

## References
- vLLM PR: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/32553
- vLLM RFC: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/32733
- Reference proxy implementation: `disagg_proxy_multiturn.py` in vLLM repo

records.title: [Bug :bug:]: EPP panics in default response parser on wrong-typed usage / token-count fields
records.body:
### Contact Details

dan@kd2ycu.com

### What happened?

EPP's default OpenAI HTTP response parser (`pkg/epp/framework/plugins/requesthandling/parsers/openai/openai.go`) has 10 unchecked type assertions on values pulled from `map[string]any` — three in `extractUsage` (the `usage` map, `prompt_token_details` map, and `cached_tokens` field) and seven in `extractUsageByAPIType` (the `prompt_tokens` / `completion_tokens` / `input_tokens` / `output_tokens` / `total_tokens` token-count fields, across the chat-completion / response / fallback branches of the API-type switch). Each site checks the JSON value for `nil` but never checks its **type**.

When a backend returns any of these with the wrong type — e.g. `"usage": "string"`, `"prompt_token_details": 0`, or `"prompt_tokens": "1024"` — the unchecked assertion panics. Go propagates unrecovered panics to the runtime, so the EPP process exits and every in-flight request handled by the pod is dropped; kubelet then restarts the container (~2-5s with image cached). If the bad responses persist (e.g., a misbehaving model-server release), the EPP enters CrashLoopBackoff with exponential kubelet backoff up to 5 minutes.

Note despite the parser being named `openai`, this is the **default** response parser ([`defaults.go:251`](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-inference-scheduler/blob/main/pkg/epp/config/loader/defaults.go#L251)) and applies to every model served via the OpenAI HTTP wire format — vLLM, SGLang, TGI, etc. The model itself can be Llama, Mistral, Qwen, etc.; we reproduced against TinyLlama through a vLLM-compatible simulator.

```bash
# Need: Docker (or Podman+compat), kind ≥ 0.20, kubectl, Go ≥ 1.22
```
