records.title: test(autoscaling): validate the KEDA EPP guide with the WVA Kind lifecycle
records.body:
Supports [#1431](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-workload-variant-autoscaler/issues/1431) and contributes to the validation path required before [#1326](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-workload-variant-autoscaler/issues/1326).

Depends on [llm-d/llm-d-workload-variant-autoscaler#1472](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-workload-variant-autoscaler/pull/1472).

## Background

This work started from the discussions around [#1326](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-workload-variant-autoscaler/issues/1326), where we need reliable KEDA and EPP autoscaling coverage before promoting the path into nightly qualification.

The first version of this PR introduced a standalone Kind-based validation runner inside llm-d. That implementation successfully established the direct KEDA and EPP metric contract and the bounded `1 -> 2` scaling behavior but it also added approximately ~2,5k lines of guide specific lifecycle code for:
* Kind cluster creation and cleanup
* Prometheus and KEDA installation
* readiness polling
* diagnostics
* request generation
* artifact handling

Following @mamy-CS 's guidance, we revisited that structure through #1431.

The conclusion was that llm-d should continue to own the canonical guide configuration, while the reusable Kind execution lifecycle should live in the workload-variant-autoscaler repository. Maintaining both implementations would duplicate infrastructure behavior and create a long term risk of drift between the two validation paths. WVA PR llm-d/llm-d-workload-variant-autoscaler#1472 was therefore created to make the existing WVA Kind lifecycle reusable for this contract.

This PR has now been refactored to use that lifecycle instead of maintaining a second runner in llm-d.

## What changed

### Removed the guide-local runner
The following standalone runner has been removed:

`guides/workload-autoscaling/scripts/test-keda-epp-kind.sh`

This removes ~2.5k lines of duplicated lifecycle and validation code

### Reworked the CI workflow

`.github/workflows/ci-keda-epp-kind.yaml` is now a thin llm-d caller of the reusable WVA lifecycle

The workflow:

1. Checks out llm-d

2. Checks out WVA at the immutable commit

   `8ff1ce41b1765843b99e2039c2616927d825b4fe`

3. Creates a unique one node Kind cluster through WVA

4. Uses the existing llm-d certificate generator to create the Prometheus TLS and CA material

5. Installs Prometheus and KEDA through WVA with:

   `DEPLOY_WVA=false`

6. Installs the canonical llm-d router values and Kind Kustomization

7. Runs only the label-isolated WVA contract:

   `make test-e2e-keda-epp-guide`

8. Collects sanitized diagnostics

9. Deletes only the isolated cluster created for the run

### Preserved llm-d ownership

The canonical guide configuration remains in llm-d and was not moved into WVA

llm-d continues to own:
* the `ScaledObject`
* the `TriggerAuthentication`
* router values
* monitoring and Prometheus values
* KEDA values
* the Kind Kustomize overlay
* the Prometheus TLS resources
* the Kind only CA compatibility configuration
* the CI workflow inputs

WVA owns only the reusable execution mechanics:
* Kind lifecycle
* Prometheus and KEDA installation helpers
* polling and readiness logic
* bounded request stimulus
* diagnostics
* artifact sanitation
* request-Pod cleanup
* isolated-cluster cleanup
* the direct `keda-epp-guide` contract

## What the contract validates
The test verifies that:

* the guide `ScaledObject` becomes `Ready=True`
* the guide `ScaledObject` becomes `Active=True`
* KEDA creates the expected HPA
* the HPA contains exactly two External metrics
* both metrics use `AverageValue`
* deterministic request load causes the first bounded `1 -> 2` transition
* three stable exact-two samples are observed
* no sampled HPA or Deployment value exceeds two
* KEDA produces no `x509`, unknown-authority, or `TriggerError` messages

This PR intentionally does not cover:
* sustained load
* scale down behavior
* performance qualification
* OpenShift specific behavior
* post scale inference validation
* nightly promotion

Those belong to the later [#1326](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-workload-variant-autoscaler/issues/1362) qualification layer.

## Local validation
The refactored workflow and retained guide resources were validated locally with:

* `git diff --check`
* `actionlint .github/workflows/ci-keda-epp-kind.yaml`
* YAML parsing
* Bash syntax validation for all embedded workflow blocks
* canonical Kustomize rendering
* Kind Kustomize rendering
* KEDA `2.20.0` Helm rendering
* kube-prometheus-stack `62.7.0` rendering
* router `v0.9.0` rendering
* workflow contract assertions
* Secret metadata and artifact safety fixtures

A complete fresh cluster execution also passed against WVA commit:

`8ff1ce41b1765843b99e2039c2616927d825b4fe`

Observed runtime results:

* exactly `1 of 73` Ginkgo specs selected
* first desired `1 -> 2` transition observed
* three stable exact two samples observed
* no sampled replica value exceeded two
* `1 passed`
* `72 skipped`
* `x509=0`
* `unknown_authority=0`
* `trigger_error=0`
* no PEM or private-key material retained
* no kubeconfig retained
* no Secret payload retained
* isolated Kind cluster cleanup passed

## Dependency
This PR temporarily pins the immutable head commit of WVA PR:
[llm-d/llm-d-workload-variant-autoscaler#1472](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-workload-variant-autoscaler/pull/1472)

Once that PR is merged, this workflow should be updated to reference the immutable upstream commit before this PR is merged.

records.title: feat(sglang): compose hierarchical caching and L3 lustre offloading into P/D disaggregation
records.body:
### Summary
This PR implements SGLang Prefill/Decode (P/D) disaggregation composed with Hierarchical Caching (`HiCache` / `DecodeHiCacheTransferMixin`) and GCP Managed Lustre shared storage (`L3`).

### Why HiCache in P/D Disaggregation?
In traditional P/D disaggregation, repeated multi-turn turns or shared-context queries re-execute prompt prefill or retransfer multi-gigabyte KV caches across RDMA/NIXL networks. By enabling HiCache on Decode workers (`--disaggregation-decode-enable-radix-cache`, `--enable-hierarchical-cache`, `--hicache-write-policy=write_through`):
1. **Zero RDMA Retransmission:** Subsequent turns reuse cached KV blocks directly from local Host DRAM (L2) or Shared Lustre (L3).
2. **6.1x–8.6x TTFT Speedup:** Time-to-First-Token drops from ~1,707–2,887 ms (cold prefill + NIXL) to ~256–334 ms (warm L2 radix hit).
3. **Cross-Pod L3 Persistence:** Any Decode worker mounting the shared Lustre volume (`llm-d-kv-cache-storage`) reloads cached prefixes after pod restarts without re-running Prefill GPU compute.

### Benchmark Results: L2 Host DRAM vs. L2+L3 Shared Lustre vs. Cold
*Environment: 5x GKE A3-Mega H100 GPU nodes, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, 4,000-token prompt context.*

| Caching Tier | Scenario | TTFT (ms) | E2E (ms) | Speedup vs Cold | NIXL / GPU Prefill Avoided |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Cold (Baseline)** | Turn 1 (Fresh prompt, Prefill + NIXL + Write) | **1,706.89 ms** | 1,947.01 ms | 1.00x (Baseline) | 0% (Full Prefill + RDMA) |
| **L2 Host DRAM Only** | Turn 2 (Warm in-memory Radix Hit) | **279.64 ms** | 501.36 ms | **6.10x (83.6% drop)** | **100% Avoided** |
| **L2 Host DRAM Only** | Turns 3–5 (Multi-turn session) | **256.28 ms** | 476.61 ms | **6.66x (85.0% drop)** | **100% Avoided** |
| **L2 + L3 Lustre Shared** | Turn 3 Post-Restart (Decode pod restarted, VRAM/DRAM flushed) | **554.72 ms** | 776.17 ms | **3.08x (67.5% drop)** | **100% Avoided (Reload from L3)** |
| **L2 + L3 Lustre Shared** | Turn 4 on Restarted Pod (L2 Host DRAM Hit) | **256.28 ms** | 476.61 ms | **6.66x (85.0% drop)** | **100% Avoided** |

### Architectural Guidance: L2 Only vs L2+L3
- **Pure L2 Host DRAM (`base/` & `gke/` overlays):** Zero extra storage cost and zero PVC dependencies. Allocates pinned host CPU RAM (`--hicache-size=20`) to deliver ~85% TTFT reduction and eliminate all inter-pod network retransmissions on multi-turn conversations.
- **L2 + L3 Shared Storage (`gke-lustre/` overlay):** Composes L2 DRAM with Google Cloud Managed Lustre (`llm-d-kv-cache-storage` PVC). Provides cross-worker cache migration and pod restart persistence without triggering cold prefill.

### Key Manifest Changes
1. **Base Decode Overlay (`base/patch-decode.yaml`):**
   - Added `--disaggregation-decode-enable-radix-cache` to maintain local radix prefix tree indexing.
   - Added `--enable-hierarchical-cache` and `--hicache-write-policy write_through` for L2/L3 cache population.
   - Added `--disable-custom-all-reduce` for container IPC safety on Kubernetes.
   - Set `--page-size=64` to align with `llm-d Router` EPP scorers.
   - Preserved `volumes:` for `shm` and `metrics-volume` to ensure robust overlay compatibility.
2. **GKE Lustre Overlay (`gke-lustre/`):**
   - Standardized on canonical `llm-d-kv-cache-storage` PVC (`/mnt/files-storage`).
   - Configured `SGLANG_HICACHE_FILE_BACKEND_ENABLE_METADATA_CACHE=true` (5.0s TTL) for Lustre metadata scalability.
   - Set 180Gi container memory limit to accommodate 100GB pinned Host DRAM pool.
   - Injected unprivileged `fix-lustre-permissions` initContainer.

records.title: feat(sglang): add multi-host distributed serving manifests via LeaderWorkerSet (LWS)
records.body:
### Description

This PR adds multi-host distributed serving manifests and GKE topology-aware overlays for **SGLang** using the Kubernetes **LeaderWorkerSet (LWS v0.9.0)** controller in `guides/wide-ep-lws/`.

This closes the feature parity gap with existing vLLM multi-host manifests (`guides/wide-ep-lws/modelserver/gpu/vllm/`), enabling multi-node distributed serving with Tensor Parallelism (TP) and Pipeline Parallelism (PP) across GPU clusters with Prefill/Decode (P/D) disaggregation.

---

### Key Changes

1. **Base LWS Manifests (`modelserver/gpu/sglang/base/`)**:
   - Standardized `decode.yaml` and `prefill.yaml` using `workerTemplate` under `leaderWorkerTemplate` (compatible with LWS v0.9.0+).
   - Configured automatic multi-node discovery and SPMD execution via LWS environment variables:
     - `--nnodes=${LWS_GROUP_SIZE:-2}`
     - `--node-rank=${LWS_WORKER_INDEX:-0}`
     - `--dist-init-addr=${LWS_LEADER_ADDRESS}:20000`
   - Set SGLang decode port to `--port 8001`, aligning with the `routing-proxy` sidecar (`base_port 8000 + data-parallel-size 1 = 8001`).
   - Exposed `--disaggregation-bootstrap-port 8998` and mapped container port `8998` on prefill leader for SGLang decode sidecar rendezvous discovery.
   - Configured `TRITON_LIBCUDA_PATH: /usr/local/nvidia/lib64` for Debian/COS container image compatibility.
   - Removed conflicting hierarchical cache flags (`--enable-hierarchical-cache`) on decode workers, which conflict with SGLang chunk cache in decode disaggregation mode.

2. **GKE Overlay & Scheduling (`modelserver/gpu/sglang/gke/`)**:
   - Added GKE Topology-Aware Scheduling (TAS) pod affinity targeting `cloud.google.com/gce-topology-block` and `subblock`.
   - Added secondary RoCE RDMA network attachments (`eth2`-`eth9` mapping to `rdma-0`..`rdma-7`) with `privileged: true` security context.
   - Disabled the GKE FastSocket NCCL tuner patch to avoid version symbol collisions.
   - Added hostPath SSD volume mounts for `/mnt/stateful_partition/kube-ephemeral-ssd/shared_disk/sglang-hf-cache/`.

3. **EPP Router Configuration (`router/sglang.values.yaml`)**:
   - Created standalone router values setting `matchLabels: leaderworkerset.sigs.k8s.io/worker-index: "0"` to ensure client traffic and P/D prefill requests are dispatched exclusively to SPMD Leader pods (rank 0).

4. **Documentation (`README.md`)**:
   - Updated `guides/wide-ep-lws/README.md` and added `guides/wide-ep-lws/modelserver/gpu/sglang/gke/README.md` with deployment, verification, and teardown commands.

---

### Verification & Empirical Benchmark Results

Tested and validated on an active **4-node A3-Mega cluster (32x NVIDIA H100 80GB SXM5 GPUs)** serving `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-0528` (FP8, 671B):

- **Cluster Topology**: 1 Prefill replica (16 GPUs, 2 nodes, TP=8 PP=2) + 1 Decode replica (16 GPUs, 2 nodes, TP=8 PP=2) fronted by `llm-d-router-standalone`.
- **Functional Validation**: Verified end-to-end `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/completions` requests through the router gateway.
- **`inference-perf` Benchmark (1,024 requests @ 2000 ISL / 2000 OSL, concurrency 256)**:
  - **Error Rate**: **0.0%** (1,024 / 1,024 requests succeeded)
  - **Total Token Throughput**: **5,791.5 tok/s** (2,896.3 input tok/s, 2,895.2 output tok/s)
  - **Time to First Token (TTFT)**: Mean **3,137 ms** (Median: **2,361 ms**, P90: **6,251 ms**)
  - **Inter-Token Latency (ITL)**: Mean **65.7 ms** (Median: **58.5 ms**, P90: **102.0 ms**)
  - **Time per Output Token (TPOT)**: Mean **65.7 ms** (Median: **67.0 ms**, P90: **73.4 ms**)

records.title: docs(autoscaling): rename README.hpa-epp.md to README.keda-epp.md
records.body:
## Summary

Fixes #2076.

The workload-autoscaling EPP guide was converted from Prometheus-Adapter/HPA to KEDA in #1981, but the file kept its old `README.hpa-epp.md` name "for link compatibility". The guide is titled *Autoscaling Workloads with KEDA and EPP Metrics* and every link to it is already labelled **KEDA + EPP Metrics**, so the file name is now the only place that still says HPA — which is exactly the confusion reported in the issue.

## What changed

- Renamed `guides/workload-autoscaling/README.hpa-epp.md` → `guides/workload-autoscaling/README.keda-epp.md` (git detects this as a rename; content is otherwise untouched).
- Dropped the now-obsolete sentence in the intro that explained why the old name was being kept.
- Updated the four in-repo links that pointed at the old path:
  - `guides/workload-autoscaling/README.md` (2 links)
  - `guides/workload-autoscaling/README.multi-inference-pool.md`
  - `guides/workload-autoscaling/README.replica-rebalancing.md`
  - `docs/architecture/advanced/autoscaling/hpa-epp.md`

## Scope notes

- `docs/architecture/advanced/autoscaling/hpa-epp.md` (the architecture page) and its entry in `docs/menu-config.json` are **not** renamed here — the issue asks specifically for the file in the `guides/workload-autoscaling` folder, and renaming a published docs route is a separate, user-visible change. Happy to fold it in if you'd like both in one PR.
- `docs/menu-config.json` only names guide *directories*, not individual guide files, so it needs no change for this rename.
- Verified with a repo-wide search that no other file, script, or workflow references `README.hpa-epp.md`.

records.title: Update docs to reflect 60s default metrics polling interval
records.body:
The 50ms default causes excessive memory allocations from the Prometheus TextParser on every scrape cycle, leading to potentail OOM errors. By default, none of the plugins recommended in the [optimized baseline](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/tree/main/guides/optimized-baseline) use the scraped metrics, with the exception of `KVCacheBlockSize`, which is constant. Therefore, it makes sense to increase the polling interval to 60s, to prevent memory strains.

This PR only updates documentation, whereas [this](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-router/pull/2195) PR on`llm-d-router` updates defaults.

records.title: fix: FMA guide fixes for benchmark nightly errors
records.body:
Four small fixes to the FMA guide so it (hopefully) passes the benchmark nightly.

- Cleanup ordering: delete the CRs + requester Deployment first, wait for the requester/launcher pods to drain while the dual-pods controller is still up to strip their finalizers, then uninstall the controllers.
- Requester readiness: standupnow use `kubectl rollout status deployment/fma-requester` instead of `kubectl wait --for=condition=ready pod -l app=fma-requester`. - `kubectl delete namespace / kubectl delete crd` are wrapped in `<!-- llm-d-cicd:skip -->` so the benchmark CI (shared cluster) skips the destructive/cluster-wide deletes.

- CI model detection: adds a `modelserver/gpu/vllm/base/` overlay so the benchmark's kustomize-based model auto-detection succeeds for FMA (whose model lives in an InferenceServerConfig, not a vLLM Deployment).

records.title: docs(async): fix unconsumable quickstart payload in the async guides
records.body:
## What

Fixes the test payload in both asynchronous-processing quickstarts (`redis/README.md` and `gcp-pubsub/README.md`) so it can actually be consumed by `llm-d-async`.

## Why

The documented message is the first command a new user runs after installing from the guide, and it always fails. Worse, it fails as a *consumer-side* unmarshal error, so the publisher sees a successful `ZADD` / `gcloud pubsub publish` and no indication anything went wrong.

There are two independent decode failures against `llm-d-async` v0.8.0+:

1. **Missing envelope.** `InternalRequest.UnmarshalJSON` decodes a tagged wire format (`internal` / `request_kind` / `data`) and hard-errors with `api: missing required field request_kind` when the tag is absent. The documented payload had no envelope at all.
2. **`deadline` typed as a string.** `api.RequestMessage` declares `Deadline int64`, but the guides quoted `"deadline": "1999999999"`, which fails `json.Unmarshal` even once the envelope is added.

## Change

Both payloads now use the working envelope form — `request_kind: "redis"` for the sorted-set queue, `"pubsub"` for Pub/Sub — matching the shape already exercised by `guides/asynchronous-processing/test/kind-e2e.sh` and by `docs/guides/e2e-deploy.md` in llm-d-async. Each guide also gets a short note that `deadline` and `created` are Unix-seconds numbers rather than strings, since that was the second, non-obvious trap.

Docs-only; no code or manifest changes.

Fixes llm-d/llm-d-async#353

records.title: docs(async/multitenant): make the saturation divisor a rendered SAT_CAP placeholder
records.body:
## What

Scenario C of the multitenant async guide ("priority under saturation") could never actually reach saturation with the guide's own worker-pool sizes.

Each pool's gate is:

```yaml
gate_type: wait-on-refuse
gate_params:
  gate: |
    {"gate_type":"prometheus-query","gate_params":{"query":"clamp(1 - sum(vllm:num_requests_running{inference_pool=\"POOL_A\"})/20, 0, 1)","fallback":"1"}}
```

`prometheus-query` closes at budget `<= 0` and `clamp(..., 0, 1)` floors the budget at 0, so the gate closes only once **20** requests are running on that model. But:

- the gates are per-model, and each pool has `workers: 8`;
- Scenario C's load is entirely async, so the only thing driving `vllm:num_requests_running` is that pool's own workers;
- a worker evaluates the gate while *holding a message it has not dispatched yet*, so at most `workers - 1` = **7** of the pool's requests are running at evaluation time.

The budget bottoms out around `1 - 7/20`, never reaches 0, `wait-on-refuse` never parks, and the run completes and looks healthy — the named scenario silently never happens.

## Change

Docs/values only; no chart or code changes.

- Replace the hardcoded `/20` divisor with a `SAT_CAP` placeholder in all three saturation overlays (`values/redis/saturation-prometheus.yaml`, `values/pubsub/saturation-prometheus.yaml`, `values/pubsub/saturation-gmp.yaml`), rendered by the guide's existing sed `render()` helper alongside `NAMESPACE`/`POOL_A`/`POOL_B`.
- Export a default `SAT_CAP=4` against `workers: 8` in the prerequisites block, and document the sizing rule: `SAT_CAP` must stay **below** the pool's `workers`, or async load alone can never close the gate. The margin is deliberate — `vllm:num_requests_running` counts only requests the server is actively running, not ones waiting in its queue.
- Say what the reader should observe: `model-a`'s budget hits **exactly 0** and stays there in stretches while `model-b` sits at `~1`; if it never reaches 0, the scenario is not happening. Added an in-flight query (`sum by (pool_name) (llm_d_async_async_inflight_requests)`) so parked pools are visible.
- Note that in production the divisor is a real capacity number (`ready pods × per-pod concurrency`), not bounded by this processor's workers, since the gate is back-pressure against all traffic on the pool including synchronous clients.
- Clarify in Observability that `async_dispatch_budget` is the **queue** gates' budget; the per-pool saturation gate's budget is the PromQL expression itself and must be queried directly.

## Verification

- `render()` leaves no unreplaced placeholders in any of the three overlays.
- Rendered YAML parses, and the embedded gate JSON parses, e.g. `{"query": "clamp(1 - sum(vllm:num_requests_running{inference_pool=\"pool-a\"})/4, 0, 1)", "fallback": "1"}`.
- `helm template ... --version 0.7.4 -f <rendered redis overlay>` succeeds and emits the expected `worker-pools.json`.
- No other guide uses this `clamp(...)` pattern; no CI workflow references the multitenant guide.

## Notes

Filed as llm-d/llm-d-async#365 but the defect lives here, in the guide.

A possible follow-up in `llm-d-async` (not needed for this fix, and unusable by the guide today since it pins published chart `0.7.4`): give the `prometheus-query` gate an explicit `threshold`/`baseline` param, so the closing point can be stated directly instead of relying on `clamp`'s floor coinciding with the hardcoded `0.0` threshold.

Ref: https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-async/issues/365

records.title: docs(async/multitenant): render prometheusURL, drop the MODEL_A/MODEL_B placeholders
records.body:
Fixes the defect reported in llm-d/llm-d-async#364 (filed there for triage; the code is here).

The multitenant guide's `render()` helper does not cover everything the overlays need, and it lists two placeholders that do not exist.

## 1. `prometheusURL` was hardcoded to the `monitoring` namespace

`values/{redis,pubsub}/saturation-prometheus.yaml` both set:

```yaml
prometheusURL: "http://kps-kube-prometheus-stack-prometheus.monitoring.svc.cluster.local:9090"
```

with no placeholder, and `render()` did not touch it. The guide's own Observability section installs kube-prometheus-stack into `monitoring`, so the happy path works — but a reader whose Prometheus lives anywhere else gets a URL that resolves to nothing.

**And it fails open, not closed.** The Scenario C gates are `wait-on-refuse(prometheus-query)` with `"fallback":"1"`, and a budget of 1 is a wide-open gate. So an unreachable Prometheus produces a run that completes cleanly, parks nothing, logs no error, and demonstrates nothing.

Now:

```yaml
prometheusURL: "PROM_URL"
```

rendered by `render()`, with the previously-hardcoded URL as the default:

```bash
-e "s#PROM_URL#${PROM_URL:-http://kps-kube-prometheus-stack-prometheus.monitoring.svc.cluster.local:9090}#g"
```

so **an unset `PROM_URL` reproduces today's behaviour byte-for-byte** — no new failure mode for readers following the guide verbatim. `PROM_URL` is exported in the environment block with that same default.

`values/pubsub/saturation-gmp.yaml` keeps its own URL: it points at the GMP query frontend in `NAMESPACE`, which is already rendered. Its header now says so.

## 2. Make the silent case visible

Scenario C now grep-checks the rendered `prometheusURL`, and after the `helm upgrade` runs three checks before any conclusion is drawn from a run:

1. the URL answers from inside the cluster (`/api/v1/query?query=up`),
2. `vllm:num_requests_running{inference_pool="${POOL_A}"}` is actually present — an empty result means the PodMonitor is not matching,
3. the processor is not logging `using fallback value`.

`Notes & gotchas` gains an entry recording that an unreachable Prometheus fails open.

## 3. `MODEL_A` / `MODEL_B` are not placeholders

All four overlays listed them under `Replace:`. They are not substitutable anywhere:

| overlay | `MODEL_` occurrences | what they are |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `redis/saturation-prometheus.yaml` | 1 | the `Replace:` line itself |
| `pubsub/saturation-prometheus.yaml` | 1 | the `Replace:` line itself |
| `pubsub/saturation-gmp.yaml` | 1 | the `Replace:` line itself |
| `redis/quota-only.yaml` | 4 | `Replace:` line + prose (`payload.model = MODEL_A`) |
| `pubsub/quota-only.yaml` | 4 | `Replace:` line + prose |

Model names reach the system through `payload.model`, which the guide's `publish()` helper fills in from `${MODEL_A}` / `${MODEL_B}`. Dropped from every `Replace:` list; the two quota-only headers and the README now say plainly that they are the guide's shell variables, not overlay placeholders. The explanatory prose is kept.

## Verification

Ran the new `render()` over all four overlays with `PROM_URL` pointed at a different namespace (`llm-d-monitoring`):

- every placeholder resolves — zero occurrences of `PROM_URL`, `POOL_A`, `POOL_B`, `IGW_HOST` remain in any rendered output,
- all four render to valid YAML,
- `ap.prometheusURL` comes out as the overridden URL on both self-hosted overlays, `http://gmp-frontend.llm-d-async.svc.cluster.local:9090` on the GMP overlay, and absent on quota-only,
- with `PROM_URL` unset, `redis/saturation-prometheus.yaml` renders the original hardcoded URL unchanged.

## Note for reviewers

`values/pubsub/saturation-prometheus.yaml` is not referenced anywhere in the README — only `redis/saturation-prometheus.yaml` and `pubsub/saturation-gmp.yaml` are. Pre-existing, out of scope here, but worth a follow-up.

This overlaps #2135, which edits the same `Replace:` header lines in the three saturation overlays to add `SAT_CAP`. Whichever merges second needs a small rebase; happy to do it.

records.title: docs(guides): make the multitenant publish() helper burst
records.body:
Fixes the defect reported in llm-d/llm-d-async#366 (filed there for triage; the code is here).

`guides/asynchronous-processing/multitenant/README.md` publishes one request per round trip — one `kubectl exec` on Redis, one `gcloud` invocation on Pub/Sub. The scenarios that follow call `publish batch a 100` (Scenario B) and `publish premium a 200 & publish batch a 200` (Scenario C). At roughly a second apiece that is several minutes of enqueue per scenario, and the cost is not just patience:

- **The burst is not a burst.** Scenario B's premise is that batch's flood exceeds its reserved quota of 1 while premium runs within quota. Spread over minutes, the workers drain the queue as fast as the loop fills it, so the backlog the classification is supposed to act on may never form. Scenario C's saturation has the same problem.
- **Concurrent `publish ... &` calls interleave their round trips**, so relative arrival rates are set by exec latency rather than by the counts the scenario asks for.

## Redis — one `ZADD` for the whole batch

`ZADD` takes any number of score/member pairs, so the pairs are built first and sent in one exec:

```bash
pairs+=("$dl" "$(printf '...' ...)")
...
kubectl -n ${NAMESPACE} exec -i deploy/redis -- redis-cli ZADD "team-${team}-${model}" "${pairs[@]}"
```

Same envelope, same key, same score — one round trip instead of *n*. The `>/dev/null` is dropped: the count `ZADD` returns is now one line instead of *n*, and it is the only confirmation the burst landed.

## Pub/Sub — bounded parallelism

`gcloud pubsub topics publish` has no multi-message form, so the invocations run concurrently with `PUBLISH_PAR` (default 8) in flight. Each invocation is a fresh Python process, hence the cap rather than backgrounding all *n*.

The issue only proposed the Redis fix, but the scenarios are backend-agnostic and a reader on the Pub/Sub path hits the identical defect, so fixing one and not the other would leave Scenarios B and C unreproducible on Pub/Sub.

## Two consequences of batching, handled

1. **Shared score.** All members of a batch now carry the same score, so `ZPopMin` breaks ties on the member string rather than on arrival. Zero-padding the index (`%04d`) makes that lexicographic tie-break equal to publish order — previously it was FIFO only by accident, because the loop was slow enough for `date +%s` to tick over.
2. **Shared deadline.** Every request in a batch expires at the same instant instead of getting its own `now+300` as the loop crawled. `PUBLISH_TTL` (default 300 — unchanged) is documented next to the helper so a long Scenario C run can raise it rather than watch the tail return `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`.

Message ids also gain a per-call `${RANDOM}` token. Without it, two bursts to the same queue within the same second would produce identical members, and the second `ZADD` would silently re-score the first instead of enqueuing anything.

## Verification

No cluster here, so both helpers were extracted from the README and run against stub `kubectl`/`gcloud` binaries that record their argv.

Redis, `publish batch a 200`:

- **1** exec (was 200), 400 pair-args, 49 KB of argv,
- all 200 members parse as JSON, are unique, and sort lexicographically into publish order,
- `deadline` in the payload matches the score; `PUBLISH_TTL=900` propagates.

Scenario B (`publish batch a 100 & publish premium a 20 & publish premium b 20 &`): 3 execs for 140 requests, correct key/team/model on each, globally unique members. Scenario C (`PUBLISH_TTL=900 publish premium a 200 & publish batch a 200 &`): 2 execs for 400 requests. Two back-to-back `publish batch a 3` calls in the same second produce disjoint member sets.

Pub/Sub, with the stub sleeping 300 ms per invocation to stand in for gcloud's startup:

| `PUBLISH_PAR` | wall clock, n=16 | peak concurrent processes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (serial, old behaviour) | 7s | 1 |
| 4 | 1s | 4 |
| 8 (default) | 1s | 8 |

100 messages: all valid JSON, unique ids, correct topic and `team` attribute.

Both blocks pass `bash -n`, and the array/`local` syntax works on bash 3.2 (macOS) as well as bash 5.

## Note for reviewers

This touches the same README as #2145 (`PROM_URL` in `render()`), though different sections — #2145 edits the env block, `render()`, Scenario C and Notes & gotchas, this one only the two `publish()` blocks. Whichever merges second may need a trivial rebase; happy to do it.

records.title: Fix: Bind In-Flight Token Accounting to the Precise Prefix Cache Producer
records.body:
The precise-prefix-cache-routing configuration enables only `precise-prefix-cache-producer`, which derives each endpoint’s cache residency from real KV-cache events. However, `inflight-load-producer` was configured without `prefixMatchInfoProducerName`. Its default data key targets `approx-prefix-cache-producer`, which is not enabled in this guide. As a result, the producer cannot find cache-match information and falls back to charging every routed request its full prompt token count, including the portion already present in the selected endpoint’s KV cache.

`inflight-load-producer` should explicitly set `prefixMatchInfoProducerName: precise-prefix-cache-producer`. This makes its cached-prefix discount consume the same exact KV-cache match data as the affinity filter, so in-flight token load reflects only tokens that still require prefill.

records.title: [ROCM] optimized-baseline: persist model cache for AMD vllm via component
records.body:
## Problem

The AMD optimized-baseline overlay (`guides/optimized-baseline/modelserver/amd/vllm`) mounts `HF_HOME` on an `emptyDir`. `emptyDir` is ephemeral, so every run starts with an empty cache and re-downloads the model (`Qwen/Qwen3-32B`, ~65GB) from HuggingFace before the benchmark can start. This is slow and, on bandwidth-constrained networks, fragile - a stalled download can hang or fail the run.

## Change

Add a reusable **`model-cache` component** that backs the cache with a persistent `ReadWriteMany` PVC and points `HF_HOME` at it, so the model downloads once and is reused across runs (and across the decode replicas that share the volume).

- **New component** `guides/recipes/modelserver/components/model-cache/`:
  - `model-cache-pvc.yaml` - an RWX `PersistentVolumeClaim` (`model-cache`, 200Gi).
  - `kustomization.yaml` (`kind: Component`) - declares the PVC and patches the Deployment: `HF_HOME=/model-cache`, volumeMount, and the PVC-backed volume.
- **Isolated to CI, opt-in:** the guide base is moved to `amd/vllm/base/` and left as upstream (`emptyDir` - unchanged behavior). A new `amd/vllm/amd-ci/` overlay layers the component on top. This matches the existing `pd-disaggregation/modelserver/amd/vllm/{base,amd-ci,...}` structure.

Design notes:
- The volume is named generically (`model-cache`), independent of the model source - `HF_HOME` (the framework's cache var) simply points at it.
- The PVC omits `storageClassName` so it binds the cluster's **default** StorageClass, consistent with how the reusable benchmark CI workflow already probes for a default RWX StorageClass (`llm-d-infra` `reusable-ci-nightly-benchmark.yaml`). No storage class is hardcoded.
- The component is reusable: any other guide can include it from its own `amd-ci/` overlay. Per-guide namespace isolation means each guide gets its own PVC, so removing/refactoring one guide can't affect another's cached data.

## Test plan

- [x] `kubectl kustomize guides/optimized-baseline/modelserver/amd/vllm/base/` renders the upstream Deployment with no cache (emptyDir).
- [x] `kubectl kustomize guides/optimized-baseline/modelserver/amd/vllm/amd-ci/` renders the PVC + patched Deployment (`HF_HOME=/model-cache`, volumeMount, PVC-backed volume; PVC name matches claimName).
- [ ] On a cluster with an RWX default StorageClass: first run downloads the model and populates the PVC; a subsequent run starts without re-downloading (cache hit).
- [ ] Nightly AMD optimized-baseline benchmark completes successfully.

records.title: fix(ci): stop tiered-prefix-cache GKE GPU nightly lanes from cancelling each other
records.body:
#2125 flagged tiered-prefix-cache-gke-cpu-gpu-vllm-native for having 6 of its last 7 scheduled runs cancelled. i think the cause is just in the workflow files.

the native and the lmcache lane both declare concurrency group nightly-e2e-tiered-prefix-cache-gke-gpu with cancel-in-progress: true, and both sit on cron '0 12 * * *'. so they fire together every night and whichever starts second kills the other. its the only duplicated concurrency group in the whole nightly fleet, every other lane has its own.

the shared group looks intentional though. both lanes use the same cluster_namespace, helm_release and workspace_dir and only differ by connector, so they really cant run side by side. so instead of splitting them up i set cancel-in-progress: false on both so the second one queues, and moved lmcache to 14:00 UTC so theyre not racing in the first place. 12:00 already has 5 lanes on it and 14:00 has 1. also left a comment on both files so the shared group doesnt look like a leftover to whoever reads it next.

one thing i didnt touch. both lanes pass the same badge_name (tiered-prefix-cache-gke-cpu-llmcache), so the native lane has no badge of its own and its result ends up on the lmcache one. thats probably the other half of the not producing verdicts thing here, but renaming it makes a badge nothing points at yet so i left it alone. can add it to this PR if you want.


Part of #2125

records.title: ci: collapse duplicated platform-parsing steps in build-image
records.body:
## Summary

The `detect-changes` job in `.github/workflows/build-image.yaml` parsed
`inputs.platforms` **twice**, with byte-identical logic, in two separate steps:

| Step | Guard |
| --- | --- |
| `platforms-input` | `inputs.force_build != true && inputs.platforms != ''` |
| `dispatch` | `github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'` |

This PR merges them into a single `platforms-input` step and removes the
now-unused `steps.dispatch.outputs.*` references from the job outputs.

Net **-10 lines**, single file touched. No behavior change on any trigger path.

## Why

- **Drift risk.** Adding a new build platform required editing both blocks; it
  was easy to update one and forget the other.
- **Redundant execution.** On a `workflow_dispatch` run both steps executed and
  computed identical values — `platforms-input` simply won `||` precedence in
  the job `outputs:` block. The `dispatch` copy was only ever *decisive* in a
  single case (dispatch with `platforms` cleared to empty), which the merged
  guard covers.

A bash function can't be shared across `run:` steps (each is a fresh shell), so
collapsing the two steps is the way to remove the duplication without adding a
new script file.

## What changed

1. Merged the two steps into one, widening the guard to cover both entry points:

   ```yaml
   if: inputs.force_build != true && (inputs.platforms != '' || github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch')
   ```

2. Deleted the `dispatch` step; moved its explanatory shim comment onto the
   surviving step.
3. Dropped `|| steps.dispatch.outputs.*` from the six `detect-changes` outputs.

The `grep -q` parsing body is **byte-for-byte unchanged** — this PR is purely
structural, deliberately not folding in any parsing-logic changes.

## Problem

The guide instructs users to store helm flags in shell variables and then expand them in helm commands. This pattern breaks with helm due to how shell argument expansion works, especially when combined with empty variables.

Users get: `open /path/base.values.yaml: no such file or directory`

## Solution

Store only the file path in variables (without the `-f` flag) and inline the flags directly in helm commands.

## Changes

- Remove `-f` from variable definitions (lines 143-152)
- Add `-f` flags inline in helm commands (lines 184-190, 206-214)
- Update setup notes to clarify this approach

records.title: feat(autoscaling): add OpenShift support to the KEDA+EPP queue guide
records.body:
**What type of PR is this?**

/kind feature

**What this PR does / why we need it**:

Enables the queue-based KEDA + EPP autoscaling guide (`optimized-baseline-autoscaling/keda-epp-queue/`) to work on OpenShift. Follows #2181, which relocated the guide.

Previously the guide shipped only a bundled kube-prometheus-stack configuration with a CA-only `TriggerAuthentication`. On OpenShift, cluster metrics live behind Thanos Querier, whose `:9091` endpoint rejects unauthenticated queries with a 401 — and KEDA suppresses trigger errors and silently serves `fallback` replicas. The result is an autoscaler that reports healthy while never actually scaling.

This PR:

- **Restructures `keda-epp-queue/` into a `base/k8s/ocp/` sibling layout** (matching `optimized-baseline-autoscaling/keda/`). A nested `overlays/ocp` that references its parent (`../..`) hits a kustomize containment cycle and fails to build; the sibling layout is the pattern that builds cleanly. `base/` holds the ScaledObject (unchanged), `k8s/` is a passthrough for generic clusters, `ocp/` is the OpenShift overlay.
- **Adds the `ocp/` overlay:**
  - Points both triggers at `thanos-querier.openshift-monitoring.svc.cluster.local:9091` and enables `authModes: bearer`.
  - Provisions a dedicated `keda-epp-metrics-reader` ServiceAccount granted the `cluster-monitoring-view` ClusterRole, plus a `service-account-token` Secret. On OpenShift the service-ca operator injects `service-ca.crt` (the CA that signs Thanos's serving cert) into that Secret automatically, so no CA copying is required.
  - Repoints the `TriggerAuthentication` at the SA token Secret (`bearerToken` + `service-ca.crt`).
- **Updates `README.hpa-epp.md`**: platform-aware apply/delete paths (`/k8s` for generic clusters, `/ocp` for OpenShift) and a concrete OpenShift section.

The `k8s` overlay is an unchanged passthrough of `base` (bundled Prometheus, CA-only auth), so non-OpenShift behavior is preserved.

**Verification:**
- `kubectl kustomize` builds all three targets (`base`, `k8s`, `ocp`); the rendered `ocp` output has both triggers on Thanos with `authModes: bearer`, the TriggerAuthentication using the SA token Secret, and the SA/ClusterRoleBinding/token Secret present with the namespace propagated to the CRB subject; the `k8s` output is unchanged from the previous base.
- Live-validated on an OpenShift cluster: applied the `ocp` overlay against a dummy scale target with TLS verification on. The ScaledObject reached `Ready=True` and held `Fallback=False`, and the KEDA-generated HPA resolved a real external-metric value from Thanos (no 401 / no fallback). Confirmed the SA token Secret's `service-ca.crt` bundle includes `openshift-service-serving-signer`, the CA that signs Thanos's serving certificate.

**Which issue(s) this PR fixes**:

N/A — enables the KEDA+EPP queue autoscaling guide on OpenShift (follows #2181).

**Release note**:

```release-note
The KEDA + EPP queue-based autoscaling guide now supports OpenShift via a new `ocp` overlay that authenticates to Thanos Querier with a bearer token (a dedicated `cluster-monitoring-view` ServiceAccount; no CA copying needed). The guide is now applied per platform: `kubectl apply -k .../keda-epp-queue/k8s` for generic Kubernetes, or `.../keda-epp-queue/ocp` for OpenShift.
```

records.title: fix(autoscaling): repair OpenShift overlay for the KEDA+EPP saturation guide
records.body:
**What type of PR is this?**

/kind bug

**What this PR does / why we need it**:

Fixes the **KEDA + EPP saturation** autoscaling guide (`optimized-baseline-autoscaling/keda-epp-saturation/`), which did not work on OpenShift as shipped.

Two independent bugs:

1. **The `overlays/ocp` overlay does not build.** It uses a nested `overlays/ocp` referencing its parent via `bases: [..]`, which kustomize rejects as a containment cycle — `kubectl kustomize .../keda-epp-saturation/overlays/ocp` fails outright (reproduced on kustomize v5.5.0).
2. **The base ScaledObject is malformed.** `metricType` and `authenticationRef` are nested *inside* each trigger's `metadata`. `authenticationRef` there fails KEDA strict decoding (`unknown field "spec.triggers[0].metadata.authenticationRef.name"`), so the ScaledObject is rejected / never authenticates. The guide also relied on a manually copied `prometheus-token` Secret whose `ca.crt` is the bundled-Prometheus CA (not the service CA that signs Thanos's serving cert), and was missing `authModes: bearer`. (The queue guide had these at the correct trigger level, which is why it worked.)

This PR:

- **Moves `metricType` and `authenticationRef` to the trigger level** on both triggers, making the ScaledObject valid.
- **Converts the guide to the `base/k8s/ocp/` sibling layout** used by the sibling `keda-epp-queue` guide.
- **`ocp/` overlay:** points both triggers at `thanos-querier.openshift-monitoring.svc.cluster.local:9091` with `authModes: bearer`; provisions a dedicated `keda-epp-metrics-reader` ServiceAccount granted `cluster-monitoring-view` plus a `service-account-token` Secret (OpenShift's service-ca operator injects `service-ca.crt` automatically); and repoints the `TriggerAuthentication` at that Secret (`bearerToken` + `service-ca.crt`). No `prometheus-token` copy is needed on OpenShift.
- `unsafeSsl` stays `"false"` — TLS verification remains on and works via the correct service CA.
- **`k8s/`** is an unchanged passthrough of `base/`, preserving the generic-Kubernetes path.
- **README** updated: platform-aware apply/delete paths (`/k8s`, `/ocp`), OpenShift skips the token-copy step, and the incorrect CA note is removed.

**Verification:**
- `kubectl kustomize` builds all three targets (`base`, `k8s`, `ocp`); the `ocp` render has both triggers on Thanos with `authModes: bearer` and `unsafeSsl: "false"`, `metricType`/`authenticationRef` at the trigger level, the TriggerAuthentication using the SA token Secret (`token` + `service-ca.crt`), and the SA/ClusterRoleBinding/token Secret present with the namespace propagated to the CRB subject. The `k8s` render is unchanged from the previous base.
- Live-validated on an OpenShift cluster: applied the `ocp` overlay against a dummy scale target with TLS verification on. records.title: feat(precise): Serve render from the model server pods
records.body: ## Summary In the `precise-prefix-cache-routing` guide, the render (tokenizer) Service no longer has pods of its own by default. Instead of three GPU-less `vllm launch render` replicas, it selects the vLLM model server pods the guide already deploys, since `vllm serve` exposes `/v1/completions/render` and `/v1/chat/completions/render` out of the box. The old renderer pool moves to `render/standalone/`, still required for SGLang (it doesn't implement vLLM's render endpoints). Both overlays publish the same Service name, so the router's `vllm.url` is unchanged. Apply exactly one. ### Why Every request is tokenized before it's routed, so the render call sits inside TTFT. A separately-scheduled pool saturates before the model servers do as QPS climbs; fronting the model servers makes render capacity scale with the serving fleet. At higher RPS, latency is more contained with this approach than with the CPU renderers. See below the benchmarking data for `Qwen3-32B` and [this workload](https://github.com/albertoperdomo2/benchflow/blob/main/profiles/benchmark/x-70r-6kSys.yaml). ## Notes - `modelName` **mismatches now fail loudly** instead of silently scoring against the wrong tokenizer. - Added the render paths to `--disable-access-log-for-endpoints`, otherwise each model server logs a line per routed request. - Unaffected by standalone vs. gateway mode, verified by templating both charts: identical `token-producer` params and InferencePool selectors.

records.title: feat(autoscaling): add queue-based KEDA+EPP autoscaling nightly (OCP GPU)
records.body:
**What type of PR is this?**

/kind feature

**What this PR does / why we need it**:

Adds a nightly test lane for the **queue-based KEDA + EPP** autoscaling guide (`guides/workload-autoscaling/README.hpa-epp.md`), which has no CI today. The existing `workload-autoscaling` nightly tests the legacy WVA path (`wva_desired_replicas`); this lane tests the EPP-direct path. KEDA scales the decode Deployment straight from `llm_d_epp_flow_control_queue_size`, with **no WVA controller**.

This is the "wiring / signal-liveness" gate: it validates that the guide deploys, the EPP emits the queue metric with the right labels, user-workload-monitoring scrapes it into Thanos, KEDA authenticates to Thanos, and the HPA is driven by the real signal (`Fallback=False`) the silent-failure class (401 / wrong CA / label drift / missing metric) that breaks autoscaling invisibly. Load-driven scale-up actuation is a planned follow-up as V2.

Files:

- **`scripts/nightly-deploy-ocp-keda-epp.sh`** — the EPP-direct sibling of `nightly-deploy-ocp.sh`. Installs the EPP router as helm release `optimized-baseline` (matching the guide → EPP Service `optimized-baseline-epp`) with the `monitoring` + `keda-epp-queue/router.values.yaml` values (the latter enables `featureGates: [flowControl]`, the source of the queue metric), applies `keda-epp-queue/ocp`, discovers the EPP Service name at runtime and templates both trigger queries' `namespace`/`service`/`model_name` to it, labels the namespace for UWM scraping, starts the decode Deployment at 1 replica, waits for it to be ready (the queue metric is per-model and only exists once the EPP has a ready backend endpoint), then gates on `Fallback=False`. `maxReplicaCount` is capped at the GPU budget (2).
- **`nightly-e2e-workload-autoscaling-keda-epp-ibm-acc-gpu-vllm-x.yaml`** — the nightly workflow, calling `reusable-nightly-e2e-openshift.yaml@main` with the deploy script as `custom_deploy_script` (no WVA image-build job). Distinct namespace (`llm-d-nightly-keda-epp-queue`), concurrency group, badge (`keda-epp-queue-ocp`), and schedule (`0 5 * * *`) from the WVA lane. Declares the inputs `/test-nightly` passes so it can be triggered by comment.
- **`consolidate-status-workload-autoscaling-keda-epp-ibm-acc-gpu-vllm-x.yaml`** — the companion past-status query (flake-tolerant "green ≥1× in 5 days").
- **`guides/workload-autoscaling/README.md`** — adds the status badge for the new lane; relabels the existing badge "WVA" so the two are distinguishable.

- `kubectl kustomize` builds the generated overlay; both trigger queries are templated to the deployed EPP's `namespace`/`service`/`model_name`; the Thanos endpoint, `authModes: bearer`, and SA-token auth are inherited from `keda-epp-queue/ocp`; the decode Deployment is patched to 1 replica with the nightly GPU priority class. `bash -n` clean; all referenced value files resolve; both workflow YAMLs parse; the consolidate-status file and README badge reference the nightly by filename.

records.title: feat(precise): enable KV event replay buffer for index recovery
records.body:
## Summary

- Enable vLLM's ZMQ replay buffer on the GPU model server backend so the router can rebuild its KV-block index after an EPP restart without waiting for live traffic
- Bump GPU vLLM image from v0.25.0 to v0.26.0 (includes the replay topic frame fix, vllm-project/vllm#45177)
- Add `replaySocketPort: 5557` to the router's `podDiscoveryConfig` so the EPP connects to each pod's ROUTER socket for replay requests

## Details

Each GPU model server now binds a ZMQ ROUTER socket on port 5557 alongside the existing PUB socket on 5556. On first connect (or after an EPP restart), each subscriber requests a replay of buffered events from the model server to rebuild the prefix-cache index without waiting for live traffic. vLLM retains the last 10,000 event batches in memory by default.

Non-GPU backends (CPU, AMD ROCm, XPU, TPU) remain unchanged — their vLLM images are on v0.23.0 or earlier which lack replay support. Replay will be enabled for those backends when their images are updated to include vllm-project/vllm#45177.

Depends on: llm-d/llm-d-router#1887 (merged)

## Test plan

- [ ] Deploy precise-prefix-cache-routing guide on GPU cluster with v0.26.0 image
- [ ] Verify KV events flow normally (prefix affinity routing works)
- [ ] Kill the EPP pod, verify it recovers and rebuilds the index via replay (check EPP logs for "Replay complete")

records.title: Update nightly matrix
records.body:
## Summary

The nightly testing matrix in `release/README.md` was missing badges for several
nightly workflows that have been running for a while. Three separate causes, all
in the shared discovery layer (`scripts/matrix_common.py`) rather than in the
README itself:

1. **Workflow stems with an extra segment were silently dropped.**
   `_parse_workflow_stem` required *exactly* four segments after the
   `-{provider}-` marker. The AMD ROCm runs are named
   `nightly-e2e-{guide}-amd-ci-acc-rocm-vllm-x.yaml` — five segments, because of
   the extra `ci` — so they failed to parse and were discarded with no warning.
   This hid the AMD column for P/D Disaggregation, Precise Prefix Cache Routing
   and Predicted Latency-Based Routing.

2. **One workflow had no `update-badge` job.**
   `nightly-e2e-precise-prefix-cache-gke-acc-tpu-vllm-x.yaml` declared the
   `update_badge` input but never used it, so it had no `badge_name` for
   `discover_workflows` to pick up and was skipped.

3. **Two `GUIDES` entries did not match reality.**
   The Workload Autoscaling row used the slug `wva` (which is the *badge* name
   prefix, `wva-ocp` / `wva-cks`) while the workflows parse to
   `workload-autoscaling` — so the WVA row rendered empty despite two nightlies
   running. And `flow-control` had a nightly workflow but no row at all.

## Changes

- `scripts/matrix_common.py`
  - `_parse_workflow_stem`: accept `len(parts) >= 4` and unpack from
    `parts[-4:]`. Segments between the provider and `offload_dest` are treated
    as environment detail and ignored; the trailing four fields are what
    identify a run. Updated the filename-convention comment and the docstring to
    document this.
  - `GUIDES`: `wva` → `workload-autoscaling`; added a `Flow Control` row,
    positioned before WVA to match the ordering in `guides/README.md`.
- `.github/workflows/nightly-e2e-precise-prefix-cache-gke-acc-tpu-vllm-x.yaml`
  - Added the missing `update-badge` job, mirroring
    `nightly-e2e-pd-disaggregation-gke-acc-tpu-vllm-x.yaml`, with
    `badge_name: precise-prefix-cache-routing-gke-tpu` and
    `badge_label: "VLLM TPU"` per the existing `{guide}-gke-tpu` convention.
- `release/README.md`
  - Regenerated via `python3 scripts/sync-nightly-matrix.py --fix`.

Chose to relax the parser rather than rename the three AMD workflow files, since
renaming would break the existing badge and workflow-run URLs.

## Testing

```
touch .release-team
python3 scripts/sync-nightly-matrix.py --check   # exit 0, "Nightly matrix is up to date."
rm -f .release-team
```

- Workflow discovery: 37/37 `nightly-e2e-*.yaml` files now resolve to a badge
  (36/37 before this PR; 33/37 with the old parser).
- No workflow guide slug is left without a matching `GUIDES` row.
- The edited workflow parses as valid YAML and its `update-badge.with` block has
  the same keys as the `pd-disaggregation` TPU reference workflow.

## Note for reviewers

- `precise-prefix-cache-routing-gke-tpu.json` does not exist on `gh-pages` yet —
  it will be created by the first nightly run after this merges. Until then that
  one badge will render as unknown/broken. Expected for a new badge, but worth
  knowing before merging.

records.title: guides(wide-ep-lws): precise prefix-cache routing variant
records.body:
Addresses #2201 (see the placement discussion there).

The wide-EP guide routes on the approximate prefix index. This adds an opt-in variant that routes on the exact KV-event-backed index (`precise-prefix-cache-producer` with load-gated affinity), following the guide's existing extension idioms:

- `components/kv-events`: sets `ENABLE_KV_EVENTS`, `KV_BLOCK_SIZE`, and `PYTHONHASHSEED` on the GLM prefill/decode engines. The base manifests gain an env-driven branch (same mechanism as `OFFLOADING_MODE`) that enables per-rank ZMQ publishers with the publisher port compensated by the pod's start rank (llm-d-router#2227). Off by default - existing deployments produce byte-identical pods.
- `router/precise-routing.values.yaml`: overrides the `wide-ep-lws-config.yaml` plugins key (same layering as `glm-5.2-overrides.values.yaml`) with the token-producer, precise producer (block 64, `podCacheSize` sized to endpoints x tiers, gpu/cpu tier weights), affinity filter, and token-load scorer.
- `render/`: a pod-less Service fronting the prefill pods' `/v1/*/render` endpoints for the token-producer (prefill, because decode port 8000 belongs to the routing-proxy sidecar; per llm-d#2188).
- README section with prerequisites (EPP with per-rank KV-event attribution llm-d-router#2233, GIE bundle >= v1.5.0-rc.2 for multi-port target pools) and three verification gates: render returns token IDs, every rank's KV-event socket subscribed (counting only ZMQ-range ports - the render Service adds EPP HTTP connections that would inflate a naive count), repeated prefixes route back to their holder.
- Cross-link from `precise-prefix-cache-routing`.

Validated on a GLM-5.2-FP8 2-prefill + 1-decode DP8 LWS cell on two clusters: all per-rank subscriptions connect (24/24), render serves token IDs from a prefill pod, and a repeated 6K-token prompt routes back to its holder with a full-prompt prefix-hit delta. records.title: fix(autoscaling): make the queue-based KEDA+EPP nightly deploy and validate reliably
records.body:
**What type of PR is this?**

/kind bug

**What this PR does / why we need it:**

The queue-based KEDA+EPP autoscaling nightly (added in #2192) fails on the shared
OCP GPU cluster. This fixes the deploy script and workflow so the path installs,
discovers the EPP, and validates cleanly. Four independent issues:

1. **Unique release name** (deploy script). Installing the router as
   `optimized-baseline` collides with existing optimized-baseline InferencePools on
   the shared cluster, sending the EPP into a hot reconcile loop (NOT_SERVING).
   Renamed the release to `keda-epp-queue`; the EPP Service is discovered at runtime
   and the ScaledObject query is templated to it.

2. **Pin the router chart to a released version** (deploy script). `guides/env.sh`
   pins every guide to the mutable `v0` tag, which picked up llm-d-router#1681 and
   stopped creating the EPP `-epp` Service with flowControl/monitoring — `helm
   install` reports `deployed` but the Service never appears. Pinned to the released
   `v0.9.0` (predates #1681; verified it creates the Service). Repo-wide env.sh fix
   tracked in #2207; chart bug in llm-d-router#2323.

3. **Poll for the EPP Service** (deploy script). It isn't present the instant `helm
   install` returns; poll up to 5m and dump `all,inferencepool` on failure.

4. **Fix stale `gateway_host`** (workflow). e2e-validate.sh curls
   `http://<gateway_host>:80/v1/models` and exits 1 if unreachable. The rename makes
   the EPP Service `keda-epp-queue-epp`, so `gateway_host` now points there (was
   `optimized-baseline-epp`).

5. **Warm up the EPP before the gate** (deploy script). The v0.9.0 EPP creates the
   per-model `flow_control_queue_size` / `request_running` series lazily on the first
   request, not at idle — so the deploy sends a few `/v1/completions` after the decode
   is Ready, before the Fallback gate, or the trigger errors on an empty series.

6. **Fix the ClusterRoleBinding subject namespace** (deploy script). kustomize's
   `namespace` transformer doesn't rewrite a CRB subject's namespace when the inner
   `ocp/` overlay already set it, so the metrics-reader SA was bound in the wrong
   namespace → KEDA's Thanos queries 403 → `TriggerError`. Now rewritten explicitly.

**Which issue(s) this PR resolves:**

Related to #2207, llm-d-router#2323

- The `v0.9.0` pin is a local workaround via `ROUTER_CHART_VERSION_OVERRIDE`; the
  broader fix is pinning `guides/env.sh` repo-wide (#2207). Verified no guide
  depends on a post-`v0.9.0` chart feature.
- Validated end-to-end on OpenShift, everything including the GPU decode
  tail: v0.9.0 creates the EPP Service, the InferencePool selects the decode pods
  by `llm-d.ai/guide`, the EPP exposes `llm_d_epp_flow_control_queue_size` /
  `llm_d_epp_request_running` (model_name-labelled), and the Thanos bearer-auth
  path (metrics-reader SA + cluster-monitoring-view) returns HTTP 200.

**Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?**

```release-note
NONE

records.title: fix(flow-control): repair user-facing guide breakages
records.body:
1. **`objectives.yaml` binds to a pool that does not exist.** All three InferenceObjectives hardcode `poolRef.name: default-pool`; this guide's InferencePool is `flow-control`. Priority and fairness headers resolve to nothing and every request lands in band `priority="0"` (observed: 450/450 burst requests dispatched at priority 0 despite `best-effort-traffic` headers), so Use Case 1 silently no-ops. After the fix, a premium request lands in `priority="100"`.

2. **The CRD manifests URL 404s.** The command interpolates `ROUTER_CHART_VERSION` (`v0`), a floating OCI chart channel with no matching GitHub release. `env.sh` gains a distinct `ROUTER_RELEASE_VERSION=v0.9.0` and the README prerequisite uses it.

3. **The verification grep matches nothing.** `grep "Flow Control enabled"` has no counterpart in the EPP. Current `main` logs `Initializing Flow Control layer` (the `experimental` qualifier was dropped at GA graduation), and the disabled path logs `Flow Control layer is disabled...`. The doc now greps the init line and names the disabled-path line, so no output stays diagnosable.

4. **Monitoring ordering is backwards.** Step 3 ("Enable monitoring") tells the reader to add values during the step 1 install, two sections after they installed, and the ServiceMonitor CRD requires the monitoring stack first. The README now states the ordering up front and gives the re-run path for readers who already installed.

5. **Duplicate metrics port fails the install.** `flow-control.values.yaml` declares a 9090 `extraServicePort` the chart already templates unconditionally on the EPP Service, so the install fails with `INSTALLATION FAILED ... duplicate entries for key [port=9090,protocol="TCP"]` regardless of whether `monitoring.values.yaml` is layered (that file never touches `extraServicePorts`). With the entry removed, the chart's own 9090 port remains, so the README's no-monitoring `curl :9090/metrics` check still works.

6. **Cleanup path drifted from the deploy path.** The deploy step renders `modelserver/gpu/vllm/${INFRA_PROVIDER}/`; cleanup rendered `modelserver/gpu/vllm/`, which no longer resolves the same manifests. Cleanup now matches, with a reminder to set `INFRA_PROVIDER` to the deploy-time value.

records.title: Exclude non-serving requester pods from the InferencePool
records.body:
## Problem

The `fast-model-actuation` guide stamps `llm-d.ai/guide: fast-model-actuation` on **both** halves of
FMA's dual-pods design:

- **bound launcher pods** — run vLLM, listening on `:8000`
- **requester pods** — reserve the GPU and hold the pod identity, and **never listen on `:8000`**

The router's `InferencePool` selects on that single label with `targetPorts: 8000`, so the EPP
load-balances across a mix of live vLLM endpoints and endpoints that refuse the connection. Callers
see intermittent:

```
upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before headers.
reset reason: remote connection failure,
transport failure reason: delayed connect error: Connection refused
```

## Fix

Add the launcher component label to the pool selector so only bound launchers are routable:

```yaml
  modelServers:
    matchLabels:
      llm-d.ai/guide: "fast-model-actuation"
+     app.kubernetes.io/component: "launcher"
```

Unbound launchers need no special handling — FMA stamps the `InferenceServerConfig` labels onto a
launcher only once it is bound to a requester, so they were already excluded.

The requester's `llm-d.ai/guide` label is deliberately **left in place**: `llm-d-benchmark`'s
kustomize standup waits for pods matching `llm-d.ai/guide=<guide_name>`, and requesters are the pods
reliably present at that point.

## Changes

- `guides/fast-model-actuation/router/fast-model-actuation.values.yaml` — the selector, plus a
  comment explaining why the guide label alone is insufficient.
- `guides/fast-model-actuation/README.md` — a `> [!NOTE]` documenting the routing topology.

No manifest, image, or version changes.

## Validation

Verified on a live GKE cluster (`Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B`, FMA `v0.6.2`, `GATEWAY_CLASS=epponly`,
2 requesters / 16 launchers):

| Check | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `/v1/completions` loop through the EPP | 3 of 8 | **10 of 10** |
| Pods matching the pool selector | 4 (2 launchers + 2 requesters) | **2 bound launchers** |
| EPP `Pod added` entries for `fma-requester-*` | 2 | **0** |

Also confirmed:

- The rendered `InferencePool` carries both labels with `targetPorts[0].number: 8000` unchanged
  (`helm template` against the committed values).
- The selector survives sleep/wake: scaling requesters to `0` unbinds every launcher and the
  selector correctly matches **zero** pods; scaling back to `2` rebinds exactly 2, and traffic is
  10/10 again.
- `scripts/guide.py check` and `render --check` both clean — the README note sits outside the
  `<!-- guide:… -->` markers.

## Follow-ups (not in this PR)

- **`llm-d-benchmark`:** standup `step_10_smoketest.py` and `step_11_inference_test.py` have no
  kustomize branch, so they resolve `{model_id_label}-router-epp` via `find_epponly_endpoint()`
  instead of using the existing `find_kustomize_endpoint(guide_name)` → `{guide_name}-epp`. That
  service does not exist for a guide deployment, so the standup smoketest likely never reaches the
  request path for this guide. Worth its own issue. **Consequence for reviewers: a green nightly does
  not by itself confirm this fix** — the live loop above is the evidence.
- Separately, the `_RETRYABLE_INDICATORS` list in `step_11_inference_test.py` does not include the
  connection-refused text, so `max_retries=3` never engages for this class of failure.
- An unrelated requester replica explosion (245 replicas) observed in an earlier nightly run.

records.title: docs(flow-control): make use-case verification observable and fix guide friction
records.body:
The Use Case 2 load test could not demonstrate the queuing it claims to verify, and an audit of the rest of the guide surfaced more breakage in the same file. Every changed command was validated on a live cluster (GKE, Helm 4.2.0, one Qwen3-32B TP=2 replica).

## Use Case 2

- Replace the dead `hey` download (S3 returns 403; the debug image's busybox wget lacks TLS) with a curl loop using tools already in the debug image.
- Sustain the load so the queue is observable: `max_tokens: 500`, `ignore_eos: true`, ~2k-token prompt; burst in the background and poll while it runs. The old payload drained in under a second.
- Derive the test sizing from the values file instead of hardcoding it. `MAX_CONCURRENCY` is read out of `router/flow-control.values.yaml` with awk and passed into the debug pod; the burst is `MAX_CONCURRENCY + SURPLUS` and the expected queue peak is `SURPLUS` (20, kept below the best-effort band's `maxRequests`). A retuned values file changes the test with it, so the guide's numbers cannot drift out from under the config.
- Scale the pool to one replica for the burst, recording the prior replica count and restoring it afterward rather than assuming 8.
- Pre-flight a single request (expect 200) before the burst; sum all `priority="-10"` series in the poll; the peak-0 diagnosis covers poll timing and replica count.

## Rest of the guide

- Use Case 1: add a verification step; `llm_d_epp_flow_control_request_queue_duration_seconds_count` must show a `priority="100"` series (records on every outcome, including immediate dispatch).
- `helm install` → `helm upgrade --install` in both install commands; the re-run instructions already assumed it.
- Add `-c epp` to the verification grep as an in-block comment; kubectl defaults to the Envoy sidecar, whose log never matches.
- Pass `MODEL_NAME` into the debug pod; the UC1 request body and UC2 payload use it in-pod.
- Document the router pod's 8 vCPU / 16 GiB request at the install step, citing `base.values.yaml` as the source.
- Drop the stale `[Experimental]` title, a duplicate QoS caveat, and the hardcoded `--model` value.

## helpers/benchmark.md

Harness- and provider-specific material moved to the benchmarking helper (the declared single source of truth for benchmarking), which the guide now links instead of duplicating:

- New troubleshooting entry for `ProvisioningFailed ... multi writer with mount access type`: the RWX StorageClass requirement, the `storage.workloadPvc.storageClassName` scenario override, a GKE Filestore walkthrough, and stale-claim recovery (PVC StorageClass is immutable and the CLI reuses an existing claim).
- New troubleshooting entry for the harness pod stuck `Pending` on its 16 vCPU / 32 GiB request.
- New "Cleaning up harness resources" section; the guide's Cleanup links it. The workload PVC is backed by shared storage that bills until removed.
- The guide's benchmark section keeps a single NOTE pointing at both.

Follow-up: a `llmdbenchmark cleanup` subcommand upstream would replace the hand-maintained resource list in benchmark.md entirely; issue to be filed on llm-d/llm-d-benchmark.

## Observed on the live run

- UC1: `outcome="Dispatched", priority="100"` count 1 after one premium request.
- UC2 (pre-parameterization commands): peak queue depth 18 from a 150-request burst against `maxConcurrency` 132 — the same arithmetic the derived commands now encode with `SURPLUS=20` (expected peak 20). <!-- update after re-running UC2 with the derived sizing -->
- Benchmark: the documented GKE failure mode reproduces; with the StorageClass override on a fresh claim, Filestore bound in ~2.5 min and `shared_prefix_synthetic.yaml` ran end to end.
- Not covered on a 2-GPU cluster: detector behavior while ready endpoints drain, 8-replica scale-back timing.

records.title: fix(observability): honor selected kubeconfig
records.body:
## What changed

The observability installer now uses the kubeconfig selected with `-g/--context` for every Kubernetes client it starts.

The change:

- exports the selected path through `KUBECONFIG`
- keeps the `kubectl` and `helm` command variables as executable names
- lets child scripts, including TLS generation and dashboard loading, inherit the same target
- adds a hermetic regression test to the existing path-filtered guide dry-run workflow

## Why

Before this change, some commands used the selected kubeconfig while bare `kubectl` and `oc` commands used the ambient configuration. A validation check could therefore pass against one cluster while a later operation changed another cluster.

For example, suppose the ambient kubeconfig points to production and the user runs the installer with `-g staging.kubeconfig`. Before this fix, Helm could install resources in staging while the reachability check, OpenShift commands, or dashboard helper still used production. One installer run could therefore read from or modify two different clusters. After this fix, every command uses staging.

The old command-string approach also broke when the selected path contained spaces.

## How to reproduce

Use different ambient and selected kubeconfigs, then run the CRD-only installer path:

```bash
export KUBECONFIG=/path/to/production.kubeconfig
guides/recipes/observability/install-prometheus-grafana.sh \
  -g "/path/to/staging kubeconfig" \
  -c
```

The regression test reproduces the dangerous case without real clusters:

1. The ambient target is configured to succeed.
2. The selected target is configured to fail `kubectl cluster-info`.
3. The installer is invoked with `-g` pointing to the selected target.

Before this fix, the initial bare `kubectl` could validate the ambient target and execution could continue. The path containing spaces could also be split as part of a command string. After this fix, validation uses the selected target and exits before any mutation; the path remains one value.

## Tests

- Bash syntax checks for the changed scripts and test clients
- Committed hermetic test covering selected-target validation, mutation prevention, paths with spaces, ambient configuration without `-g`, and TLS helper inheritance after changing directory
- External hermetic checks for the OpenShift path and dashboard helper
- YAML parse and whitespace checks

The committed test uses fake client binaries and does not require a live cluster, credentials, network access, or a new test dependency. It runs as a step in the existing guide dry-run workflow, which is path-filtered to guide or workflow changes, keeping the ongoing CI cost bounded.

## Related issue

No separate GitHub issue was opened for this bug. This PR contains the problem statement, concrete reproduction, fix, and regression coverage. `#2215` is the pull request number, not an issue number.

## Follow-up

The TLS helper still has the existing limitation that a relative kubeconfig path can stop resolving after it changes directory. Resolving that path before the directory change should be handled separately.

records.title: fix: align multimodal modelServers selector with multimodal-aggregation guide label
records.body:
fix predicted-latency-routing : update the cross-guide label consumer missed by the multimodal-aggregation rename 

The multimodal deployment flow in guides/predicted-latency-routing/README.md is:

```
# for Multimodal
# line 174
helm install ${GUIDE_NAME} \
    ${ROUTER_STANDALONE_CHART} \
    -f ${REPO_ROOT}/guides/recipes/router/base.values.yaml \
    -f ${REPO_ROOT}/guides/${GUIDE_NAME}/router/predicted-latency-multimodal.values.yaml \
    -n ${NAMESPACE} --version ${ROUTER_CHART_VERSION}

kubectl apply -n ${NAMESPACE} -k ${REPO_ROOT}/guides/multimodal-serving/aggregation/modelserver/gpu/vllm/${INFRA_PROVIDER}/
```

`router.modelServers.matchLabels` in predicted-latency-multimodal.values.yaml is rendered by the Helm chart into the InferencePool's label selector. EPP (Endpoint Picker) uses that selector to discover the vLLM model server Pods in the same namespace, so it knows which backends are candidates in its pool.

On the producer side, `guides/multimodal-serving/aggregation/modelserver/*/kustomization.yaml` stamps the label onto the Pods:

```
labels:
  - pairs:
      llm-d.ai/guide: multimodal-aggregation
    includeSelectors: true
    includeTemplates: true
```

So predicted-latency-multimodal.values.yaml must use the same label:

```
llm-d.ai/guide: multimodal-aggregation
```

The stamped label value and the selector value have to match literally.

records.title: fix: Disable USE_SCCACHE when the sccache fallback kicks in
records.body:
Fixes #2223

### Problem

`docker/scripts/common/setup-sccache.sh` degrades gracefully when sccache cannot start, but the degrade path leaves the build broken in two separate ways.

**1. `USE_SCCACHE` is never cleared.**

The script removes the binary, unsets the CMake launcher variables and returns success — but the input variable still says `true`. Every consumer sources the script and then branches on it, so they still believe sccache is available:

```bash
. /usr/local/bin/setup-sccache
...
if [ "${USE_SCCACHE}" = "true" ]; then
    export CC="sccache gcc" CXX="sccache g++"   # binary was just deleted
fi
```

gdrcopy builds with a plain Makefile rather than CMake, so unsetting the `CMAKE_*_COMPILER_LAUNCHER` variables has no effect on it. The hardcoded `sccache` in `CC` is what actually breaks the build:

```
make[1]: sccache: No such file or directory
make[1]: *** [<builtin>: gdrapi.o] Error 127
make: *** [Makefile:63: lib] Error 2
```

`build-ucx.sh:29` and `build-nixl.sh:32` set `CC` the same way and fail identically. `build-gdrcopy.sh:62`, `build-ucx.sh:62`, `build-nvshmem.sh:147`, `build-lmcache.sh:88` and `build-compiled-wheels.sh:106` call bare `sccache --show-stats` after the binary is gone, which aborts under `set -e`.

**2. Deleting the binary breaks the final image layer.**

`docker/Dockerfile.cuda:493-494` copies sccache out of the builder stage, and its comment states the invariant the degrade path violates:

```dockerfile
# sccache binary is always installed in builder; only configured/started when USE_SCCACHE=true
COPY --from=builder /usr/local/bin/sccache /usr/local/bin/sccache
```

Once the builder stage stops failing, the build gets one step further and dies here instead:

```
ERROR: failed to build: failed to solve: failed to compute cache key:
failed to calculate checksum of ref ...: "/usr/local/bin/sccache": not found
```

Together these fail every CUDA-family image build — both architectures, both base OSes, plus the debug, gb200 and aws variants.

**3. The install-time smoke test uses the binary as a success proxy.**

`install-sccache.sh:40` decides whether to run its verification compile by testing whether the binary still exists:

```bash
source /usr/local/bin/setup-sccache

# verify sccache works with a simple test (only if binary still exists after setup)
if [ -x /usr/local/bin/sccache ]; then
    echo "int main() { return 0; }" | sccache gcc -x c - -o /dev/null
```

That check is only meaningful because of the `rm -f` in (2), and it contradicts the file's own header comment: "Always install sccache binary (small download) so `COPY --from=builder` works in downstream stages regardless of `USE_SCCACHE` setting." With the binary preserved, the smoke test runs even though the cache is unreachable and aborts the builder stage under `set -Eeux`:

```
+ sccache gcc -x c - -o /dev/null
sccache: error: Server startup failed: ... InvalidAccessKeyId
#24 ERROR: process "/bin/sh -c /tmp/install-sccache.sh ..." did not complete successfully: exit code: 2
```

### Fix

Export `USE_SCCACHE=false` in both fallback branches, stop deleting the binary, and gate the smoke test on the flag rather than on the binary's existence.

The script is sourced, so the export covers every consumer in one place, and it matches the pattern `build-nvshmem.sh:32` already uses when it opts out of sccache. Every reference to the `sccache` binary in every consumer script is inside an `if [ "${USE_SCCACHE}" = "true" ]` guard, so the `rm -f` no longer protects against anything — its stated purpose ("so meson/cmake can't accidentally try to use it") is already covered by the unset launchers plus the disabled flag.

Only the degrade paths and the one guard are touched; the successful-sccache path is unchanged.

### Verification

Ran the real `build-gdrcopy.sh` in a container with no working sccache, which is exactly the CI condition:

| | exit code | output |
|---|---|---|
| before | `2` | `make[1]: sccache: No such file or directory` / `Error 127` |
| after | `0` | `cc -shared -Wl,-soname,libgdrapi.so.2 -o libgdrapi.so.2.5 ...` → installed |

And confirmed the resulting state after sourcing the script with a stub sccache that fails to start the way CI's does:

```
+ '[' true = true ']'
+ source /usr/local/bin/setup-sccache
++ /usr/local/bin/sccache --start-server
sccache: error: Server startup failed: InvalidAccessKeyId
Warning: sccache failed to start, continuing without cache
++ export USE_SCCACHE=false
+ '[' false = true ']'
---- results ----
exit code: 0
binary PRESENT
```

### Why this surfaced now

`detect-changes` lists `docker/common-versions` as a trigger for every platform. PRs touching only one platform's Dockerfile skip the CUDA jobs entirely, so the bug stays hidden; any PR that edits the shared `common-versions` file turns all platform builds on and hits it immediately. #1230 is the PR that ran into it.

The three failure modes masked each other: the builder stage died at gdrcopy before reaching `COPY --from=builder`, and the smoke test was skipped only because the binary had been deleted. The CI credentials for the `vllm-nightly-sccache` bucket currently return `InvalidAccessKeyId`, so the degrade path is taken on every run rather than occasionally.
